Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ (1)

We have already discussed the opening letters of the surahs (1) at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah and Surah Al 'Imran, and we said that the openings of some surahs of the Qur'an begin with disjointed letters, which we pronounce when we read them by the names of the letters, not by what the letters denote.

Every letter has a name and a referent (musamma). The name of the letter is known to the elite who know reading and writing, whereas the common people who cannot read or write speak in terms of the referents of the letters and do not know their names.

When an illiterate person is asked to spell out any word and to pronounce its letters separately, he cannot do it, and the reason is that he has not learned reading and writing. The learned person, however, knows the names of the letters and their referents.

We know that the Qur'an was revealed to be heard. For this reason I say: beware of reading the Book of God unless you have first heard it, for if you read it before you hear it, then when you read at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1)﴾ [Al-Baqarah], it will be the same to you as when you read at the beginning of Surah al-Sharh ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim... (1)﴾ [Al-Sharh]. (Note: this is a reading of the disjointed letters as the author presents them.)

But when you hear the Qur'an, you read the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard it from Jibril (peace be upon him): "Alif Lam Mim," and you read the beginning of Surah al-Sharh as "Alif Lam Mim."

I say this because the Qur'an, as we know, is not like any book that you approach to read without hearing it. No. It is a book that you read after you have heard it and corrected your recitation under a reciter, so that you know how to pronounce every noble word. Then after that you may read, once you have learned the manner of recitation, because every letter in the Noble Book is placed with measure and due proportion.

We also know that the verses of the Qur'an include clear verses (muhkamat) and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat) (2). The clear verses comprise the rulings that you must carry out in order to be rewarded for them, and if you do not carry them out you will be punished, and everything in the clear verses is evident.

As for the ambiguous verses, they came ambiguous only because human comprehension differs from one person to another, from one stage of life to another, and from one society to another. Comprehensions have means in which people resemble one another, such as the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the hand.

These means of perception have laws that govern them:

Your eye is governed by the law of sight, which extends until the lines of rays meet at a focal point beyond which your seeing is impossible; for this reason objects gradually shrink as you move away from them until they vanish from the limits of your vision.

Your voice has a law: it is governed by the vibrations of the air that reach the organs of hearing inside your ear.

Likewise smell has limits, for you cannot smell a rose that is in a distant country.

Likewise the human mind has limits by which it perceives. God has known how a human being perceives things, so He did not forbid contemplating a beautiful rose, but He did command the lowering of the gaze (3) when seeing any woman.

Thus the Truth defines for you the lawful that you see, and defines for you the unlawful that you must refrain from looking at. Likewise in the intellect: it may understand one matter and may not understand another matter, and your failure to understand that matter is itself a kind of understanding. If you ask how:

Look at the situation of a pupil in preparatory school to whom his teacher brings an engineering exercise of the kind studied by university students. Here the intelligent pupil will say to his teacher: "We have not taken the necessary foundations for solving such an engineering exercise." This statement means that the pupil has understood his limits.

Thus God teaches us good manners in using the means of perception. There is a matter that it is permitted for you to understand, and there is a matter that you hear from your Lord and obey, and you may not try to understand it before carrying it out, because it is above the level of your perception.

I always give this example, and to God belongs the highest likeness: when you stay in a large hotel, you find that every room has its own key that opens no other room, and on every floor of the hotel there is a key that fits the opening of all the floors. This matter is understood only by the specialist in designing such keys.

So what about the Book of God, the Most High, which is the comprehensive Book in designing such keys?

So what about the Book of God, the Most High, which is the comprehensive Book in which the Truth, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are clear verses, they are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous. As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation (ta'wil). But none knows its interpretation except God. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾ (7) [Al 'Imran]

Thus, the ambiguous matter is considered by the people of deviation an opportunity to achieve their aims, which is to nullify the religion by any means and in any way, and they try to practice arrogance toward the Book of God.

To these people we say: God willed that some surahs of the Noble Book begin with letters pronounced by their names, not by their referents.

The Truth, glory be to Him, also willed this in order to test minds. Just as He, glory be to Him, permitted the human intellect to reflect on many matters, there are some matters in which reflection fails, so the intellect cannot comprehend things that exceed its limits.

The Truth, glory and exaltation be to Him, places trials for a human being in his means of perception; He made limits for every means of perception, and He willed to bring the ambiguous to test the human being and to see: what does the believer do?

The saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:
﴿But none knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly grounded in knowledge... (7)﴾ [Al 'Imran]

It may be understood from it that it is a conjunction, meaning that those firmly grounded in knowledge also know its interpretation, and therefore they will teach people what they arrive at of knowledge of the interpretation. But the interpretation of those firmly grounded in knowledge is their saying:
﴿All of it is from our Lord... (7)﴾ [Al 'Imran]

So the end of their interpretation is: it is from our Lord, and we have believed in it.

And the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to us to resolve the difficulty of the ambiguous:
"Whatever in it is ambiguous, believe in it." (4)

Because the ambiguous is among the trials of faith.

The example I give here is his (ﷺ) command to us to touch (5) the Black Stone and kiss it, and to stone the stone that represents Iblis (Satan), and both are stones, but we comply through faith with what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded us.

If you approach every command with your reason and want to know the wisdom behind every command, you would be worshipping your reason, whereas the Truth, glory be to Him, wants you to approach matters with His judgment, glory be to Him.

If you tell someone: "Alcohol damages the liver," and you place on his liver an ultrasound device that shows an image of the liver, then you hand the man a cup of wine, and he sees what the cup of wine does to the liver, and this frightens him, so he says: "By God, I will never drink it," does he do that because he is a believer? Or has he tied his behavior to experiment?

He has tied his behavior to experiment, and this differs from the believer who carries out the teachings of heaven, so he abstains from wine because God commanded it. We cannot postpone the teachings of heaven until their wisdom appears to us.

Thus the reason for the ambiguous is faith in it, and the ambiguous may have wisdom, but we will not postpone faith until we know the wisdom.

I always say: a person must treat his faith in his Lord as he treats his physician. The patient goes to his doctor to present his complaint of an illness that pains him, so that the doctor prescribes the medicine for him. Likewise the work of your intellect: it must stop at the threshold of your faith in God.

Among the sayings of the people of knowledge of God is one that says: reason is like a riding beast; it brings you to the gate of the sovereign, but it does not enter with you.

Thus, whoever debates the causes of things is one who wishes to converse with an equal in wisdom, and is there an equal to God?

Certainly not. Therefore take the openings of the surahs that came with disjointed letters as they came, and our disagreement about their meanings confirms that they are a treasure of giving that never runs out, until they are explained, if God wills, by God (6).

It is remarkable that all the verses of the Qur'an are built on continuity (wasl). At the end of Surah Hud we find the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:
﴿Your Lord is not unaware of what you do. (123)﴾ [Hud]

It was expected that we would pause on it and pronounce the word "ta'malun" (you do) with a sukun on the nun, but it is connected to "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"; therefore the nun came with a fatha.

Also, since the verses are built on continuity, it was expected that we would pronounce the beginning of Surah Yusuf as "Alif Lam Ra" but the Messenger of God (ﷺ) taught us to read it "Alif Lam Ra" and to pronounce it with a sukun.

This is evidence that it is a word built on pausing, and evidence that God, glory be to Him, has wisdom in this and in that.

We know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to review the Qur'an once every Ramadan with Jibril (peace be upon him), and he reviewed it twice in the Ramadan before his death (ﷺ) (7).

Thus the Qur'an reached us as the Truth, glory be to Him, sent it down upon His Noble Messenger (ﷺ).

Here the Truth says: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book. (1)﴾ [Yusuf]

"Those" (tilka) is an indication of what follows "Alif Lam Ra," and it is the verses of the Book.

That is: take from them that the verses of the Qur'an are composed of such letters. This is what some understood by the meaning of "Alif Lam Ra" (Yusuf 1).

But this is not the whole understanding.

Like the tailor who places in the front of his shop some of the threads from which the cloth was woven, to show the precision of his craft.

It is as if God, glory be to Him, is showing us that "Alif Lam Ra" are names of letters, of the names of the letters that we speak, and the words of the Qur'an are composed of such letters, but the verses of the Qur'an are miraculous, and humans cannot, even with the help of the jinn, produce its like (8).

Thus the excellence is not in the material that makes up speech, but the miracle is that the speaker is the Truth, glory be to Him, so His speech must be miraculous, even if it is composed of the same letters that we humans use.

There is another meaning: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) pronounced the names of the letters "Alif Lam Ra," and he (ﷺ) was illiterate (9), as testified by his contemporaries, including his opponents, even though whoever is able to pronounce the names of the letters must be learned, since the illiterate pronounces the referents of the letters and does not know their names (10). In this pronunciation there is a testimony that the one who taught him that is his exalted Lord.

The Truth says: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Clear Book. (1)﴾ [Yusuf]

The word "Book" (al-kitab), when it is used, its meaning refers to the Noble Qur'an (11).

And we find the word "clear" (al-mubin), that is, the one that makes clear everything the movement of the human being, the vicegerent on earth, needs. If something becomes clear to you and you think the Qur'an did not address it, then you must search for a material or a verse that draws your attention to what makes clear to you what was hidden from you.

It is narrated of Imam Muhammad 'Abduh (12) that he met one of the orientalists (13) in Paris, and the orientalist directed a question to the Imam, saying:
"Since there is a verse in the Qur'an that says: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book (14) of anything... (38)﴾ [Al-An'am],
then let me ask you: how many loaves does an ardab of wheat produce?"

The Imam said to the orientalist: "Wait," and he summoned a baker and asked him: "How many loaves can we make from an ardab of wheat?" The baker answered the question.

Here the orientalist said: "I asked you for an answer from the Qur'an, not from the baker."

The Imam replied: "If the Qur'an has said: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book of anything... (38)﴾ [Al-An'am],
then the Qur'an has also said:
﴿Ask the people of remembrance if you do not know. (43)﴾ [Al-Nahl]"

Imam (15) Muhammad 'Abduh perceived that the human mind is too narrow to contain all the knowledge that life requires; therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, willed to distribute talents among human beings, so that each person who excels in a field becomes one of the people of remembrance in his field.

We, for example, when we encounter a matter of inheritance, turn to one who specializes in inheritance, so that he may guide us to the precision of distributing the shares of this inheritance.

When a Muslim of the common folk performs the pilgrimage (Hajj), it is enough for him to know that Hajj is an obligation, and he seeks at the start of the Hajj someone who teaches him...

It was also said: i.e., in the Qur'an, meaning: We have left nothing of the matter of religion without having indicated it in the Qur'an, either by a clear and explained indication, or by a general indication whose explanation is received from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or from *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), or from *qiyas* (analogical reasoning) established by the text of the Book."

31 - Imam Muhammad ʿAbduh is one of the eminent imams. He is a *mujaddid* (renewer) of his age, has intellectual works, and has a reformist school. He was a contemporary of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani. Imam Muhammad ʿAbduh had his own directions in the education of individuals and peoples, such that education begins with the individual first and then with the community. This gradual educational approach was distinctive to the Imam and set him apart from Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, although there was a general and specific relationship between them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 2:

﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an.. (2)﴾ [Yusuf]

In the preceding verse He said: ﴿These are the verses of the Book.. (1)﴾ [Yusuf]

So at one time He describes it as a Qur'an, meaning "that which is recited," and at another time as a Book, because it is inscribed. This is one of the miracles of naming.

We know that the Qur'an, when it was collected (1) to be written down, the scribe of the Qur'an wrote only what he found written, and it was attested by two of the memorizers.

We also know that hearts may differ according to desires, whereas written lines are fixed and free of ambiguity.

And it is an Arabic Qur'an because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was to proclaim the call openly among an Arab nation, and it was necessary that there be a miracle that demonstrates the truthfulness of eloquence from Allah, and that it be of the kind in which the Arabs excelled (2), because a miracle is conditioned by challenge, and it is not possible for Him to challenge them in a matter in which they have no preeminence and to which they have no connection, lest anyone say: "We were not taught this; and had we been taught it, we would have brought something better than it."

The Arabs were a people of eloquent expression, literature and excellence in rhetoric and poetry. They would gather in the markets (3), each tribe boasting of its poets and its eloquent orators (4). Competitions in recitation were held, challenges were carried out in this field, and judges were appointed for them.

That is to say, skill in the language was a widely practised and widely circulated craft, judged upon by people in the markets. They were a nation of expression (5), rhetoric and eloquence.

Therefore, the True One, glorified is He, willed that the Qur'an be a miracle of the same kind as that in which the Arabs excelled, and they were the first people to whom the Qur'an was sent. When these people believe, the challenge will not be by the eloquence of words and the arrangement of speech alone, but by the principles that surpass the principles of the Persians and the Romans.

These are principles that were sent down to a nomadic nation (6), having no law that unites them, and no homeland that gathers them under one allegiance; rather, every tribe had its own law, and they were all Bedouins moving from place to place.

When the Qur'an was sent down among them, the people of Persia and Rome knew that this nomadic nation had acquired what would build a civilization without precedent before, even though the Prophet was unlettered and the nation in which the Qur'an was revealed was an unlettered nation.

The Persians and the Romans knew that the Messenger who was sent to that nation had challenged them in what they excelled in, and not one of them was able to stand against the challenge; from here they felt that they were facing a civilizational challenge of another kind that they had not known.

The True One, glorified is He, willed that the Qur'an be sent down in Arabic, because the Truth would not send a messenger except in the tongue of his people. He says:

﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language (7) of his people, to make clear to them.. (4)﴾ [Ibrahim]

Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent with the Qur'an, which was distinguished from the books of the messengers who preceded him in that it is at once a book and a miracle, whereas the miracles of the messengers before him, peace and blessings be upon him, were separate from the books of rulings that were sent down to them.

The Qur'an remains a miracle carrying a method until the Hour is established. Since the first believers in it spread throughout the world, there was fulfilled what Allah promised: that this Book be comprehensive, attracting everyone who has not believed in it to be astonished by what it contains of rulings.

Therefore, when they seek the causes of the spread of Islam in that brief period, they find that Islam spread not by the strength of those who believed in it, but by the strength of those who were drawn to it, bewildered (8) by the systems in it that free them from their hardships.

In the Qur'an there are laws that truly make a person happy, and in it are prophecies of what will happen in the universe, which make those who believe in it recall with humility that the Book which Allah sent down to their Messenger has neglected nothing.

If a certain orientalist says: "How can you say that the Qur'an was sent down in a clear Arabic tongue, despite the presence of foreign words such as the word 'Amin,' which you say after the imam's supplication; and there are also Roman words and Persian words (9)?"

These orientalists did not notice that the Arab received words of various kinds from many nations as a result of his mixing with those nations, and then these words circulated on his tongue and became Arabic words. In our modern age we too Arabize words, and we introduce into our language any word we use and that circulates on our tongues, as long as we understand what is meant by it.

Allah, the Most High, concludes the noble verse with His saying:

﴿So that you may understand (2)﴾ [Yusuf]

This is to rouse the energy of reason, so that one reflects on the matter. The one who is just to the truth wants people to receive what he presents to them through reason, unlike the deceiver (10), who wants to conceal reason to one side so that he may slip through behind reason.

In our daily life, when a merchant draws your attention to a commodity and displays its solidity and merits, he does so as evidence that he is confident of the quality of his goods.

But if the workmanship is not good, he will not call you to think with your reason, because when you ponder the matter with your mind you discover the deceiver and the non-deceiver; therefore he deceives you, blinds you, and leaves you no opportunity to think.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿We relate to you the best of narratives (11) by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, and though you were before it among the unaware.. (3)﴾

1 – Al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak: the Qur'an was collected three times:
The first: in the presence of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.
The second: in the presence of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.
The third: in the time of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him.
What is meant here is the second collection of the Qur'an, which was carried out by Zayd ibn Thabit by the command of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "You are a young, intelligent man; we do not accuse you, and you used to write down the revelation for the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, so trace the Qur'an and gather it." Zayd said: "I traced the Qur'an and gathered it from the palm-stalks, the flat white stones, and the chests of men. Zayd would not accept anything from anyone until two witnesses testified to it." As-Suyuti said: "This indicates that Zayd did not suffice with merely finding it written until one who had received it orally testified to it, even though Zayd himself had memorized it; he did this as an exaggeration in caution." [See: al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an 1/164–167], abridged.
2 – Naba' al-shay': appeared. Naba' minhum sha'ir: emerged; and al-nabigha: the well-known poet, so named for his prominence [Lisan al-Arab, root: nb'].
3 – The Arabs had markets where they gathered, such as 'Ukaz and Dhu al-Majaz; the tribes of the Arabs would gather there every year and boast to one another, and poets would attend and recite to one another what they had composed of poetry.
4 – Mufawwah: one whose speech is fine and whose discourse is eloquent, able to speak well with simplicity and fluency. See some of this in [Lisan al-Arab, root: fwh].
5 – Bayan: the manifestation of the intended meaning in the most eloquent wording; it derives from understanding and keenness of heart together with fluency of tongue, and its origin is disclosure and manifestation. [Lisan, root: byn]. Bayan: disclosure, clarification and eloquent speech. Allah said: ﴿This is a clarification for mankind.. (138)﴾ [Al 'Imran], i.e., a disclosure and clarification or an eloquent discourse. And His saying: ﴿He taught him the bayan (4)﴾ [al-Rahman], i.e., the utterance that expresses what is in the soul of meanings and thoughts. [al-Qamus al-Qawim, root: byn].
6 – Mutabaddiyah: attributed to the badiyah (desert); it is said: tabadda al-rajul: he resided in the desert. The badiyah is the opposite of the hadar (settled life), and it was named badiyah for its appearance and exposure away from the places where people gather in settled life around water and other things, adapted from [Lisan al-Arab, root: bdw].
7 – Lisan: one of the senses of taste and speech. Allah said: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes (8) and a tongue and two lips (9)?﴾ [al-Balad], so Allah bestows upon man the blessing of sight and speech. Lisan also means language and speech. Allah said: ﴿And my brother Aaron is more eloquent in tongue than I..(34)﴾ [al-Qasas], i.e., more capable than I of eloquent speech. And Allah said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your tongues and colors..(22)﴾ [al-Rum], where "your tongues" means your languages and dialects. [al-Qamus al-Qawim, root lsn].
8 – Siyaha: going about the earth for various purposes, including worship, preaching and trade, and its origin is from sayh (flowing) of water over the surface of the earth. [Lisan al-Arab, root: sayh], adapted.
9 – Shadda al-rajul shaddan: he was bewildered; al-dahash also means bewilderment: dahash: he was bewildered, or his mind departed, from dhahala or walah, so he is madhush, and another made him dhahish. [Lisan, roots: shdh, dhh].
10 – Al-tamin: saying "Amin." Amin: a word said after supplication. Al-Farisi said: it is a compound sentence of a verb and a noun, meaning: "O Allah, respond to me." [Lisan al-Arab, root: amn]. On the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When the imam says Amin, then say Amin, for whoever's Amin coincides with the Amin of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven." Related by Imam Malik in his Muwatta' [1/87], Ahmad in his Musnad [2/238, 321], al-Bukhari in his Sahih [780], and likewise Muslim [410].
11 – Examples of Roman words found in the Noble Qur'an:
- [al-Raqim] in His saying: ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the Raqim were among Our signs a wonder? (9)﴾ [al-Kahf]. Al-Suyuti in al-Itqan [2/112] said that three opinions have been given concerning it: the tablet, the book, the inkwell.
- [al-Sirat]: al-Naqqash and Ibn al-Jawzi related that it is the road in the Roman language.
- [Tafiqa] in His saying: ﴿And they began to join over themselves some of the leaves of the Garden.. (22)﴾ [al-A'raf], its meaning being: they set out, in Roman.
12 – Examples of Persian words in the Noble Qur'an:
- [Abariq]: al-Tha'alibi in Fiqh al-Lugha related that it is Persian; al-Jawaliqi said: al-ibriq is Persian arabized, and its meaning is: the path of water, or pouring water in a certain manner.
- [Dinar]: in His saying: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you constantly stand over him.. (75)﴾ [Al 'Imran]; al-Jawaliqi and others mentioned that it is Persian.
- [Sijjil]: from Mujahid, who said: sijjil is Persian; its first part is stones and its last part is clay.
13 – Al-Suyuti in his book al-Itqan [2/105–108] mentioned the scholars' disagreement concerning the Arabness of these words and their foreignness, and mentioned the proofs of each of the two groups. Then he said: Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: "The correct view in my opinion is one that affirms both sayings together. These letters have foreign origins, as the jurists say, but they came to the Arabs, and the Arabs Arabized them with their tongues and converted them from foreign words into their own words, so they became Arabic. Then the Qur'an was revealed when these letters had become mixed with the speech of the Arabs. Whoever says they are Arabic is truthful, and whoever says they are foreign is truthful." Al-Jawaliqi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others inclined to this view.
14 – Tadlis: concealing a defect; al-mudalasah: deception; tadlis in sale: concealing a defect of the commodity from the buyer; indalasa al-shay': when it became hidden. [Lisan al-Arab, root: dls].
15 – Qass al-kalam or al-akhbar: he narrates them, qassan and qasasan: he traced them, transmitted them and related them. Allah said: ﴿So when he came to him and related to him the stories, he said, "Fear not..(25)﴾ [al-Qasas], i.e., he related to him his news and told him of it. Al-qasas: a verbal noun applied to what is transmitted of reports. Allah said: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding..(111)﴾ [Yusuf]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim (2/120)].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

When the Truth, glory be to Him, speaks of one of His acts and uses the plural pronoun, the reason is that every single act of His requires the existence of multiple attributes. It requires knowledge, wisdom, power and capabilities.

And who other than Him, glory be to Him, possesses all the attributes by which one does what one wills, at the time one wills?

No one besides Him is able to do that, because He, glory be to Him, alone is the possessor of the attributes that accomplish everything required and decreed in life.

But when He, glory be to Him, speaks of His Essence, He affirms the oneness of God (tawhid), so the form used is not the plural. He, may He be exalted, says:
﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ [Ta-Ha]¹ ²

Here He, glory be to Him, speaks in a manner that expresses acts which no one else can perform, with the precision He willed, when He says:
﴿We relate to you the best of stories...﴾ [Yusuf]³

He specified that it is He who relates. When an act is attributed to Allah, we take the act in its own particular meaning and do not try to derive from it a name to apply to Allah, unless the act has a attribute of His that we know from His Most Beautiful Names (al-Asma' al-Husna), because He is the Most Holy Essence.

In everything related to Him, in His Essence, attributes and acts, we observe adab (proper courtesy), because we know nothing of the Essence of Allah except what Allah has told us about Himself. Therefore it is not correct to say of Allah that He is "qassas" (a narrator of stories). Rather, we take the act as He informed us of it, and we do not derive from it a name for Allah, because He did not describe Himself by that in His Beautiful Names.

What is required is that what He, glory be to Him, named as a name, we take as a name, and what He named as a verb, we take as a verb.

Here He, glory be to Him, says:
﴿We relate to you the best of stories...﴾ [Yusuf]³

We know that the word "qassa" (قص) means to follow. Some scholars said: the story (qissa) is so called because each word follows another word, and it is derived from qassa al-athar, which is tracing the traces of a traveler on the ground, so that a person may know the destination of the one he follows and not deviate far from the direction in which the one he seeks went.

Consider the words of the Truth, glory be to Him:
﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she observed him from afar while they did not perceive.﴾ [Qasas]⁴
And "qusiyyihi" (﴿قصيه﴾) [Qasas 11]⁵
meaning: follow his trace.

So, qass is not the word that follows a word; rather, qass is following what has actually happened.

The Truth, glory be to Him, gives us an example from the story of Musa, peace be upon him, with a young man:
﴿He said, "Did you see when we retreated to the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish, and none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea, astonishingly."* He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they went back, retracing their footsteps.﴾ [Kahf]⁶
That is: they followed the steps.

Thus we know that qass is the following of what has actually occurred, so every word is a depiction of a reality, not ambiguous (lubs) or imaginary, and it adds nothing. This is unlike modern fictional storytelling, in which the storyteller adds imaginary scenes for the sake of the artistic plot (hubka), excitement and attracting attention.

As for the stories of the Qur'an, their situation is entirely different, for all the Qur'an's stories follow what actually happened, so that we may take a lesson from them, because a story is a kind of history.

The story in the Qur'an sometimes comes for the sake of the event, and sometimes to strengthen the heart (fu'ad) of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The story of one messenger did not come in the Qur'an in full, except the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

As for the rest of the messengers, their stories came as scattered scenes on occasions to strengthen the heart of the Messenger Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. So a scene from the life of one messenger comes, then a scene from the life of another messenger, and so on.

No one should say that the Qur'an was unable to bring a complete and comprehensive story. Rather, the Truth, glory be to Him, willed to bring the story of Yusuf from its beginning to its end, in full. In it there is an event around which persons revolve, and in it there is a person around whom events revolve.

The story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the Qur'an is distinguished not only by its plot, but it combines both types of story: the event around which characters revolve, and the person around whom events revolve.

The story of Yusuf came with Yusuf and the events that passed over him, beginning with the dream, passing through the envy and plotting of the brothers, then the attempted seduction by the wife of the Aziz, then prison, then the ability to interpret dreams, then assuming authority, then the meeting with the brothers and kindness to them, and finally the reunion with the father again.

Thus the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:
﴿We relate to you the best of stories...﴾ [Yusuf]³
shows us that the excellence came to it from the fact that earlier scriptures spoke of the story of Yusuf, but when the rabbis of the Jews read the story as it came in the Qur'an, some of them abandoned their book and relied on the Qur'an in narrating it. The events of the story are the same, except in the wording of the expression, the touches of inner feelings, the highlighting of positions hidden within the human soul, and the fulfillment of unseen visions. All of that came in a plot with an eloquent expression that is miraculous, making it the best of stories.

Or: it is the best of stories in what it contains of many lessons: lessons of childhood in confrontation with old age, the envious hatred among brothers, rebellion, throwing him into the well and plotting against him, imprisoning him unjustly, and the position of Yusuf, peace be upon him, toward false accusation, and his pride in the truth until victory and establishment (tamkin) were achieved for him.

And how Allah cast love for Yusuf, peace be upon him, into hearts, so that everyone who met him loved to serve him.

And how Yusuf preserved the inheritance of prophethood, with its gentleness and its capacity to pardon when able. He pardoned his brothers, as the surah relates:
﴿He said, "No reproach upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ [Yusuf]⁷

The master of mankind, Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said the same to his people on the day of the conquest of Makkah: "Go, for you are free (al-Tulaqa')."⁸

Thus Surah Yusuf is filled with extreme lessons, some of which appear in the matter of his being imprisoned unjustly, and then pardon and judgment come to him. Therefore it is the best of stories, either because it combined an incident and the persons around it, or because it brought the person and the events that revolved around him.

Or: it is the best of stories in that it conveyed what was agreed upon and common among all the earlier books, and it came on the tongue of Muhammad the Unlettered (al-ummi), who had no acquaintance with those books. Yet the presentation of the subject came in an attractive, compelling, convincing and delightful style.

Or: it is the best of stories because Surah Yusuf is the surah that included multiple scenes that correspond to: the chronological age, the intellectual age, and the emotional age of a human being in all his stages, weak and overpowered, and strong and dominant, empowered over everything.

Whereas we find that the news of the earlier messengers came as scattered scenes distributed as verses within other surahs, and each verse came in its appropriate place.

Thus, the outstanding excellence came from the miraculous style of the Qur'an, which no one among mankind can produce its like.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:
﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, though before it you were certainly among the unaware.﴾ [Yusuf]⁹

The meaning of "ghafil" (unaware) here is that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was unlettered, and no one knew before the revelation of the Qur'an that he was an orator or a poet. All that was known of him was his high moral qualities of truthfulness and trustworthiness, and these are qualities required in one who conveys from Allah. Since he had never lied to any human before, how would he lie while conveying the message of heaven to the people of the earth?

Lying is utterly improbable for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, before the prophetic mission (ba'tha) and after it.

An example of others affirming the Messenger of Allah is the affirmation of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed him that revelation had descended upon him. He told him nothing more than that he was a messenger from Allah, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You have spoken the truth."

When the Night Journey (al-Isra') occurred, some denied it, asking: "How can we travel to it on the backs of camels for a month, and Muhammad says he covered it in one night?" Abu Bakr asked them: "Did he say that?" They said: "Yes." Abu Bakr said: "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth."¹⁰

Thus we find that the basis of his truthfulness before the mission is what indicated his truthfulness when he conveyed what was revealed to him.

An example of this: the affirmation of Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her and content her, of him, when he informed her of the descent of revelation. She said to him: "By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. Indeed, you join the ties of kinship, bear the burdens of the weak, earn for the destitute, honor the guest, and assist in the calamities of truth."¹¹

In the sincerity of her insight and the depth of her sensitive nature were reasons that supported her affirmation of him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in his prophethood.¹²

When some matters occurred that did not agree with the logic of premises and conclusions, causes and effects, some minds among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah would stand questioning: "How?" Abu Bakr would clarify for them: "Pay attention, he is the Messenger of Allah."

An example of this is what happened at the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, when Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, questioned, almost rejecting the conditions of that treaty: "Are we not upon the truth? Why should we accept humiliation in our religion?"

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, replied to him: "Hold fast to his stirrup, O Umar, for he is the Messenger of Allah."¹³

That is: be attentive and know that you are speaking with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is not blind submission; rather it is obedience out of believing insight.

And the Truth, glory be to Him, says here:
﴿...though before it you were certainly among the unaware.﴾ [Yusuf]⁹

The unaware (al-ghafil) is one who does not know, not out of ignorance or deficiency of intellect, but because what he is unaware of is a matter that does not occupy his mind.

Or: the intended meaning of His words:
﴿...among the unaware.﴾ [Yusuf]⁹
is: that you, O Muhammad, would not have been among those who know the story of Yusuf, because you did not learn to read so as to read it from a book, nor did you sit with a teacher who narrated that story to you, nor did you gather some parts of the story from here or there.

Rather, you did not receive the revelation of it until some of the People of the Book said to some people of Makkah: "Ask him about the sons of Ya'qub and the brothers of Yusuf; why did they leave Syria and go to Egypt?"

It was a form of miracle that this clear exposition, in all its details of the story, should descend upon you, O Messenger of Allah, as a practical proof that the teacher of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is Allah, and that it was He, glory be to Him, who revealed it to him.

Revelation, as we know, is informing in secret. He, glory be to Him, reveals to the angels, saying:
﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe..."﴾ [Anfal]¹⁴
And He, glory be to Him, reveals to whom He chooses from among mankind, to their elite, in confirmation of His words:
﴿And when I revealed to the disciples, "Believe in Me and in My Messenger." They said, "We have believed, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ [Ma'idah]¹⁵
And the Truth, glory be to Him, casts inspiration into the heart as a revelation that a human cannot repel, like the revelation to the mother of Musa that she should cast her infant son Musa into the river:
﴿And when We revealed to your mother what is revealed: "Cast him into the chest and cast it into the river, and let the river deliver him to the bank, and there will take him an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his. And I bestowed upon you love from Me, so that you might be raised under My eye."﴾ [Ta-Ha]¹⁶
And He, glory be to Him, reveals to the earth, which is inanimate, as in the saying of the Truth:
﴿Because your Lord has inspired it.﴾ [Zalzalah]¹⁷
And He, glory be to Him, revealed to the bee, and the Truth said:
﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee: "Take for yourself dwellings in the mountains and in the trees and in what they build. Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, submissively..."﴾ [Nahl]¹⁸

The Truth, glory be to Him, reveals to whom He wills what He wills. Everything, inanimate, plant, animal and human, is of His creation, and He, glory be to Him, addresses them with the secret of their creation, and the difference in the means by which they comprehend that.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says after that:
﴿When Yusuf said to his father, "O my father, indeed I have seen eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾ [Yusuf]¹⁹

5. Al-hut: the fish, whether large or small; its plural is hitan. He, exalted is He, said about Musa's words: ﴿Indeed, I forgot the fish...﴾ [al-Kahf 64]: meaning the fish. And He said: ﴿When their fish came to them on their Sabbath, openly...﴾ [al-A'raf 163]: the fish would appear to them in the water on the Sabbath, and they would hunt them, defying the command of their Lord. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/176]. Ibn Manzur said in Lisan al-Arab, article "hawt": "al-muhawwata: evasion; huwa yuhawituni means he evades me; and hata al-tair 'ala al-shay' yahuwt means the bird circled around the thing."

6. Al-'ajab: a wonder and astonishment that seizes a person upon admiring something whose secret is hidden, or magnifying it; and the matter astonished him: it delighted him or made him marvel at it. A matter is "ajib" and "ajjab" with doubled jim for emphasis. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, this is a thing astonishing.﴾ [Sad 5]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/7].

7. Baghā al-shay': sought it, and ibtaghāhu: sought it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They seek to cause you fitnah...﴾ [al-Tawbah 47]: meaning they seek it for you. And He said: ﴿seeking bounty from Allah...﴾ [al-Fath 29]. And His saying: ﴿Certainly they sought fitnah...﴾ [al-Tawbah 48]: meaning they sought it and strove to spread and disseminate it. Al-ibtigha' is seeking: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not be weak in pursuit of the people...﴾ [al-Nisa' 104]: in their pursuit to fight them. And He said: ﴿And those who patiently seek the face of their Lord...﴾ [al-Ra'd 22]: meaning seeking His pleasure. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/76-77].

8. Al-labs and al-lubs: confusion of a matter. "Labasa 'alayhi al-amr yalbisuhu labsan" means he mixed it up for him until he did not know its direction; "iltabasa 'alayhi al-amr" means the matter became confused and ambiguous; "talabbasa bi al-amr" means the matter became mixed and entangled. [Lisan al-Arab, article "labs"].

9. Al-habk: tightening. Al-hubka: a rope tied around the waist; al-tahbik: documentation. "Jad ma habakahu" means he did well in its weaving; "habaka al-thawb yahbukuhu habkan" means he wove the garment well and beautified the craftsmanship in it. [Lisan al-Arab, article "habk"]. The term is borrowed for the plot of a story, as if it were a cloth well woven and crafted, so it is not flimsy.

10. This is in His saying: ﴿Certainly there was in their stories a lesson for those of understanding.﴾ [Yusuf 111]. "Ibra" is the name of that by which a person is admonished; "ibra" means admonition. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson...﴾ [al-Nur 44], and He said: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ [al-Hashr 2]: meaning take admonition. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/4].

11. The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And all We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We strengthen your heart. And there has come to you in this the truth and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.﴾ [Hud 120]: meaning We strengthen your heart by it in conveying the message and patience over the harm you receive in it. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3435].

12. Al-ghiwaya: error and immersion in deviance and corruption. "Ghawa yaghwi": he immersed himself in ignorance, and it is the opposite of rectitude. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from error.﴾ [al-Baqarah 256]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/64].

13. *Al-Ahbar*: the plural of *habr*, meaning a scholar. God says: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God﴾ [At-Tawbah]. The root meaning of the word *habr* is the ink with which one writes, and anything of fine quality in handwriting, speech, poetry or otherwise is described as *habr*. One says: he *habara* (wrote finely) a *habr* (fine writing) and *habr*. [Lisan al-Arab, root: h-b-r].

14. *Tharraba*: he blamed him and reproached him. *Tharraba* with the doubled letter means he blamed him excessively, reproached him for his sin, and admonished him for his bad conduct. God says: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today. God will forgive you﴾ [Yusuf, 92]. That is: there is no blame and no reproach. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/106].

15. Ibn Ishaq said: "Some of the people of knowledge related to me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood at the door of the Ka'bah in his address and said: 'There is no god but God alone, without partner. He fulfilled His promise, supported His servant, and defeated the confederates alone.' Then he said: 'What do you think I will do with you?' They said: 'Good. A noble brother and the son of a noble brother.' He said: 'Go, for you are the freed ones.'" [See: Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham 4/412].

16. Ibn Hisham mentioned in *Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah* (1/398), in summary, that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) woke up after his return from Jerusalem, he went to the Quraysh and informed them of the news. They denied it, and they went to Abu Bakr and presented this matter to him with denial. Abu Bakr said to them: "You are lying about him." They said: "Yes, there he is in the mosque, telling people about it."
Abu Bakr said: "By God, if he said it, then he has spoken the truth, so what amazes you about that? By God, he tells me that news comes to him from God, from the heaven to the earth, in an hour of the night or the day, and I believe him. This is further than what you find amazing."

17. *Al-Kall*: one who cannot manage his own affairs. God says: ﴿and he is a burden upon his master﴾ [An-Nahl, 76]. *Al-Kall* is the weak, heavy burden with no good in him. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/169], abridged.

18. *Al-Ma'dum*: like the dead person who has no way of acting. The meaning is that you give people what they do not find with anyone else. [Fath al-Bari 1/24].

19. *Qira al-Dayf*: he hosted the guest, and *al-qira* is the food of guests. [Lisan al-Arab, root: q-r-y].

20. *Al-Nawa'ib*: the plural of *na'ibah*, which is what befalls a person, that is, what descends upon him of troubles, calamities and events. *Al-Na'ibah* is a misfortune among the misfortunes of time that descends upon a person. [Lisan al-Arab, root: n-w-b], with adaptation.

21. The hadith of the beginning of revelation was recorded by al-Bukhari in his *Sahih* [3], and likewise Muslim in his *Sahih* [160], from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her.

22. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You believed in me when people disbelieved, you affirmed me when people denied me, you comforted me with her wealth when people deprived me, and God granted me children from her and not from other women." Ahmad included it in his *Musnad* [6/118], from the hadith of 'A'ishah.

23. *Al-Dinyah*: a blameworthy trait. A man is *dani* (base) from a people who are *adna'* (lowly), and he is the weak and despicable one. [Lisan al-Arab, root: d-n-w], abridged.

24. *Al-Gharz*: the stirrup of the saddle. Everything that holds the two feet in a mount is a *gharz*. The *gharz* of a she-camel is like the girth of a horse and like the stirrup of a mule. From it comes the hadith of Abu Bakr, that he said to 'Umar: "Hold fast to his stirrup", meaning: cling to him, hold on to him, follow his words and actions, and do not oppose him. He borrowed the word *gharz* for this, like one who holds the stirrup of a rider and moves with his movement. [Lisan al-Arab, root: gh-r-z].

25. Ahmad included it in his *Musnad* [4/323-325], from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah al-Zuhri and Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and its complete form is: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab came to Abu Bakr and said: 'O Abu Bakr, is he not the Messenger of God?' Or are we not Muslims? Or are they not polytheists?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then why should we accept humiliation in our religion?' Abu Bakr said: 'O 'Umar, hold to his stirrup wherever he is.'" The hadith...

26. Al-Qurtubi mentioned it in his *Tafsir* from the words of al-Nahhas [4/3440]: "It is narrated that the Jews said: 'Ask him why the family of Ya'qub moved from Syria to Egypt, and about the story of Yusuf.' So God, may He be exalted, sent this down in Mecca, agreeing with what is in the Torah, and in it there is an addition that is not in their books."

27. *Al-Darb*: the category of things. It is said: "This is of the *darb* of that", meaning of its kind and category. The plural is *durub*. *Darab Allah mathalan* means God described and explained. Their saying *darab lahu al-mathal bi-kadha* means only: he explained to him a kind of parables, that is, a category of them. [Lisan al-Arab, root: d-r-b].

28. *Al-Hawariyyun*: the plural of *hawari*, which is the pure and clean one from everything. Its use became common for the sincere companions and chosen ones of the prophets. God says: ﴿The disciples said: "We are the helpers of God"﴾ [Al 'Imran, 52]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/177].

29. *Al-Yamm*: the sea or the sweet river. God says: ﴿So We drowned them in the sea﴾ [Al-A'raf, 136], and it is the Gulf of Suez, whose water is salty, and it is an extension of the Red Sea. His saying: ﴿Cast him into the river, and let the river cast him ashore﴾ [Ta-Ha, 39] refers to the sweet River Nile. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/372].

30. *Al-Tabut*: the chest or box. God says: ﴿Indeed, the sign of his kingdom is that there will come to you the ark, within which is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left, carried by the angels﴾ [Al-Baqarah, 248]. *Al-Tabut* is also the ribs and what they contain, such as the heart and liver and others, by comparison with the box in which goods are kept. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/96], [Lisan al-Arab, root: th-b-t].

31. *Sahalahu*: he peeled it and carved it. The winds *tasahhil* the earth: they scrape off the dirt on it. *Al-Sahil* is the bank of a river, because the waves eat from it, carve it and erode it. God says: ﴿So let the river cast him ashore, and an enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him. And I placed upon you love from Me, so that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha, 39], meaning: on the riverbank. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/306].

32. *'Arsh al-bayt*: its roof. God says: [﴿How many a city have We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, and it is fallen on its roofs﴾ [Al-Hajj, 45]. [Lisan al-Arab, root: '-r-sh].

33. *Dhall*: he became gentle and submitted without compulsion after being difficult. So he is *dhalul* (docile), and its plural is *dhull*. These are *matayا dhull* (docile mounts) or *turuq dhull* (smooth, easy roads). God says: ﴿It is He who made the earth docile for you, so walk through its slopes and eat of His provision, and to Him is the resurrection﴾ [Al-Mulk, 15]. And His saying: ﴿So follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾ [An-Nahl, 69], that is, made smooth for the bee so that it gathers honey from them. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/245], abridged.

34. Al-Qurtubi said in his *Tafsir* [4/2441]: "Abu al-Hasan al-Aqta' was asked about Yusuf, and he was wise, and he said: 'Al-asaf in the language is sorrow, and al-asif is the slave, and both have come together in Yusuf, so for that reason Yusuf was named.'"

35. *Al-Kawkab*: in the expression of the Qur'an, it includes the cold planet that takes its light from another, and it includes the blazing star, as if it were a great ball of fire. God says: ﴿as if it were a brilliant star﴾ [An-Nur, 35], that is, a star of bright light. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/177], abridged.

Thus begins the story of Yusuf, when he says to his father Ya'qub, peace be upon them both, "O my father" (yā abat). The original word is "yā abī," and in the Arabic language we find the words "abā," "abat," "abatā'" and "abah," all of which convey the meaning of fatherhood, though each has its own linguistic nuance.

Yusuf continues in his speech:

﴿O my father, I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]

We have all seen the sun and the moon, each at the time of its appearance; but Yusuf's dream shows that he saw them together. We have all seen the stars scattered across the sky in countless thousands, so how did Yusuf see just eleven stars?

These must have possessed special attributes that distinguished them from other stars, and he was seeing them after others had passed.

Yusuf's vision shows that he saw them as the sun, the moon and eleven stars; then he saw them afterwards prostrating.

This means that he saw them first with their qualities by which we see the sun, the moon and the stars without prostration; then he saw them prostrating to him, with the marks of submission to a command from God. For this reason the word "I saw" is repeated, and it is not mere repetition but serves to clarify the matter.

We find that the word ﴿prostrating﴾ [Yusuf: 4] is the sound masculine plural (jam' mudhakkar sālim). The sound masculine plural is used only when the singular is rational, and reason is characterised by the capacity to choose between alternatives. The rational believer is one who makes his choices in this world within the framework of the religion, and the highest form of submission to religion is prostration to God.

Those who prostrated to Yusuf did so only by command of God; they therefore understood the command of the Truth, glory be to Him.(1)

Their case is similar to what is stated in the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:

﴿When the sky is split open, and it hearkens to its Lord and is obliged to do so﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1-2]

This sky understands the command of its Lord who built it.

He also said of it that it has no fissures:

﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾ [Qaf: 6]

And it also hears the command of its Lord, in confirmation of His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿and it hearkens to its Lord and is obliged to do so﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 2]

That is, it has possessed the faculty of hearing; for "adhinat" derives from "udhun" (ear). It is as though, merely upon hearing the command of God, it is moved and split open.(4)

Thus we find that every world of the cosmos is a community like the community of mankind.(5) Man communicates with other humans who share his language, and may communicate with people like himself who do not know their language by signs, through an interpreter, or by learning the language itself.

But man does not understand the language of inanimate things, or of plants, or of animals, unless God bestows upon a servant the ability to understand from inanimate things, or allows inanimate things to understand from him.

An example is the glorification of the mountains with David; his glorification together with theirs formed a "choir" (jawqah) (6) of harmony, consisting of a glorifying human, the highest of creatures, and the mountains echoing the glorification, which are the lowest of creatures among the inanimate.

We know that all creatures glorify, but we do not comprehend their glorification.(7) However, the Truth, glory be to Him, chooses from among His servants one whom He teaches the speech of other creatures, as He said, glory be to Him, of Sulayman:

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud, and he said: O people, we have been taught the speech of birds...﴾ [al-Naml: 16]

Thus we learn that birds have a speech, and the Truth, glory be to Him, taught Sulayman the language of the ant, for we read the saying of the Truth:

﴿When they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive. So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said: My Lord, inspire me to give thanks for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteous deeds that please You, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 18-19]

Therefore: every community of creatures has a language, and it understands from its Creator, or from whomever God, glory be to Him and exalted, wills that it should be understood by. By this we know that the sun, the moon and the stars, when they prostrated by the command of their Lord to Yusuf in his dream, were understanding the command of their Lord.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿He said: My son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they devise a plot against you. Surely Satan is a manifest enemy to man﴾ [Yusuf: 5]

1 - al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3443): The view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that, since these things were described with obedience and prostration, which are acts of one who has reason, they were described as one who has reason is described.
It may be drawn from the implicit meaning of al-Imam al-Sha'rawi's reflections that the verse shows Yusuf's standing within the family, his standing with his Lord, and that in the end they will acknowledge his merit and greatness, and this is evidence of victory after siege. Let us know that dream visions have laws that differ from visual sight, and that the symbolism of dream visions contains secrets that yield what is intended, since they carry explanatory indications of their meaning, such as Yusuf's vision of their prostration to him, and that he saw all of them at one time, with the time element between them omitted.
2 - adhina al-kalam fulan, and adhina ila sawtihi: he listened to it with his ear and attentively, admiring it and loving it. This meaning is given for the saying of the Exalted: "wa-adhinat li-rabbiha wa-huqqat" (84:2), i.e., she listened to the command of her Lord, responded, obeyed and submitted willingly. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/16, abridged].
3 - al-Furuj: plural of furj, which is a gap between two things; and al-furj: a split. The Exalted said describing the sky: "wa-ma laha min furuj" (50:6), i.e., cracks; it is firmly held together without any gap, but on the Day of Resurrection it will be split. The Exalted said: "wa-idha al-sama'u furijat" (77:9). [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/74].
4 - An example of this is the Exalted's saying: "thumma istawa ila al-sama'i wa-hiya dukhan fa-qala laha wa-lil-ard'i'tiya taw'an aw karhan qalata ataina ta'i'in" (41:11).
5 - The Exalted said: "wa-ma min dabbatin fi al-ardi wa-la ta'irin yatiru bi-janahayhi illa umamun amthalukum..." (6:38).
6 - al-Jawq in the language: every mixture of herdsmen whose affair is one; al-Layth said: al-jawq is every flock of herders whose affair is one; al-jawq also: a group of people. [Lisan al-Arab, root: j-w-q].
7 - The Exalted said: "...wa-in min shay'in illa yusabbihu bi-hamdihi wa-lakin la tafqahuna tasbihahum innahu kana halimān ghafura" (17:44).
8 - hatama yahtimuhu: broke it violently; the origin of ḥaṭm is breaking a dry thing, and it is applied to any breaking. The Exalted said: "la yahtimannakum Sulayman wa-junuduhu" (27:18), and al-huṭām: what has broken of the dry. The Exalted said: "law nasha'u laja'alnahu huṭaman" (56:65).
9 - awza'ahu an yaf'ala kadha: impelled him, urged him, or incited him, or inspired and guided him. The Exalted said: "rabbi awza'ni an ashkura ni'matak" (27:19), i.e., inspire me to thank You and impel me to it and make it beloved to me. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/334].
10 - kada fulanan yakiduhu kaydan: deceived him, plotted against him and schemed to inflict harm upon him. Kayd is a verbal noun, and it is applied to the action or means by which the schemer seeks to prevail over his adversary. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/180].

Whenever the Qur'an relates a father's address to his son, the phrase ﴿O my son﴾ appears, and it is an address of tenderness that indicates closeness to the heart (1). "Bunayya" is the diminutive of "ibn" (son).

As for when the Qur'an relates a father speaking about his son, it says "my son," as the Real (Exalted is He) says about Noah speaking about his son who chose disbelief over faith:

﴿Indeed, my son is of my family..﴾ (45) [Hud]

The phrase "O my son," with what it contains of tenderness and affection, will benefit us greatly in what follows of the positions of Yusuf and the positions of his father toward him.

Ya'qub's saying to Yusuf, "O my son," implies that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was still young. Ya'qub is the origin and Yusuf is the branch, and the origin is always full of tenderness toward the branch. At the same time, we find that any father says: whoever eats of my bread must listen to my word.

A father's saying "O my son" implies that the son is still young, without a self separate from the father by which he may decide what is suitable and what is not.

When Yusuf is alarmed by something that disturbs him or harms him, or by any difficult matter (2), he turns to the one who loves him, and that is the father, because the father is—in the eyes of the son—the most capable of facing difficult matters.

When Yusuf, peace be upon him, related the vision to his father, the father Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said:

﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers..﴾ (5) [Yusuf]

From the word "ru'ya" we understand that it is a vision seen in sleep, because the sun, the moon and the stars do not prostrate to anyone [in waking life]. This makes clear to us the precision of the Arabic language: one word, "ra'a" (to see), may have a different meaning according to what is seen. Your seeing while awake is called "ru'ya" (ru'ya being the vision in waking), and your seeing while asleep is called "ru'ya" (ru'ya being the vision in sleep). [Note: the author here distinguishes the two forms, "ru'ya" and "ru'ya", in the sense of the vision seen awake and the dream.]

Seeing (ru'ya in waking) is a noun agreed upon by all; you see what others see. As for "ru'ya" (the dream-vision), it comes to the sleeper.

Thus we find the convergence in "ra'a" and the difference in the state: whether it is the state of sleep or the state of wakefulness. Grammatically, both are feminine, because the sign of feminine gender is either a "ta'" or a long "alif" or a short "alif" (3).

The true seeing that occurs in wakefulness took the "ta'" (ة), which is the pillar of feminine marking; while the dream-vision took the feminine "alif."

Nothing casts doubt on the word "ru'ya" being a dream except one verse in the Qur'an, when the Real (Exalted is He) speaks of the moment when the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken up in the Ascension; He said:

﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people..﴾ (60) [al-Isra']

But those who say, "It is a dream-vision," have not understood the meaning behind this statement. The meaning is: what happened was a marvelous thing that happens only in dreams, but it happened in reality; the proof is that He called it "a trial for the people."

Had the Messenger (ﷺ) said it was a dream-vision, no one would have denied what he said; but he declared that it was a true vision, therefore the Qur'an described it as a trial for the people.

Here Ya'qub, peace be upon him, says:

﴿He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers..﴾ (5) [Yusuf]

Because Ya'qub, peace be upon him, as a father, is trustworthy regarding his son Yusuf; but Yusuf's brothers are not trustworthy regarding him. When Yusuf relates his vision to his father, the father will look into what is good for Yusuf and guide him to it (7).

But if he relates the vision to his brothers, human circumstances may cause them to envy their brother, and so it was.

If someone asks: why would they envy him over a dream-vision in which he saw the sun, the moon and eleven stars prostrating to him?

We say: Ya'qub, peace be upon him, must have known the interpretation of the vision, that it was a prophecy of events that would occur; and Ya'qub, peace be upon him, must also have known the ability of Yusuf's brothers to interpret that vision. Had Yusuf told them, they would have understood its intent, and they would then necessarily have plotted against him in a way that would bring him harm.

They had already been distressed by Yusuf while he was still a child, so what would their distress be if they learned of such a vision in which the father and mother and the brothers prostrate to him?

This does not mean we should regard Yusuf's brothers as wicked; they are the Asbat (8). The distress that afflicts them because of the father's excessive affection for Yusuf is among the changes that befall human beings. They are not wicked by nature (9), because the wicked by nature has evil events escalate within him, whereas the good has evil events descend upon him.

An example of this: you may find the wicked person wishing to slap another person on the cheek; but after a little while he thinks of escalating the aggression against that person, deciding to slap him twice instead of once; then he sees that two slaps are not enough, so he wants to increase the aggression by aiming a pistol at him; and thus the wicked person escalates his criminal thinking.

As for the good person, he may think of beating someone who has wronged him a "beating" (ʿalqa); but he diminishes the thought of returning the aggression by being content with thinking of slapping him twice instead of the "beating," then he calms down a little and pardons the one who wronged him.

Yusuf's brothers—and they are the Asbat (10)—began to think of a great revenge upon Yusuf, so they said to one another: ﴿Kill Yusuf..﴾ (9) [Yusuf]

Then they descended from this painful level in their expression of jealousy over their father's increased love for Yusuf, and said:

﴿Or cast him out to some land, so that your father's face will be clear for you..﴾ (9) [Yusuf]

When they wished to cast him out to a land, they hesitated, and replaced that with throwing him into the well (13), perhaps some of the caravan (14) would pick him up. They said:

﴿And cast him into the depths of the well (15); some of the caravan will pick him up..﴾ (10) [Yusuf]

This shows that they descended from severe revenge out of jealousy; indeed, they thought about his deliverance.

In the verse about which we are reflecting, the Real (Exalted is He) says:

﴿Do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they devise a plot against you..﴾ (5) [Yusuf]

Kayd (plotting): a hidden stratagem against one who cannot be confronted directly; only the weak plots, because the strong can confront.

That is why it is said: the plotting of women is great, because their weakness is greater.

The Real (Exalted is He) concludes the noble verse with His saying:

﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy.﴾ (5) [Yusuf]

This enmity is well known to us, because he went out of Paradise cursed and expelled, unlike Adam, whose repentance Allah accepted. Satan swore by the might of Allah that he would mislead all, except the sincere servants of Allah (16).

That is why the Prophet (ﷺ) says: "Allah has helped me against my devil, so he has submitted." (17)

The Real (Exalted is He) describes Satan's enmity toward man as "clear" (mubin) (18), meaning encompassing; and when we read the Qur'an we find Satan's encirclement of man contains alertness:

﴿I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left..﴾ (17) [al-A'raf]

No mention is made of coming from above or from below, because whoever lives in servitude below and worship above, Satan never reaches him.

We note that the Real (Exalted is He) brought Ya'qub's words, addressing Yusuf, peace be upon him, in this verse:

﴿lest they devise a plot against you..﴾ (5) [Yusuf]

He did not say "yakīdūka" (they plot against you); and this is from the outpouring (nadh) of Ya'qub's prophethood upon his tongue, because there is a difference between the two expressions. The saying "yakīdūnaka" would mean that the hidden evil they plot against you will harm you.

But ﴿fa-yakīdū (20) laka kaydan..﴾ (5) means that their plotting, by which they intended to inflict evil upon you, will turn out to your account and bring you good.

That is why we find His saying elsewhere in the same surah:

﴿Thus did We plot for Yusuf..﴾ (76) [Yusuf]

i.e., We plotted for his benefit.

The Real (Exalted is He) then says:

﴿And thus will your Lord choose you and teach you the interpretation of narratives and complete His favor upon you and upon the family of Ya'qub, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed, your Lord is Knowing and Wise.﴾ (6)

1 - This address occurs six times in the Qur'an, in Hud, Yusuf, Luqman (three verses) and al-Saffat. Let us know that the universe and what is in it and who is in it have as their function, before Allah, obedience and prostration, in compliance with Allah's will; so it is among the things that come upon one...
2 - "Al-amr al-mu'dil": the difficult matter that is very constricting. 'Adala 'alayhi fi amrihi ta'diIan: he was constrained in his affair, i.e., restricted him from what he wanted unjustly; and 'adala bihim al-makan: the place became cramped; and the land constrained its people when it was too narrow for them due to their multitude [Lisan al-'Arab, root ʿ-dh-l].
3 - The verbal signs of feminine gender are three:
- The "ta'" of feminine: it enters verbs and nouns, such as jālisa and Fāṭima; and since it serves to distinguish masculine from feminine, it does not enter adjectives specific to women such as ḥā'iḍ, mur-ḍi', thayyib.
- The short (maqsura) alif of feminine: a fixed alif whose preceding letter is fatha, attached to the end of a feminine word.
- The extended (mamdud) alif of feminine: a syllable consisting of a hamza preceded by a long alif with fatha before it; it attaches to nouns, not verbs, such as ḥasnā', ṣaḥrā', kibriyā', ʿĀshūrā'. See: al-Qawa'id al-Sarfiyya, Dr. ʿAli Abu al-Makarim, 1979 ed., pp. 62–65.
4 - Qadaḥ: it left a mark; one says, "qadaḥa al-shay' fi ṣadri" (it left a mark in my chest). In the saying attributed to ʿAli, may Allah honor his face: "doubt strikes his heart with the first passing shubha" [Lisan al-'Arab, root q-d-ḥ].
5 - ʿAraja: to ascend, rise and go up; al-mi'raj: whatever helps you ascend, plural ma'arij. The Exalted said: ﴿and ascending stairways upon which they climb﴾ [43:33], i.e., they ride them and ascend in them to the heights [al-Qamus al-Qawim, abridged: 2/13].
6 - Al-Azhari and others said: the sum of the meaning of fitna is trial, testing and examination [see Lisan al-'Arab, root f-t-n].
7 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3447]: "This verse is a basis for not relating a vision to anyone other than a sincere, trustworthy confidant, nor to one who does not know how to interpret it."
8 - Al-Asbat: plural of sibt; al-sibt: a tree with one root and many branches; this was transferred metaphorically to the lineage tree, so the sibt is a tribe branching from one origin; and al-asbat are the tribes among the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, which are twelve tribes named after the twelve sons of Ya'qub: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations﴾ (160) [al-A'raf] [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/300].
9 - Al-salīqa: nature and disposition; so-and-so reads bi-l-saliqa, i.e., by his nature not by learning; it is also said bi-l-saliqiyya, i.e., by the nature in which he was raised. Abu Zayd said: he is noble in nature and disposition [Lisan al-'Arab, root s-l-q].
10 - The word "asbat" is mentioned five times in the Qur'an; in four of them it refers to the asbat who were prophets, and in the fifth place, asbat means the origins of the tribes of Bani Isra'il; each son of Ya'qub was the first of a sibt or the other.
11 - Tarh al-shay' yatrahuhu tarhan: he cast it away and threw it; the Exalted said: ﴿or cast him out to some land (9)﴾ [Yusuf], i.e., throw him in a distant land [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/399].
12 - Khalā fulān ila fulān: he devoted himself to him and did not occupy himself with anyone else. The Exalted said on the tongue of Yusuf's brothers: ﴿so that your father's face will be clear for you (9)﴾, i.e., your father will be free for you and turn to you with all his care, and will not occupy himself with anyone other than you [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/209].
13 - Al-jubb: a well not built with stones. Al-Layth said: al-jubb: a well not far off; al-Farra' said: a well whose interior is wide in its middle, vaulted; and it is also a well with abundant water and deep bottom [Lisan al-'Arab, root j-b-b].
14 - Sayyar: one who travels much, an intensive form; sayyara: intensive form for the feminine; al-sayyara: a traveling group on the road. The Exalted said: ﴿And there came a caravan (19)﴾ [Yusuf], i.e., a group of travelers; and His saying: ﴿as a provision for you and for the travelers (69)﴾ [al-Ma'ida], i.e., for travelers [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/340].
15 - Ghāba al-shay' yaghību ghaybān: it hid from sight or from human knowledge in the figurative sense; al-ghayb is a verbal noun and is used to name what is hidden and concealed. The Exalted said: ﴿those who believe in the unseen (3)﴾ [al-Baqara].
16 - The Lord of Might related this from Iblis the accursed, that he said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, (82) except Your sincere servants among them (83)﴾ [Sad].
17 - On the authority of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but that a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him and a companion from the angels." They said: "And you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And I, but Allah has helped me against him, so he does not command me except with truth." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [1/385].
18 - Ban al-shay' yabinu bayanan: it appeared and became clear, so it is bayyin (clear, masculine) and bayyina (clear, feminine): i.e., apparent and evident; al-bayn and al-bayyina are used in the sense of the manifest and the clarifying; and by both meanings it is explained. Bayyana al-shay', abana, bayyana and istabana: it is no longer hidden. His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy (168)﴾ [al-Baqara] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/91–92, adapted].
19 - The root of nadh is seepage: nadaḥa al-rajul bi-l-ʿaraq naḍḥan: the man sweated; and nadaḥat al-ʿayn fa-ara bi-l-dam'; and nadaḥat al-khābiya wa-l-jarra tanḍaḥ: if it is thin and water comes out of the earthenware and seeps [Lisan al-'Arab, root n-ḍ-ḥ, adapted].
20 - Kāda fulānan yakīduhu kayden: he deceived him, schemed against him, and contrived to inflict harm upon him; kayd is a verbal noun and is applied to the action or means by which the plotter seeks to overcome his opponent [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/180].
21 - Ijtabā fulānan: he chose him, selected him and preferred him; the Exalted said: ﴿Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back (13)﴾ [al-Shura], i.e., He chooses and selects whom He wills of His creation [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/117].
22 - Al-hadith: speech, its plural is aḥādīth; al-aḥādīth is the plural of uḥdūtha, the wondrous report; hadith may also be applied to visions and dreams. The Exalted said: ﴿and teach you the interpretation of narratives (6)﴾ [Yusuf]. As for His saying: ﴿and We made them narratives (44)﴾ [al-Mu'minun], it is a metaphor for death and destruction, i.e., after they were alive they became dead, and people speak of them [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/145].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 6:

I.e., just as Allah has comforted you with this joyful vision, which announces that you will have a great station with respect to your brothers and with respect to your father, "your Lord will choose you" (yajtabika rabbuka); not merely to protect you, but by making their scheming a cause of your benefit, and by teaching you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith), which will make people of rank and authority turn to you.

The meaning of the ta'wil (interpretation, i.e., knowing what a thing will ultimately lead to) of a thing is knowing what that thing will return to. We know that dreams come like riddles, and have a symbolic cipher that no one can decode except one whom Allah has granted the ability to do so; it is not a science with fixed rules and principles, because it is an inspiration from Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

Then, after that, O Yusuf, you will be placed over the treasures of the earth, when drought occurs and it covers the whole region, and you will become the 'Aziz of Egypt.

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues:

﴿And complete His favour upon you..(6)﴾ [Yusuf]

So everything that Yusuf enjoyed is among the blessings of this world, and the crown of the blessing of this world is that Allah chose him as a messenger.

Or: ﴿And complete His favour upon you..(6)﴾ [Yusuf]

meaning that the blessing will never be taken from you; for in Yusuf's life there is an important position, the position of 'Aziz of Egypt, and positions are among the transient things that can be removed.

Or: ﴿And complete His favour upon you..(6)﴾ [Yusuf]

by joining the bliss of your worldly life with the bliss of your Hereafter.(2)

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues:

﴿And upon the family of Ya'qub, as He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq. Indeed your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.(6)﴾ [Yusuf]

The Truth, glory be to Him, reminds Yusuf, peace be upon him, that his brothers' scheming against him must not turn him into an enemy, because the blessings will also be completed upon these brothers, for they are the family of Ya'qub; they and their sons are the descendants of Ya'qub, and some of the might, station and wealth of Yusuf will reach them, just as He completed it previously upon Ibrahim, the first grandfather of Yusuf, by taking him as a khalil (intimate friend) of Allah,(3) and Allah, glory be to Him, completed His favour upon Ishaq through prophethood.
