1 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3479]: "His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they were of those who were indifferent to him (20)﴾ [Yusuf]: it is said the intended were his brothers. It is said: the caravan (al-sayyara). It is said: the watering party (al-warida). In any case, he was not an object of desire (ghabitan) for any of them: not for the brothers, because their aim was his removal from his father, not his wealth; not for the caravan, because the brothers said he was a runaway slave from us; and al-zuhd is little desire; nor for the watering party, because they feared their companions would share in it with them, and they saw that a small price for him when alone was better."
2 - Thawa al-makan, and thawa bihi yathwi: he dwelt in it, remained and settled there. It is transitive and intransitive, and the Qur'an used the intransitive form, saying: ﴿You were not dwelling among the people of Madyan (45)﴾ [al-Qasas], meaning residing among them. Al-mathwa is a place noun or a noun of place from the mim-form. God says: ﴿Honour his residence (21)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning his stay. That is: honour Joseph, and he expressed the place by the state within it, as a metonymy (majaz mursal) whose relation is locality (ʿalaqah mahalliyyah). [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/113].

The purchaser had a reason for buying him. He bought him for his wife, so that he would attend to her service. She was barren and pressed him insistently to seek a cure. Most of the biographical accounts say that the man who bought him was weak in his desire for women.

This scene shows us the corruption that arises in households that adopt a child. They do not reckon with the matter when this child reaches manhood. The mistress of the house grows accustomed to carrying him and kissing him, and she lavishes on him such pampering that she finds it hard to refrain from it. And because the child grows up gradually, the forbidden may occur, and we enter the maze of sin.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said to his wife, "Make his stay honourable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." (21)﴾ [Yusuf]

This means that she should take care of the place where he will reside, and naturally this statement requires that she take care of the boy himself, in the hope that the man and his wife will benefit from him.

If someone should ask: how can the man benefit from him, when he is the Aziz of Egypt and everyone is at his service?

We say: the benefit intended here is the benefit that is bound up with the affection of the one who benefits. It is different from the benefit of the officials who work under the command and authority of the Aziz of Egypt. When Yusuf grows up as the son of the man and his wife, and as a person raised in the man's house, the matter will be different, and the benefit will be charged with the affection that the man spoke of:

﴿Or we may adopt him as a son.. (21)﴾ [Yusuf]

We know from the biographies that they had not been blessed with children.(1)

The Truth, glory be to Him, says in the same verse:

﴿And thus did We establish Yusuf in the land, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah is predominant over His affair, but most of the people do not know. (21)﴾ [Yusuf]

The establishment of Yusuf in the land began from the moment he entered the house of the Aziz of Egypt, to live a good life, and so that Allah would teach him the interpretation of events, by granting him the ability to interpret visions and dreams, and so that Allah would prevail over His affair.

If his brothers had looked at what Yusuf, peace be upon him, came to, they would have known that their intention had failed, and that the will of Allah had prevailed, through the honouring of Yusuf. Had they known that, they would have begrudged him being thrown into the well, and this is the way of all wrongdoers.

Therefore we say: if the wrongdoer knew what Allah has prepared for the one who is wronged, he would begrudge him the wrong.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And Allah is predominant over His affair.. (21)﴾ [Yusuf]

this is an enforced statement, because He alone is able to say to a thing "Be," and it is. There is no other god to oppose His will.

For this reason we said long ago that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, bore witness to Himself that there is no god but He,(2) and He possesses the absolute, assured foundation that there is no god besides Him. He alone holds dominion, and He alone is capable of everything.

But some creatures are disappointed, those who imagine that they are able to plan and scheme, forgetting or ignoring that above them is the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum),(3) who is not seized by drowsiness (sinah)(4) or sleep. If these people had paid heed, they would have known that Allah possesses, in truth, power over the one who wrongs, above the one he wronged.

We have seen in our lives and our history wrongdoers who united to oppress people, and their end was worse than imagination, and more terrible than the fate they would have suffered had those they wronged held power over them.

The Truth, glory be to Him, then says:

﴿And when he reached his maturity,(5) We gave him judgement and knowledge. And thus do We reward the good-doers. (22)﴾

1 - Ibn Abbas said: he was a eunuch (ḥaṣūr) who could not father children. Ibn Ishaq likewise said: Qitfir did not approach women and could not father children. If it is asked: how did he say "or we may adopt him as a son" when he owned him, and being a son and being a slave contradict each other? It is answered: he would free him and then adopt him as a son. Adoption was known among the nations, and it was so at the beginning of Islam. Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir [4/3482].
2 - This is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those of knowledge, maintaining justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise (18)﴾ [Ali 'Imran].
3 - Al-Qayyum and al-qiyam, in the description of Allah and His Most Beautiful Names, is the One who manages the affairs of His creation in their creation, their provision, and His knowledge of their places. Qatadah said: al-Qayyum is the One who stands over His creation with their terms, their deeds, and their provisions. [Lisan al-Arab, root q-w-m].
4 - Sana yasin sanah: he slept a light sleep. The sanah is a single act. The Most High said: ﴿Drowsiness does not seize Him, nor sleep (255)﴾ [al-Baqarah], meaning: a light slumber does not seize Him, nor any sleep, or inattention to anything does not seize Him, nor sleep of any kind, heavy or light, much or little. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/338].
5 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3484]: "its meaning is the completion of strength, after which decline follows." Mujahid and Qatadah said: al-ashudd is thirty-three years. Rabi'ah, Zayd ibn Aslam and Malik ibn Anas said: al-ashudd is reaching puberty.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 22:

Al-bulugh (puberty, maturity) is reaching the end point. The words of the Exalted:

﴿When he reached his maturity... (22)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: he reached the limit of his ripeness and full development. From the word "balagha" (to reach) the technical term al-bulugh (puberty) is derived. A person's legal responsibility (taklif) begins as soon as he reaches his maturity, and he becomes able to father a child like himself.

When a person like Yusuf reaches his maturity, and he has grown up in a house full of good things, then this maturity, if it is not guarded by wisdom (hikmah) and knowledge ('ilm), will produce in him recklessness (ra'unah)(1). For this reason, the Truth (al-Haqq) guarded him with wisdom and knowledge.

Al-hukm (judgment) is the decisive distinction between two conflicting, opposing matters: truth and falsehood. Since God has given him judgment, he is able to distinguish between right and wrong.

God has also given him knowledge which he can transmit to others, and from which will come the interpretation of dreams (ta'wil al-ru'a)(2), and other knowledge that will become apparent when he is placed in charge of the treasury of Egypt.

So here, Yusuf reached his maturity, and the Truth guarded him with wisdom and knowledge.

The Exalted concludes this verse with His saying:

﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers (22)﴾ [Yusuf]

Every person who handles well the situation he is in, God gives him the fruit of this goodness. An example: when a poor man does not rebel against God's decree that made him poor, and tries to do well and perfect what he does, God shows him through a good reward: "You accepted My decree and did your work well, so take the good recompense." This is the condition of the great ones of this world entirely.

Thus we find the saying of the Truth, the Exalted:

﴿And thus do We reward the good-doers (2)﴾ [Yusuf]

This is not revealed about Yusuf alone, but about everyone who receives God's decree well, because when He, the Exalted, brings a ruling from among the rulings, He afterwards generalises the ruling; this means that this ruling is not specific but general.

And if the Exalted mentions this on a particular occasion, He then establishes that every good-doer is given judgment and knowledge by God.

The saying of the Exalted:

﴿And when he reached his maturity... (22)﴾ [Yusuf]

suggests to us that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had reached the stage of youthful vigour (fatwah)(3), and here his troubles in the palace began. In his childhood the wife of the al-Aziz looked at him as a beautiful child, and he did not possess the features of manhood that would stir her femininity.

But after maturity, we find her condition has changed: she began to perceive his allure, and her imagination began to wander beyond perception, which is the inflaming of emotion with ardent feeling (4), and after perception and emotion comes inclination (nuz'u).

Had she been kept from him, the seduction by perception and emotion would not have occurred.

This gives us the reason for lowering the gaze from sexual stimuli, because if you do not lower your gaze you perceive, and if you perceive you feel, and if you feel you incline towards marriage or chastity through suppression within the self, and you live in the agitation of anxiety and tension; and if you do not restrain yourself, you rampage (5) against people's honour.

Likewise, God the Exalted commanded that women not display their adornment except to those whom God the Exalted specified in His saying:

﴿And let them not display their adornment except to their husbands(6), or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands, or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or what their right hands possess, or male attendants having no physical desire (ghayr uli al-israh)(7), or children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private parts of women... (31)﴾ [al-Nur]

That is: the one who has reached such an age and senility that does not make him think of desire for women.

The look of the wife of the al-Aziz at Yusuf, peace be upon him, while he was in his youthful vigour, after he had reached his maturity, was a different look, which God the Exalted clarifies in His saying:

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him, and she closed the doors and said, "Come, you." He said, "God forbid! Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my residence good. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed." (23)﴾

1 - Ra'unah: foolishness and slackness; a ra'an is one who is reckless in speech [Lisan al-'Arab, root r-‘-n].
2 - Ru'a: plural of ru'ya, what you see in your sleep; ra'a can mean "to believe" and "to know"; ra'a fi manamihi ru'ya means he dreamed; al-ru'ya means a dream during sleep [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/250].
3 - Al-fatah: youth; al-fata and al-fatiyah are the young man and young woman. Al-Qutaybi said: al-fata does not mean a young man or a youth, but rather the complete, excellent man; the poet said: "Indeed the fata bears every burden; the fata is not one who indulges the young." [Lisan al-'Arab, root f-t-y].
4 - Shabba al-nar wa al-harb: he kindled the fire or war; shabb al-nar is its blazing. Abu Hanifah reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that he said: shabbat al-nar and shabbat hiya nafsaha; he said one does not say shabbah, but mashbub [Lisan al-'Arab, root sh-b-b].
5 - A man 'arbad, 'arbad, mu'arbad: a wicked, troublesome man; the one who is 'arbad is called 'arbid, as if likened to a snake [Lisan al-'Arab, root '-r-b-d].
6 - Al-ba'l: husband or wife; it is a masculine noun used for both, so it is not feminised. Its plural is bu'ul. God says: "And this is my husband, an old man" (Hud 72) and "And their husbands have more right to take them back" (al-Baqarah 228), meaning their husbands have more right to take them back after a revocable divorce, and after a final single divorce or two final divorces, by a new contract [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/76].
7 - Al-arab: a need that requires contriving to attain it; likewise al-arbah and al-ma'rab. God says: "or male attendants having no physical desire (ghayr uli al-israh)... or children" (al-Nur 31), meaning those without need of women, that is, those who have no desire due to old age, infirmity or youth [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/17].
8 - Ghalaqa al-bab yughliquhu ghalqan: he locked it, like aghlaqahu; ghallaqahu with the doubled letter is for intensity in closing and securing doors, as in God's saying: "and the doors were locked" (Yusuf 23), meaning he firmly locked them to secure himself from those who enter [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/59].
9 - Hayya'a al-shay': he prepared it, readied it and made it easy. God says: "and prepare for us from our affair right guidance" (al-Kahf 10), meaning make easy for us from our affair the path of right guidance and truth. Ha'tu lil-amr: I prepared myself for it. It is recited in surah Yusuf as "wa-ha'tu laka", meaning I prepared myself for you; and "hayta" is a verb-form meaning "come forward" and "come here". God says: "And she said, 'Come, you.' He said, 'God forbid...'" (Yusuf 23). The meaning: come forward; the lam is for transitivity, i.e., I call you to come forward, or the call is for you [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/311, 312].

When you hear "rawada" (راود), understand that the action involves a contest between two parties, like the patterns "fa'ala" (فاعل) or "tafa'ala" (تفاعل). An example is "Muhammad shared (shaaraka) with Ali" (شارك محمد عليا), meaning that Ali shared with Muhammad and Muhammad shared with Ali. Each of them is the object once and the subject once.

*Muraawada* (المراودة) means requesting something gently and softly, while concealing what you want from the person you want it from. If the matter is easy, the *muraawada* ends in achieving something. But if the second party refuses after learning what is intended, the *muraawada* will not end in the thing you were longing for.

In this way, the wife of al-Aziz *raawada* Yusuf (peace be upon him), meaning she sought from him gently and softly, in a manner that deceives him, in order to draw him away from what he was in to what she wanted.

Previously, Yusuf used to serve her, and she would look at him as a child. But after he reached his maturity (*ashudd*), the matter changed. Let us suppose she asked him to bring her something. When he brings it to her, she says, "Why are you standing far away?" and she invites him to sit beside her. He cannot escape, because he is in her house and she has power over him, for she is the mistress of the palace.

Thus we find that the affair was compounded against him from several directions: he had been raised in her house, and she was the one who was gentle and tender with him, and he understood what she meant.

In this way, the Truth (al-Haqq), glorified is He, explained the matter from beginning to end with refined decorum and without exposing it openly, saying:

﴿And she in whose house he was sought to seduce him from himself, and she closed the doors.﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

The intensification of the action is indicated here, or the repetition of the action. She closed more than one door. When we move the *mizlaj* (المزلاج, a bolt) we are emphasising the closing of a door, and we turn the key and turn it to emphasise the closing of the door.

So this is a process greater than closing the door. If we add a second bolt, we have multiplied the closing of one door, and in this way we can describe what we did as having closed the door.

The wife of al-Aziz carried out more than one closing for more than one door, for the palaces of great men have many doors. You do not enter upon such a great man in his house to find him waiting to receive you after the first door. Rather, a person passes through several doors to meet the great one who has come to receive him.

History records the story of a man who refused to pledge allegiance to Mu'awiya in Medina, so Mu'awiya ordered that he be summoned to the seat of government in Damascus.

This was the palace which 'Umar ibn al-Khattab had once visited, and he found in it excessive grandeur, which Mu'awiya justified to him with the cunning of the shrewd, saying it was grandeur necessary to display the status of the Arabs before the neighbouring Roman state. So 'Umar remained silent about it.

When Mu'awiya summoned the man, he entered with the guard through one door, and he thought he would meet Mu'awiya immediately upon entering. But the guards led him through several doors, and the man's heart did not sink. Rather, he entered upon Mu'awiya with composure and withheld from addressing him as "Commander of the Believers," and said in a loud voice:

"Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Mu'awiya realised that the man was refusing to pledge allegiance to him.

Returning to the verse we are reflecting upon, we find that the wife of al-Aziz closed the doors because whoever commits an ugly act knows the ugliness of what he does and tries to conceal his deed. She tried to do that away from those who work or live in the palace. The seduction took place and took time, but it appears that he did not respond to her.

﴿And she said, "Come, [I am] yours."﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

That is, she moved from the stage of seduction to the stage of clarity in requesting the act, by saying, "I have prepared myself for you." His response was:

﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah."﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

The *mu'aadh* (المعاذ) is that in which you seek refuge, and you do not seek refuge except when your means fail before the event you are passing through, so that perhaps you may find someone to rescue you. It is as if the matter had become difficult for him, so he found no refuge except Allah.

No one is able to act in this way except one whom Allah has guarded with the wisdom and knowledge He gave him, and made able to distinguish between the lawful (*halal*) and the unlawful (*haram*).

To demonstrate the gravity and power of seeking refuge, we mention what the books of prophetic biography (*sira*) narrate: that the Prophet (ﷺ) contracted marriage with the daughter of al-Jawn (or Malik), who was extremely attractive. Some of the Prophet's wives felt jealous of her, and one of them, perhaps 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), said: "If he marries her and consummates the marriage with her, she may surpass us." She said to the bride, "The Prophet loves a certain word, and he loves whoever says it." The girl asked about the word, and 'A'isha said to her, "When he comes near you, say, 'I seek refuge in Allah from you.'"

So when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went in to her and approached her, she said: "I seek refuge in Allah from you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left her and said: "You have sought refuge with one who grants refuge," and he released her with a gracious release.

There, in the case of Lady Maryam (peace be upon her), we find that when the angel appeared to her as a well-formed man, she said:

﴿Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you should be fearing of Allah.﴾ (18) [Maryam]

So she sought refuge in One who is able to save her.

And here, in the verse we are reflecting upon:

﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my residence excellent. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

This statement gives two meanings:

The first: he did not agree to her request after she had made clear what she wanted.

The second meaning: he sought help from Allah, for He is the One who saved him from the plotting of his brothers, rescued him from the well, prepared for him the best place in Egypt in which to live, and granted him knowledge and wisdom when he reached his maturity.

After all this, would he meet such generosity with disobedience? Certainly not.

Alternatively, he said: ﴿He has made my residence excellent.﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

to remind the wife of al-Aziz that she has a husband, and that this husband had treated Yusuf well when he said to her:

﴿Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.﴾ (21) [Yusuf]

So the difficulty comes not only from her inviting him to herself; the difficulty grows worse because she has a husband, so she is not free, and this husband had asked her to honour Yusuf and to choose for him a place of residence fitting for a son. It is not possible for him to respond to that with ingratitude and betrayal.

Thus Yusuf's words, ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord﴾ (23) [Yusuf], may refer to Allah, glorified is He; and they may refer to the al-Aziz of Egypt. This is a feature of the style of the Qur'an: it uses an expression that encompasses all the levels of understanding. Since Allah is the One who rewards good, and He is the One who said in the same context:

﴿And thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ (22) [Yusuf]

the meaning is that whoever does evil, Allah brings about the opposite, so he does not succeed, because the two matters are contrasted:

﴿And thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ (22) [Yusuf]

and

﴿The wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ (23) [Yusuf]

After that, the Truth (al-Haqq), glorified is He, says:

﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Thus [it was], that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants.﴾ (24)

1 - *Saba yasbu* (صبا يصبو): he inclined and loved. Yusuf (peace be upon him) said: ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant.﴾ (33) [Yusuf], meaning: I might incline to them and do what they entice me to do. *Saba ila al-lahw* means he yearned for and longed for amusement and accompanied it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/368].

2 - *Al-zalaj* and *al-mizlaj* (الزلاج والمزلاج): the bolt of a door, named so for the speed with which it slides. One says *azlajtu al-bab*, meaning I closed the door. The *mizlaj* is a bolt that can be opened by hand, whereas the *mighlaq* (a lock) can only be opened with a key. [Lisan al-Arab, root z-l-j].

3 - *Al-arib* (الأريب): the intelligent person. *Al-irb* and *al-arab* mean cunning and insight into affairs, and it derives from reason. The root *irb* means cunning and guile. [Lisan al-Arab, root a-r-b].

4 - *Al-abha* (الأبهة): majesty and splendour. *Al-bahaa'* and *al-abha* mean majesty and pride, and a man of *abha* is one of pride and majesty. [Lisan al-Arab, root a-b-h].

5 - Abu 'Ali al-Qali mentioned in his *Amali* [2/136]: "Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba said: When 'Umar looked at Mu'awiya, he would say, 'This is the Chosroes of the Arabs.'"

6 - It is mentioned in al-Tabari that she was Mulaika bint Dawud al-Laythiyya [3/123], or Fatima bint al-Dahhak al-Kilabiyya [3/139].

7 - Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari* [9/359]: "It occurred in Ibn Sa'd's [*al-Tabaqat*] that 'A'isha and Hafsa entered upon her when she first arrived, and they groomed her and dyed her, and one of them said to her: The Prophet (ﷺ) likes it of a woman, when he comes in to her, that she says, 'I seek refuge in Allah from you.'"

8 - Narrated by al-Bukhari in his *Sahih* [5255], *Kitab al-Talaq*, from the hadith of Abu Usayd (may Allah be pleased with him).

9 - *Al-sarah* (السراح): a verbal noun or noun of action meaning divorce: ﴿So come, I will provide for you and release you with a gracious release.﴾ (28) [al-Ahzab], meaning a good divorce without deceit or harm. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/309].

10 - *Al-sawiyy* from men means one who has no defect in his creation and no disease or affliction in his body. So His saying, ﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights while sound."﴾ (10) [Maryam], means while you are complete in creation, neither mute nor deaf, nor having any incapacity. And His saying, ﴿So He appeared to her as a well-proportioned man﴾ (17) [Maryam], means one of proportioned creation in the form of a complete, beautiful, radiant human. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/339].

11 - *Al-mathwa* (المثوى): a place noun or a mimi verbal noun. Allah says: ﴿And wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers﴾ (151) [Al 'Imran], a place noun referring to the Fire. And He says: ﴿Make his residence comfortable﴾ (21) [Yusuf], meaning his stay, that is, honour Yusuf. He used the name of the place to express the condition within it, as a metonymy (majaz mursal) with a figurative link. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/113].

12 - *Hamma bihi yahummu hamman*: he intended it and turned his intention towards it without doing it. Allah says: ﴿When a people intended to extend their hands to you, but He withheld their hands from you﴾ (11) [al-Ma'ida], meaning they resolved and turned their intention to fighting you, transgressing against you and harming you, but Allah restrained them. Allah says concerning the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾ (24) [Yusuf]. *Hammat bihi* (she desired him) means a resolve and determination; *wa hamma biha* (he desired her) means abandonment, aversion and resistance, that is, he resisted her, and Allah knows best. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/307, adapted].

13 - *Al-burhan* (البرهان): the clear, decisive proof. Allah says: ﴿Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."﴾ (111) [al-Baqara]. And His saying: ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ (24) [Yusuf] means: had he not seen the proof of his Lord that strengthened him upon the truth and turned him away from what he intended. Or: had he not seen the proof of his Lord, that is, the evidence of his master's arrival and presence. Allah decreed that his master would come to the house at that time to avert evil from him. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/65].

14 - *Akhlasahu Allah* means He made him pure, clean and unblemished. The passive participle is *mukhlas* with a fatha on the lam. Allah says: ﴿Indeed, he was of Our chosen servants﴾ (24) [Yusuf], meaning the chosen, pious, purified ones. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/202].

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah Yusuf, verse 24

*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)*

*Hamm* (intention, resolve) is the soul's inner speech about a thing, whether or not the person acts on it. Among the mercies of our Lord toward His creatures is that when someone resolves on an evil deed and his soul prompts him to do it, but he does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him.(1)

The expression here concerns the solicitation that came from her and the refusal that came from him. That situation requires a reciprocal action between two parties who contend over something.

One of the two is the wife of the Ruler (*al-'Aziz*). Allah speaks of her:

﴿And she certainly desired him..(24)﴾ [Yusuf]

In the preceding verse the Truth, glorified is He, had already made known her position when she said, "*Hayta lak*" (Come, I am yours). Likewise He showed the position of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when he said, "*Ma'adh Allah*" (God forbid).

Here He shows us that his soul also spoke within him, and that the inner speech was equal on both sides. But for Yusuf there occurred the seeing of the proof of his Lord.

Our understanding of the phrase is: "Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." We know that *lawla* (had it not been for) is a particle indicating that a thing is prevented because another thing exists, as when we say: "Had Zayd not been with you, I would have come to you."

Someone might ask: How is the conditional structure of existence and prevention absent for those who say that the *hamm* did occur in him?

And why did the Truth not say: "She certainly desired him, but he did not desire her," so that we might escape that difficult question?

We say: Had the Truth said that, this wording would not have given us the required meaning. The wife of the Ruler desired him because she had the impulses of action within her. Had He not told us that he had desired her, we would have supposed him impotent, or that his castration or the situation (of her being his mistress) had caused his strength to fail.(2)

Therefore, had the Truth, glorified is He, said that he did not desire her, the barrier to desire would have been either something natural in him, or something accidental, such as that she was his mistress, and shame might have prevented him from desiring her.

But the Truth, glorified is He, wants to make clear to us that Yusuf was a normal man, for he had reached his full strength and maturity. Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her.

Thus Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not fail to do what that requires because of a defect in him. The situation was a sudden shock that unmanned him all at once,(3) like what happens to some young men on the wedding night, when a man cannot approach his bride, and days pass until he regains his balance and approaches his bride.

Therefore, if the Qur'an had intended to deny the *hamm* absolutely and without any cause, it would have said: "And she certainly desired him, but he did not desire her."

But such a statement would negate the event without implying chastity and protection, since the absence of desire might be due to some defect. Also, so that we would not be led to compare him to some servants, who are shy to look at the beautiful daughters of the household in which they work, and whose eyes turn instead to the maidservant who works in the neighboring house, because feelings have their meeting points.

Among the kindnesses of Allah toward His creation is that He creates interactive meeting points between equals. So the servant's feeling does not, at certain times, fall upon the daughters of the house where he works. He may ask the people of the house to go out to buy anything from outside the home, hoping to obtain a fleeting meeting with the neighbor's maidservant.

It may also be that the servant has considered that if he desired one of the daughters of the family he works for, the family might dismiss him from work, while he lives happily with that family.

Thus the Truth, glorified is He, wills to distribute these matters with order and balance in many cases.

Now in the verse about which we are reflecting, the Truth, glorified is He, said:

﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord..(24)﴾ [Yusuf]

Therefore, the proof of his Lord preceded the *hamm*. He resolved, but did not commit what the *hamm* requires, because the proof of his Lord was in his heart. Yusuf had known the proof of his Lord from the beginning.

With this the matter is settled. Therefore there is no need for people to enter into labyrinths, such as the claim that he desired her, sat between her four limbs,(4) and only trembled when the image of his father Ya'qub appeared to him and forbade him this act.(5) For the most dissolute of the dissolute, if his father had appeared to him in such a situation, would have fainted.

When someone who holds this view is debated, he replies that his aim is to affirm the virility of Yusuf, because the *hamm* existed and he struggled against it.

We say to the holder of this view: Are you speaking about Allah, or about Satan?

If you look at the characters of the story, you find them: the wife of the Ruler; Yusuf; the Ruler himself; the witness who showed that Yusuf had tried to escape from that situation; then the women whom the wife of the Ruler invited to see his beauty. And Allah had ordained his protection.

All of these cooperated(7) in showing that nothing happened from Yusuf.

Yusuf himself said:

﴿She solicited me against myself..(26)﴾ [Yusuf]

The wife of the Ruler herself, confirming what he said, said:

﴿And I did solicit him against himself, but he held firm..(32)﴾ [Yusuf]

And she said: ﴿Now the truth has come to light: it was I who solicited him against himself, and he is surely one of the truthful. (51) That he may know that I did not betray him in his absence..(52)﴾ [Yusuf]

Yusuf said at that moment:

﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I shall incline towards them and be among the ignorant.(33)﴾ [Yusuf]

*Al-Sabwa* (inclination, youthful passion) is the inner speech of the soul toward a thing. It affirms Yusuf's capacity to act, peace be upon him, and Allah protected him from *al-sabwa*, because the Truth, glorified is He, said:

﴿So He turned away from him their plot..(34)﴾ [Yusuf]

Consider the scene of the women who whispered gossip about the wife of the Ruler and her affair with Yusuf. Did they not say:

﴿This is no mortal; this is none other than a noble angel.(31)﴾ [Yusuf]

When he entered upon them, their eyes turned to him, and eyes have their languages, and emotion has its languages. Otherwise, why would Yusuf have said:

﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot..(33)﴾ [Yusuf]

Thus we know that there were preliminaries showing that the women had intentions toward him like those of the wife of the Ruler, and they thought that the wife of the Ruler would expel him, so they would seize him. This is the habit of corrupt households.

And was there any household more corrupt than the house of the Ruler himself, after the witness judged that it was she who had solicited Yusuf against himself? Then the Ruler was vexed by the affair and said:

﴿Yusuf, turn away from this. And you, [woman], ask forgiveness for your sin; surely you were of the sinners.(29)﴾ [Yusuf]

The aim of the Ruler was to protect his standing from gossip and talk.

When the witness questioned the women, what did they answer?

The Truth, glorified is He, says that the women said:

﴿We know no evil against him..(51)﴾ [Yusuf]

Allah turned away from him Satan, who always undertakes seduction, and who never enters into battle with Allah. Rather, he enters into conflict with the creatures of Allah, because the Truth, glorified is He, attributes to him:

﴿He said: "By Your might, I shall surely mislead them all, (82) except Your chosen servants among them."(83)﴾ [Sad]

So Satan himself acknowledges that whoever Allah chooses for Himself from among His servants, he, as a devil, is unable to lead astray, and does not dare to approach him.

The witness from the wife of the Ruler's family, whom the Ruler summoned to learn the truth, said:

(And if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied, and he is of the truthful.(27)) [Yusuf]

After all this evidence, no one has the right to ask: Did Yusuf desire the wife of the Ruler, or did he not desire her?

In the verse about which we are reflecting, the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord..(24)﴾ [Yusuf]

*Al-burhan* (the proof) is the argument for a ruling. The Truth, glorified is He, is the One who says:

﴿We never punish until We have sent a messenger.(15)﴾ [Al-Isra']

And in another verse the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people may have no argument against Allah after the messengers..(165)﴾ [An-Nisa']

That is: it is necessary that the Truth send a messenger to people, supported by a miracle that makes them believe the path they follow, so that they may live their lives in faithful harmony, and so that Allah does not punish them in the Hereafter.

The Truth, glorified is He, concludes the verse by saying:

﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality; surely he was of Our sincere servants.(24)﴾ [Yusuf]

*Al-fahsha'* (immorality) is adultery and the act itself; *al-su'* (evil) is the notion of the *hamm*. Some moderate scholars said: after she solicited him and moved, in fact, to the stage of frenzied passion, at the moment he preceded her to the door, she considered killing him, and he tried to defend himself and to kill her. Had he killed her, he would have been punished as a killer.(17)

So the Truth turned away from him the thought of killing, and by this He meant here His saying "*al-su'*" (evil). But I am reassured that *al-su'* is the notion of the *hamm*, which is the preliminary to the act.

The Truth, glorified is He, affirms that Yusuf, peace be upon him, is one of His servants who are sincere. In this there is a refutation of Satan, because Satan said:

﴿except Your chosen servants among them (83)﴾ [Sad]

And the Truth's statement here:

﴿Surely he was of Our sincere servants.(24)﴾ [Yusuf]

confirms Satan's acknowledgment that he will not approach the sincere servants of Allah. There are two kinds of "sincere" (*mukhlasin*): the *mukhlis* and the *mukhlas*. The *mukhlis* is one who strove and thereby gained Allah's obedience; the *mukhlas* is one whom Allah purified and chose for Himself, having first struggled.(18)

There are people who reach Allah's honor through obedience to Allah, and there are people whom Allah honors so that they obey Allah. (And to Allah belongs the highest similitude; He is exalted above every comparison.) For example, someone may come to your door asking for a share of Allah's bounty upon you, and you deem him weak and honor him. Another time you may walk in the street and call someone to give him some of Allah's bounty upon you. That is: there are those who ask and you grant them, and there are those whom you yourself seek out to give to.

After the discussion of the solicitation, with its gentleness and its back-and-forth, the Truth, glorified is He, moves us to what happened in terms of movement. He, exalted is He, says:

﴿And they raced to the door, and she tore his shirt from the back, and they met her husband at the door. She said: "What is the penalty for one who intended evil against your wife, except imprisonment or a painful punishment?"(25)﴾

1 - On the authority of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever resolves on a good deed but does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him; and whoever resolves on a good deed and does it, ten to seven hundred times its reward is recorded for him. And whoever resolves on an evil deed but does not do it, nothing is recorded; and if he does it, it is recorded against him." Related by Muslim in his Sahih, Kitab al-Iman, hadith 206.

2 - *Al-'anin*: the one who does not come to women and does not desire them. One says *'anna* and *'anin*. A man is said to be *'unna* (impotent) toward his wife if the judge rules so, or if he is prevented from her by sorcery. A woman who is *'anina* likewise does not desire men nor seek them. He is called *'anin* because his member turns toward the woman's private part from his right or left and so does not intend it. [Lisan al-'Arab, root '-n-n]

3 - *Baghtahu baghtan wa baghtatan*: he surprised him unawares and heedlessly. The Almighty said: ﴿So We seized them suddenly, while they perceived not.(95)﴾ [Al-A'raf]. *Al-mubagh'ata* is surprise; *al-bagh* and *al-baghta* are sudden occurrence, when a thing comes upon you unexpectedly. [Lisan al-'Arab, root b-gh-t]

4 - In a hadith: "When a man sits between the four limbs of a woman, the ghusl becomes obligatory for him." Her four limbs are her two hands and two feet; it is also said her two feet and the two lips of her private part, a euphemism for the insertion of the glans into her private part. [Lisan al-'Arab, root sh-'-b]

5 - Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He saw the image of Ya'qub on the walls, biting on his finger and threatening him, so he calmed down, and his desire went out through his fingertips. [Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir 4/3492]

6 - *Rajul fahil*: a man of *fahl* (virility), and he is truly of full virility; not castrated, but fertile. [Lisan al-'Arab, root f-h-l]

7 - *Tadafara al-qawm 'ala fulan* and *tazaharu 'alayhi* and *tazahru* have one meaning: they cooperated and gathered against him. *Ta'allabu* and *tasabaru* are similar. Ibn Sayyida said: *tadafara al-qawm 'ala al-amr* means they backed one another and cooperated in it. [Lisan al-'Arab, root d-f-r]

8 - *Ista'sama*: he sought protection for himself and held to it. The Almighty said: ﴿And she certainly solicited him against himself, but he held firm..(32)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning he refrained, holding to his protection and the chastity of his soul and guarding it from evil. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/24]

9 - *Hasahsa al-haqq*: the truth became clear and manifest after being hidden. The Almighty said: ﴿The wife of the Ruler said: "Now the truth has come to light..(51)"﴾ [Yusuf]. Ibn Manzur said in Lisan al-'Arab: "*al-hasahasa* is the manifestation of the truth after its concealment." [root h-s-s]

10 - Scholars have many opinions on the speaker of this statement, which the commentators mention. Among them: it is Yusuf; and among them: it is the wife of the Ruler. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir [2/481]: "This view is the most famous, most appropriate and most suited to the context of the story and the meanings of the speech. Al-Mawardi related it in his tafsir, and Imam Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, undertook to defend it and devoted a separate work to it."

11 - *Da'aba 'ala al-amr*: he became accustomed to it. *Al-da'b* and *al-da'b* mean custom and habit. The Almighty said: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah..(31)﴾ [Ghafir], meaning their habit and way. He said: ﴿He said: "You shall sow for seven years, as usual..(47)"﴾ [Yusuf], meaning persistently and diligently. He said: ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant..(33)﴾ [Ibrahim], meaning continuously moving without cessation, likened to the diligent human being. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/219]

12 - *Aghwahu*: he misled him and brought him into error and straying. The Almighty said: ﴿We led them astray as We ourselves went astray..(63)﴾ [Al-Qasas], meaning we misled them as we were misled. *Ghawa yaghwa ghayyan wa ghawaya*: he plunged into ignorance, the opposite of rectitude. The Almighty said: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become distinct from error..(256)﴾ [Al-Baqara]. *Ghawiya* means he failed and went astray, because he plunged into ignorance. *Al-ghawi* is the active participle; the Almighty said: ﴿And Hell will be brought forth for those who go astray (91)﴾ [Al-Shu'ara'], meaning the misguided who plunge into the works of ignorance. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/64]

13 - *Qadda al-thawb*: he tore the garment. The Almighty said: ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind..(25)﴾ [Yusuf]. *Al-qadda* is the torn piece of cloth, and also a group differing in opinion within a community, as if it had been torn and cut off from it. The Almighty said: ﴿We are of diverse ways (qidadan)(11)﴾ [Al-Jinn], meaning groups differing in opinion, plural of *qidda*. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/102]

14 - *Al-dubur*: the rear of anything, its end, its back, opposite of *al-qubul* (front). The Almighty said: ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind..(25)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning from behind. A warrior who turns his back (*dubur*) signifies his flight. The Almighty said: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs (45)﴾ [Al-Qamar], meaning they will flee. Its plural is *adbar*. The Almighty said: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped (111)﴾ [Al 'Imran], meaning they will flee from you in defeat. His saying: ﴿And during the night glorify Him, and after the prostrations (40)﴾ [Qaf] means after each prostration or after each prayer. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/220]

15 - *Al-sarf*: turning a thing from one state to another. *Sarf al-nuqud* is changing or spending money. *Sarf al-sajin* is releasing the prisoner. *Sarf al-qulub* is turning hearts from guidance to error. The Almighty said: ﴿God has turned their hearts away (127)﴾ [Al-Tawba]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/374]

16 - *Al-si'ar*: intense hunger. One says: "the man was *mas'ur*" when his hunger and thirst intensified. *Al-sa'r* is desire together with hunger; *al-sa'r* is also madness; *si'ar al-'atash* is its burning. *Al-sa'ir* and *al-sa'ura* are fire, and it is said: its flame. *Al-si'ar* and *al-sa'r* are its heat. [Lisan al-'Arab, root s-'-r]

17 - Al-Qurtubi mentions in his tafsir that among the interpretations of Yusuf's *hamm* toward the wife of the Ruler is that he resolved to strike her and push her away from himself, and the proof (*burhan*) was that he held back from striking her, for had he struck her, it would have seemed that he intended her for the forbidden, so she resisted and struck him. [See Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3488]

18 - *Akhlasahu Allah*: Allah made him pure, clean and purified. The passive participle is *mukhlas* with a fatha on the lam. The Almighty said: ﴿Surely he was of Our sincere servants (24)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning the chosen, pious, purified ones. *Akhlasa dinahu lillah*: he purified his religion for Allah and cleansed it of the impurities of polytheism and ostentation. The Almighty said: ﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His (2)﴾ [Al-Zumar]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/202]

19 - *Alfa al-shay'*: he found it. The Almighty said: ﴿They found their fathers astray (69)﴾ [Al-Saffat], and He said: ﴿And they found her husband at the door (25)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning they both found him. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/197]

20 - *Sada qawmahu yasuduhum siyadatan*: he was honored above them and led them; he is *sa'id* and *sayyid*, its plural *sada*. ﴿And they found her husband at the door (25)﴾ [Yusuf]: *sayyidaha* means her husband. The Almighty said: ﴿And a leader and chaste (39)﴾ [Al 'Imran], meaning noble and a leader in religion and knowledge. He said: ﴿Surely we obeyed our leaders and our great ones (67)﴾ [Al-Ahzab], meaning our chiefs, kings and rulers. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/334]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 25:

We understand that both of them tried to reach the door before the other, and they raced each other in this race. We note that the Truth, glory be to Him, mentions here only one door, whereas the wife of the ruler had earlier locked more than one door.

But the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:

﴿And they found her master at the door.. (25)﴾ [Yusuf]

shows us that she caught up with Yusuf at the last door, for she had raced with Yusuf to all the doors until the last door, because she wanted to lock the door so as to block off his last escape route. This racing differs according to the one doing it: she wanted him for herself, while he wanted to flee the situation. Then she tore his shirt from behind.

This is evidence that he had reached the door before her, so she seized him by his shirt from behind, and the shirt was torn in her hand. The witness, who was from her family(1), examined that matter in order to deduce from the events the truth of what had happened.

And His saying, exalted be He:

﴿And they found her master at the door.. (25)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: the surprise befell them both, namely the appearance of the ruler of Egypt before them. The scene became threefold: the wife of the ruler, Yusuf, and her husband.

Here the woman cast the accusation upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, in the form of a self-justifying question, to escape the responsibility of the solicitation, by casting the charges upon Yusuf.

﴿She said: What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your family, except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment?(25)﴾

Then she specified the punishment.

The Truth, glory be to Him, then brings the words of Yusuf, peace be upon him:

﴿He said: It was she who sought to seduce me from myself. And a witness from her own family testified: If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken truly and he is among the liars. (26) And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied and he is among the truthful.(27)﴾

1 - This is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And a witness from her family testified: If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has spoken truly and he is among the liars. And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she has lied and he is among the truthful (26-27)﴾ [Yusuf].
2 - Shahida (شهد): indicated by a statement or an action. Exalted is He who said: ﴿And a witness from her family testified (26)﴾ [Yusuf] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/358]. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3494]: "A witness from her family testified, that is, a judge from her family gave a ruling, because it was a ruling from him and not a testimony."
3 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3494, 3495]: "Scholars differed concerning this witness, giving several opinions. Among them: that he was an infant in the cradle who spoke. Al-Suhayli said: this is the sound view, because of the hadith transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this subject, which says: 'None spoke in the cradle except three,' and he mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. Among them also: that he was a wise man of sound intellect whom the minister used to consult on his affairs, and he was one of the woman's kinsmen." Adapted.
4 - Qadda al-thawb (قد الثوب): he split it. Exalted is He who said: ﴿And she tore his shirt from behind (25)﴾ [Yusuf]. The qidda (قدة) is the piece torn off from a garment; and a group divided in opinion, together with the whole community, is as if it were torn and cut from it. Exalted is He who said: ﴿We were of divergent ways (11)﴾ [al-Jinn], that is, groups differing in opinion, plural of qidda. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/102].

Here the Chieftain of Egypt found himself between two conflicting statements: her statement accusing Joseph, and his statement accusing her. He had to bring someone who would separate the two accounts, and this person needed precision in receiving and understanding events.

The Exalted continues: ﴿She said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself." And a witness from her own household testified: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is one of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is one of the truthful."﴾ (12:26-27)

The word "witness" (shāhid) appears in the Qur'an with several meanings.

Sometimes it means "to be present" (ḥaḍara), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur]

Sometimes it means "to know" ('alima), as in His words: ﴿And we testify only to what we know...﴾ [Yusuf: 81]

And "shahida" comes to mean "to judge and decide" (ḥakama wa qaḍā), that is, to weigh one statement against another in order to deduce the truth in one of the two directions. In this case, the Qur'an has established that the witness is a relative on the side of the accused, namely the wife of the Chieftain. Had he been from the side of the one in whose favour the judgment went, his testimony would have been rejected.

Thus the situation became fourfold: the wife of the Chieftain, Joseph, the Chieftain of Egypt, and the witness. The verse conveys the witness's statement in half: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is one of the liars.﴾ [Yusuf]

Because the meaning (though the reality was not so) is that Joseph, peace be upon him, was the one who approached her; his garment hung down to the ground, so he tripped over it, and the shirt tore.

God continues the witness's statement: ﴿But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is one of the truthful.﴾ (12:27)

Notes:

1. That is: the punishment of the adulteress and the adulterer and the infliction of the penalty upon them, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress — flog each one of them with a hundred lashes. And let not pity for them overtake you in the religion of Allah, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾ [al-Nur] ...

2. The qamīṣ (shirt): that which encloses the body. It may be called shi'ār (undergarment), and what is over it is dithār (outer garment). Every garment may also be called a qamīṣ. The Exalted said: ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood...﴾ (12:18) [Yusuf]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/133].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 27:

I mean: if Joseph's shirt was torn from behind, then Joseph is truthful and the wife of the ruler (al-'Aziz) is lying.

We observe that the witness here gave this opinion before he saw the shirt; indeed, in his words he laid down the basis by which he would look at the matter, which is the framework of the evidence of proof.

This is what the next verse explains. He, glorified is He, says:

﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile, O women. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ (28)

1 - Kayd (guile, scheming): a verbal noun, and it is applied to the action or the means by which the schemer resorts to overcome his opponent. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿So settle your plan, then come forward in a row﴾ [Ta-Ha 64], meaning: gather the means by which you scheme. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/180].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 28:

﴿So when he saw that his shirt was torn from behind, he said: "Indeed, it is from your guile, [O women]. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾

And the saying of the Truthful, Glorified is He, about the witness who judged:

﴿So when he saw his shirt...﴾ [Yusuf]

This indicates that he set down the ruling before he saw the shirt, and established the principle first in the absence of seeing the shirt, then he saw it afterwards. Thus he made the absent consideration (al-hay'a al-ghA'iba) the judgment in the matter that was occupying them.

Therefore he followed his words with what condemns the wife of the 'Aziz:

﴿He said: "Indeed, it is from your guile. Indeed, your guile is great."﴾ [Yusuf]

Guile (kayd), as we know, is the scheming to bring about harm secretly, and it is carried out by one who does not possess the ability to confront openly, and the guile of women is great because their weakness is greater.

After that, the verses of the surah return to the situation of the 'Aziz of Egypt, and the Truthful, Glorified is He, says what came on the tongue of the husband:

﴿Yusuf, turn away from this, and [O wife], ask forgiveness for your sin. Indeed, you were of the wrongdoers.﴾

1 - Kayd (guile): a verbal noun, and it is applied to the action or means by which the schemer seeks to overcome his opponent. From it is His saying: ﴿So gather your plan, then come in ranks﴾ [Ta-Ha], i.e., gather the means by which you scheme. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/180].

2 - I'raD 'an al-shay' (to turn away from a thing): to turn and depart from it, not desiring it. The Exalted said: ﴿He turns away and withdraws to his side...﴾ [al-Isra'] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/16]. Al-Qurtubi said: "That is: do not mention it to anyone and conceal it." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3497].

3 - Khaṭa' and khaTA' (error, sin): the opposite of correctness; one says "khaTi'a yakhTa'u khaTa'an," meaning he sinned absolutely or deliberately committed a sin. The Exalted said: ﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for our sins; indeed, we were sinners."﴾ [Yusuf], i.e., sinful. [Editor's note: the surrounding text is left as given.]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 29:

With this statement from the husband, Allah, glorified is He, brings this four-sided situation to an end at this point, the point at which the Aziz of Egypt acknowledges that his wife has erred, and asks Yusuf to turn away from this matter and conceal it.

This shows us the policy of some people of standing toward their households, and it is a matter we witness in our own age as well. We find the man of standing who refuses to see his family in sin, and refuses even more to let others see his family in such a case, and tries to keep the matter hidden within himself. The humiliation of the situation he has already suffered is enough for him, and he does not want his adversaries or enemies to gloat over him.

Here there is a point we must pause at, namely the question of faith, which still permeates even those who deviate and those who conceal the deviants. The Aziz of Egypt says to Yusuf:

﴿Turn away from this..(29)﴾ [Yusuf]

And he says to his wife:

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin, for you were of the sinners (29)﴾ [Yusuf]

In this statement of his, he acknowledges that a sin has been committed; and he would not acknowledge this unless he had known of Allah a heavenly method, and he is in a position in which he cannot do otherwise than ask her to seek Allah's forgiveness.

Having been a four-sided scene, in which there were Yusuf, the wife of the Aziz, the Aziz himself, and then the witness who examined the case and judged it, Allah, glorified is He, now moves us to a wider scene, namely the circle of the society in which the case occurred.

This shows that the secrets of palaces have no secrecy, for the palaces have eyes that spy on them and tongues that speak of them, so that no one supposes that he can protect himself from wrongdoing, because there will be someone who will expose it, however great the capacity of its doer to conceal and hide it.

Some of the palace servants spied on it, until the story became on the tongues of the women.

The Qur'an relates the scene, saying:

﴿And women in the city said, "The wife of the Aziz is seeking to seduce her young man from himself. He has affected her with love; indeed, we see her in clear error." (30)﴾

1 - The origin of 'as (ʿass) is circling at night, and from it the hadith of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to patrol (yaʿassu) in Madinah, i.e., he would go around at night and watch over the people and examine those in need of discipline. The ʿassas is a noun derived from it like al-talab, and it may be a plural of ʿass as ḥāris is to ḥaras. [See Lisan al-Arab, root: ʿ-s-s.]
2 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3498): "It is said: the wife of the Aziz's cupbearer, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, and the wife of the keeper of his prison. It is also said: the wife of the chamberlain, from Ibn ʿAbbas and others."
3 - Shaghafa: it reached the shaghaf of his heart, meaning its covering, or it reached its inner part and core. Allah, the Exalted, said: {And he had affected her with love (30)} [Yusuf], i.e., it reached the shaghaf of her heart with a strong, piercing love like an arrow. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/350.]

The words "al-niswa" (النسوة) and "nisa'" (نساء) both denote a group, but the singular of each is not used in the language in the same way: the singular of "niswa" is "imra'a" (woman), and the singular of "nisa'" is also "imra'a."

What is remarkable is that the singular, the word "imra'a," has a dual form, "imra'atan" (two women), but in the plural form there is no "imra'at." Instead, the word "niswa" is a collective noun for groups of females, whose singular is "imra'a" and whose plural is "nisa'."

The women said:

﴿The wife of the Ruler is seeking to seduce her young man away from himself...﴾ [Yusuf: 30]

What they said was true; but they did not say it out of zeal for the truth, or zeal for virtue.

God, glorified is He, willed to clear them of this statement, so He exposed the hidden aim behind this saying in the following verse, when He said:

﴿So when she heard of their scheming, she sent for them and prepared for them a banquet, and gave each one of them a knife, and said, "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they were amazed at him and cut their hands, and said, "Perfect is God! This is not a human; this is none but a noble angel." She said, "That is the one about whom you blamed me..."﴾ [Yusuf: 31–32]

The Qur'an, the ruse of others is the concealment of one thing behind another, and it seems that the Truth (Allah) is alerting us that the women's words did not stem from anger for the sake of the truth, nor from zealotry for virtue. Rather, it was a desire to humiliate the wife of al-Aziz and to expose the misguidance in which she was living.

They also wanted something else: to bring the wife of al-Aziz down from her pride and to spread her disgrace. So they brought together two opposites, and in both the situation could only be carried out by someone of base method.

She is the wife of al-Aziz (2), that is, the most exalted woman in society, who had lowered herself from her pride as the wife of a man described as the mighty one who cannot be overcome, because the word "al-Aziz" is derived from sensory meanings.

It is said "al-ard al-azaz" (3), meaning the rocky land that is difficult to walk on, which no one can tread. From this meaning came the word "al-Aziz."

So how will the wife of al-Aziz be when she becomes a morsel (4) on people's lips, because she solicited her young servant to himself, and he was, in her view, of the lowest rank? That is a disgraceful and shameful scandal.

The women also said:

﴿She has been seized by love for him...(30)﴾

Love has stages. The first of these stages is "al-hawa" (passion), like the sprouting of plants (7), and it is said: "he saw something and was smitten by it."

This passion may end at the moment of sight. But if a person becomes attached to what he sees, he moves from passion to attachment (8).

After that comes "al-kalaf" (ardent devotion) (9), that is, the effort to reach what he seeks from this attachment. Then he moves to a stage of mutual meeting, which is "al-ishq" (passionate love) (10), in which feelings are exchanged and each party declares its devotion. For this reason they call them "lover and beloved."

Then he moves to a stage called "al-tadlih" (infatuation) (11), that is, he almost loses his mind. Then the body becomes emaciated, and it is said "tabbalat al-fu'ad" (his heart has been wasted), meaning the person has lost his way in the matter.

After that comes the stage of "al-hiyam" (wandering), that is, the person wanders aimlessly, without knowing any goal. If this is followed by a burning, it is called "al-jawa" (inner torment) (14).

These are the stages of love that pass through the heart (15). The heart, as we know, is the cone-shaped organ, and they call it the seat of the settled beliefs, which a person has examined and actually believed.

A person perceives things through his outward senses: he sees, smells, hears, tastes and touches. When he perceives some matters, he presents them to the intellect to weigh them, and he chooses what is most acceptable to him. After that, those accepted matters go to the heart to settle there as a conviction from which it does not deviate.

As for intellectual questions, other matters may come that shake them; therefore, the matters that have settled in the heart are called "aqa'id" (creeds), meaning something tied that never comes loose.

What reaches this level shows its effect in directing the course of life's conduct, and when the principle settles in a person's soul, all his movement is under the shade of this principle that he has believed.

Thus we know how a belief passes through several stages before it settles in the soul: perception (16) occurs first, then reasoning second, and after that the person believes the matter, and every conduct thereafter becomes in accordance with what he has believed.

As for the words: ﴿...has been seized by love for him...(30)﴾, they mean that feelings passed from her perception to her intellect to her heart. "Shaghaf" is the thin membrane that covers the heart; that is, love had fully taken possession of her heart.

﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error (30)﴾

This is a true statement, but it was intended for falsehood.

Therefore, after that, the Truth (Allah), exalted is He, says what exposes their intention:

﴿So when she heard of their scheming, she sent to them and prepared for them a banquet (mut'a'an) and gave each one of them a knife, and said: "Come out before them." And when they saw him, they were amazed by him (akbarnahu) and cut their hands, and said: "Allah forbid! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel." (31)﴾

And one might ask: how did the talk about what had happened between her and Yusuf pass to the women?

There must have been a stage between what happened in the palace, whose protagonists were four: al-Aziz, his wife, Yusuf, and the witness. Whoever carried the talk outside the palace must have had two connections: a connection with the palace, so he heard, saw and perceived, and then conveyed what he knew to someone connected to him outside the palace.

The scholars investigated the relationship of the women who gossiped about the matter, and the scholars said: they were five women: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the chamberlain, the wife of the keeper of the animals [that is, the groom of the horses], and the wife of the jailer.

These women lived inside their homes. So who conveyed the secrets of the palace to them?

It must be that one of their husbands wanted to entertain his household, so he related the story of the wife of al-Aziz with Yusuf, peace be upon him. Then his wife passed the news on to other women.

When the news reached the wife of al-Aziz, and how they were scheming against her, she sent to them:

﴿And she prepared for them a banquet, and gave each one of them a knife...(31)﴾

Al-muttaka' (the reclining place) is the thing on which a person leans so that he does not grow weary of the manner of his sitting. The intended meaning of the phrase is that the sitting would last a long time, and she had planned to reveal the effect that seeing Yusuf would have on them, so she gave each of them a knife, which suggests that there would be food to be eaten.

The Truth (Allah), exalted is He, continues:

﴿And she said: "Come out before them." So when they saw him, they were amazed by him...(31)﴾

It is said: "akbartu al-shay'" (I magnified the thing), as if you had imagined it before you saw it as it really is. Perhaps your imagination had drawn a beautiful image of it; but when you see the thing in reality, the seen reality surpasses what was imagined.

The example is that a person may tell you good things about another, but when you see this other person, you are surprised that he is better than what you had heard about him.

The poet says:

"The questioning of riders almost told me of Ja'far ibn Habib, the most truthful of values,
Until we met, and by Allah, my ear had not heard anything more pleasant than what my eye has seen."

And in contrast they say: "Hearing about al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him" (21), meaning: would that you had kept hearing about him without seeing him, because your seeing him would diminish the esteem of what you had heard.

When they had harmed the wife of al-Aziz by spreading news of her solicitation of him, they imagined for him a certain image of beauty; but when they saw him, his seen reality exceeded every image they had imagined of him, so they were dazzled.

The first stage of dazzlement is bewilderment, which makes the thing that has befallen you distract you from what you were doing; so if there was something in your hand, it may fall from you.

Each of them had cut her hand with the knife that the wife of al-Aziz had given her for cutting fruit or the food served to them.

The Truth (Allah), exalted is He, said about that:

﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed by him and cut (qat'ana) their hands...(31)﴾

Is there any depiction that more precisely shows the bewilderment they experienced than this statement (23)?

He, exalted is He, continues:

﴿And they said: "Allah forbid! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel." (31)﴾

The word "hashsha li-Llah" (Allah forbid!) is a declaration that Allah, exalted is He, is free from being unable to create this ideal beauty; or, they declared that the bearer of that image was free from committing an abomination or indecency with the wife of al-Aziz; or, Yusuf, peace be upon him, must have departed from a form more exalted than the human form they knew, so they said: "He must be a noble angel."

The image of an angel, as we know, is an imagined image, and a person judges imagined things according to what suits their image in his imagination, just as we imagine Satan in the most hideous form.

Ugliness itself differs from one person to another; what you see as ugly may not be seen as such by others, because standards of ugliness or beauty differ from one people to another.

In central Africa, the beautiful woman in the eyes of a man is the one with very thick lips, or the one with curly and wavy hair.

Modern civilization has confirmed that this is a kind of beauty to which a man is attracted in some cases, as evidenced by the fact that some women with very straight hair go to hairdressers and ask them to curl their hair.

Thus beauty is measured by tastes: one sees a beauty that others may not see as such, and another sees a beauty that others do not see either.

The Truth (Allah), exalted is He, casts the standards of beauty into the human soul according to the measure of the components of meeting and harmony.

For this reason, in the Egyptian countryside this proverb is said: "Every bean has its measurer."

A young man may approach a girl whom he wishes to marry; as soon as he sees her he is repelled, and another young man approaches her and falls in love with her and hastens to marry her. This means that the standards of the first differ from the standards of the second.

When the Truth (Allah), exalted is He, wills to bring two people together, no one is able to prevent acceptance from each party toward the other. This is a matter whose secrets we do not know, because He, exalted is He, is the One who writes acceptance; He manifests in a woman a beauty that may attract one man and not attract another, and the same matter occurs in the woman's disposition.

Thus, when the women saw Yusuf, peace be upon him, they said: ﴿This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel. (31)﴾

This means that Yusuf is the highest image of beauty, for which there is no equivalent among humans (25).

After that, the Truth (Allah), exalted is He, mentions what came on the tongue of the wife of al-Aziz in reply to them:

﴿She said: "That is the one about whom you blamed me (lamtunnani). I did solicit him for himself, but he refrained (fa-sta'sama). And if he does not do what I command him, he will surely be imprisoned and be among the humiliated." (32)﴾

1 - "Nakaa al-'aduww nakaa'": he struck the enemy and gained from him. "Naktu fi al-'aduww anka nakaa'" means I defeated him and overcame him. So "naka" in the sense of "yankī" (he wounds) [Lisan al-'Arab, root: n-k-a].

2 - The meanings of "al-'Aziz" revolve around the one who holds authority and power, in whose hand are the reins of rule, whom no one questions, rather he holds the authority of command and prohibition. [See: Lisan al-'Arab, root: '-z-z].

3 - Ibn Manzur said in [Lisan al-'Arab, root: '-z-z]: "Al-'azz and al-'azaz: a hard place with a quick flow of water. Ibn Shumayl said: al-'azaz is what is thick of the land, and it occurs only at its edges. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade urinating in al-'azaz, lest it splash back onto him."

4 - "Madagha yamdughu": he chewed; "madgh al-ta'am" is chewing food, and "al-madgha" is a piece of meat. "Amdagha al-tamr" means the dates became ready to be chewed, and "tamr dhu madgha" is firm, sturdy dates that are chewed much. "Madgh al-umur" means its trivial matters [Lisan al-'Arab, root: m-d-gh]. The intended meaning is to liken her to a piece of meat that people chew in their mouths.

5 - "Al-izra'": belittling something; "izdaraytuhu" means I despised him; "al-izdira'" is contempt, belittling and blame, and it is a derivation of "zarayt 'alayhi ziraya" when I criticized him. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: z-r-y].

6 - "Al-shayn": defect, which is the opposite of adornment. Al-Farra' said: "al-'ayn, al-shayn and al-shinar" mean defect, and "al-mashayin" are faults and ugliness [Lisan al-'Arab, root: sh-y-n].

7 - "Shaqqa al-nabat yashuqqu shuqqan": this is at the first moment the earth splits open to bring it out; "shaqqa naab al-sabi yashuqqu shuqqan" is at the first appearance of a child's tooth [Lisan al-'Arab, root: sh-q-q].

8 - "'Alaqa al-shay' 'alqan wa 'alaqa bihi 'alaqatan wa 'uluqan": he clung to it. "Al-'alaqa" is passion and love that is fixed to the heart. He loved her ('alqan, 'alaqatan), and he became attached to her ('alaqa bi-ha) and was smitten: he loved her. Al-Lihyani said: "al-'alaq" is passion that a man has for a woman [Lisan al-'Arab, root: '-l-q].

9 - "Al-kalaf": devotion to a thing together with preoccupation of the heart and hardship; "kalifa bi-l-shay' kalafan wa kulfatan" means he persisted in it; "kalifa bi-ha ashadda al-kalaf" means he loved her intensely; a "mukallaf" man is one who loves women [Lisan al-'Arab, root: k-l-f].

10 - "Al-'ishq": intensity of love. The lover is called 'ashiq because he withers from the intensity of passion, as the "'ushqa" withers when it is cut; "al-'ushqa" is a tree that turns green then crushes and turns yellow, according to al-Zajjaj [Lisan al-'Arab, root: '-sh-q].

11 - Ibn al-Qayyim said in Rawdat al-Muhibbin [p. 59]: "As for al-tadlih, in al-Sihah: al-tadlih is the loss of mind due to passion; one says: 'dalahahu al-hubb,' meaning it bewildered and astonished him."

12 - He said in Rawdat al-Muhibbin [p. 49]: "As for al-tabala, it is from 'tabalahu' when it consumed him. Al-Jawhari said: 'tabalahum al-dahr' and 'atbalahum' when time consumed them; and 'tabalahu al-hubb' and 'atbalahu' meaning it wore him out and corrupted him."

13 - "Al-hiyam": like madness; love has driven him mad ("hayyamahu al-hubb"). The noun is al-hiyam, and "rajul hayman" is a lover of intense longing. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-haym" is the verbal noun of "hama yahimu haymān" when he loved a woman; "al-hiyam" means lovers; "al-hiyum" is that one goes off on his face [Lisan al-'Arab, root: h-y-m].

14 - "Al-jawa": burning and intense longing from passion or grief [Lisan al-'Arab, root: j-w-y].

15 - Ibn al-Qayyim, in Rawdat al-Muhibbin [p. 25], mentioned about sixty names for love, each name having a station or degree within love.

16 - The intended meaning of the Imam agrees with what the psychologists have said when choosing things: there must be perception, then emotional response, then inclination, meaning choice.

17 - "Itakka yattaki'u": sat settled; its origin is "aw ittaka'a." He said: ﴿And reclining on couches therein (34)﴾ [al-Zukhruf] and he also said: ﴿Reclining therein on couches (31)﴾ [al-Kahf]. "Al-muttaka'": a place noun, as He said: ﴿And prepared for them a reclining place (31)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning a comfortable place where they sit settled and reclining. "Al-muttaka'" is also what a person leans on, a cushion or couch [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/353].

18 - "Akbara al-shay'": he counted it great, or its impression on him was so great that he saw it as great. He said: ﴿So when they saw him, they were amazed by him (31)﴾ [Yusuf] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/150].

19 - "Hashsha li-Llah": that is, innocence to Allah and refuge in Allah. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of "hasha" in Arabic speech is to remove a person from the description of the group by the quality of "hashan," and to remove him to one side, not including him in their number [Lisan al-'Arab, root: h-sh-w].

20 - See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi [4/3498], which he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others.

21 - This is a proverb struck for one whose report is better than his appearance. It is said of a man who has fame and reputation, so when you see him you despise his appearance. "Ma'ad" is a tribe or the name of a tribe. As for their saying in the proverb: "Hear of al-Mu'aydi, rather than seeing him," it is a lightened form contrary to the required analogy in this type [Lisan al-'Arab, root: m-'-d].

22 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir [4/3503]: "Mujahid said: 'We cut until we threw them down.' It was also said: 'We scratched them.' Ibn Abi Najih narrated: 'He cut them with the knife.' Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid means it was not a cut by which the hand is severed; it is a scratch and a notch, and this is known in the language, that when a person scratches the hand of his companion, one says he cut his hand."

23 - Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir [2/476]: "More than one has mentioned that she said to them, after she had given each of them a knife: 'Is there any desire among you to look at Yusuf?' They said: 'Yes.' So she sent to him, ordering him to come out to them. When they saw him, they began to cut their hands, then she ordered him to return, and he returned while they were still gashing their hands. When they felt the pain, they began to wail. Then she said: 'You did this from a single look; how then would I endure pain?'"

24 - Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: The women mentioned that the image of Yusuf was more beautiful than the image of human beings; rather, he was in the image of an angel. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly We created man in the best of forms (4)﴾ [al-Tin]. The reconciliation between the two verses is that their saying [Allah forbid!] is an exoneration of Yusuf from what the wife of al-Aziz accused him of, namely solicitation. Al-Qurtubi mentioned it in his tafsir [4/3505].

25 - On the authority of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yusuf and his mother were given half of beauty." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [3/286] and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak [2/570].

26 - "Lamahu yalumuhu lawman": he blamed him for an action that is not proper or fitting, so he is a blamer. "Talawama al-rajulan": each of the two blamed the other: ﴿So they turned to one another blaming (30)﴾ [al-Qalam]. "Alama" means he brought blame upon himself by doing what is not proper, so he is "mulim," deserving of blame. He said: ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy (142)﴾ [al-Saffat], meaning sinful and deserving of blame [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/208], adapted.

27 - "'Asamahu ya'simuhu": he prevented him and protected him. He said: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people (67)﴾ [al-Ma'idah], meaning He will guard and shield you. And His saying: ﴿I will take refuge in a mountain that will protect me from the water (43)﴾ [Hud], meaning will guard me. "I'tasama": he held firmly; He said: ﴿And hold fast, all of you, to the rope of Allah (103)﴾ [Al 'Imran], meaning hold to His religion. "Istasama": he sought protection for himself and held to it; He said: ﴿And she certainly sought him, but he refrained (32)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning he abstained, holding to his protection and the chastity of his soul and guarding it from evil [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/23, 24].

28 - Smallness (*al-sighar*) can be physical, in size, or figurative, in rank and standing, and it is the opposite of greatness (*al-kibar*). Something is *saghir* (small) either in its size or in its rank and standing.
