An example of the physical sense is His saying: ﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large﴾ [al-Baqarah]. An example of the figurative sense is His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are among the humiliated﴾ [al-A'raf] [*al-Qamus al-Qawim* 1/277].

It seems that she found the opportunity to establish an excuse for herself in her solicitation of him, for Yusuf, by their own admission, had reached a level of beauty not found in any human being.

Her saying: ﴿That is the one you blamed me for.. (32)﴾

It is composed of "dha", a demonstrative pointing to Yusuf, and "dhalikunna", an address to the women. The demonstrative differs from the address.

Here there is a stylistic point, for speech, whether it is uttered or written to be read, has multiple forms. Sometimes it is prose not bound by meter or rhyme(1); it may be rhymed prose (saj') (2) or free prose (mursal), and sometimes speech is poetry governed by meter and rhyme.

An example of rhymed prose is the saying of the Truthful, glorified is He:

﴿By the Mount (1), and a Book inscribed (2), on parchment unrolled (3), and the frequented House (4)﴾ [al-Tur]

This is rhymed prose without affectation. When you hear or read speech, your ear takes from it according to the loftiness of its style, but if you move from one style to another, your ear catches the difference between the two styles.

An example is found in the letter Ibn Zaydun (5) wrote, seeking the favour of Ibn Jahwar:

"This reproach has praiseworthy consequences, and this cloud is a shower followed by clearing. My master will not be troubled if its cause is slow or delayed, being not stingy in his affliction; the slowest buckets are the fullest when drawn, and the heaviest clouds move most gently. With today comes tomorrow, and for every term there is a Book. To him is praise for his seizing of the opportunity, and no blame upon him for his neglect.

If the deed that displeased was one, his deeds that delighted are thousands."

Thus you feel Ibn Zaydun's transition from prose to poetry. But when you read the Qur'an, you move from free prose to rhymed prose to poetic verse in the meter of the poetic bahr, so you can hardly distinguish in style between poetry and prose.

An example is found in the verse which is the subject of our reflections:

﴿That is the one you blamed me for.. (32)﴾

It is metered in the bahr al-basit, yet you do not feel that you have moved from prose to poetry.

Likewise the saying of the Truth:

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path (46)﴾ [al-Nur]

And also His saying:

﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful (49)﴾ [al-Hijr]

These verses come in places where what precedes them may be prose, which shows that the melody spoken by God, whether verse, poetry or prose, has no dissonance in it, and is almost one continuous flow.

This is only possible from the speech of the Truth, blessed and exalted, and you would not perceive this matter unless someone alerted you to the poetic meter in some verses.

As for human speech: if you read metered text and then move to unmetered prose, your ear senses this transition; and the same matter you feel when you read prose and then move to metered text, your ear will sense the transition.

﴿She said, "That is the one you blamed me for. I certainly solicited him, but he refrained.. (32)﴾ [Yusuf]

She said this with the boldness of one who has seen the effect of their seeing Yusuf, and declared that he "refrained", which means that he undertook hardship in restraining himself from the act. This statement establishes that Yusuf's manhood was not deficient, for he struggled against himself to suppress it from the deed.

The Truth, glorified is He, continues with what came on the tongue of the wife of the ruler:

﴿And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned and will be among the debased (32)﴾ [Yusuf]

She said this as though she were the one issuing the judgments, while the women listening to her were those who had magnified Yusuf at the moment they saw him. She announces to them that if he does not obey her in what she wants, she will imprison him and diminish his standing to humiliate and disgrace him.

As for the women who heard her, each of them longed that the wife of the ruler would expel Yusuf from the palace so that each of them could be alone with him.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, relates to us the saying of Yusuf, peace be upon him:

﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn away from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant."(33)﴾

(1) Qafiyah (rhyme) in poetry: it is called qafiyah because it follows (taqfu) the verse. al-Akhfash said: the qafiyah is the last word in the verse.

(2) Saj': rhymed speech. Saja'a yasja'u saj'an, tasjee'an: he spoke words with endings like the endings of poetry, without meter; its speaker is sajjaa', and it comes from evenness, straightness and resemblance, as if each word resembles its companion. Ibn Jinni said: it was called saj' because of the similarity of its endings and the harmony of its closing rhymes. [Lisan al-Arab, root: s-j-'].

(3) al-Tur: the mountain in Sinai where Musa, peace be upon him, descended after leaving Egypt with his people. God said: {And We raised above them the mount (154)} [al-Nisa'], and it is also called {Tur Sayna'} [al-Mu'minun 20] and {Tur Sinin} [al-Tin 2]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/408].

(4) al-Raqq: thin leather on which one writes, and it was applied to the white sheet on which one writes. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/272].

(5) He is Ahmad ibn Abd Allah ibn Zaydun al-Makhzumi al-Andalusi, Abu al-Walid, a vizier, writer and poet from Cordoba, born in 394 AH. He attached himself to Ibn Jahwar [one of the Party Kings in al-Andalus], and was the envoy between him and al-Andalus. He died in Seville in [463 AH] in the days of al-Mu'tadid's son al-Mu'tamid 'ala Allah. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 1/158], adapted.

(6) al-Azhari said: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim and al-Kisa'i recited "ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim" with ṣād, while Ya'qub recited it with sīn. He said: the original of its ṣād was sīn, changed with the ṭā' into ṣād because their articulation points are close. al-Jawhari said: al-sirat and al-sirat both mean the path. [Lisan al-Arab, root: s-r-ṭ].

(7) Nashaza al-shay' yanshuzu nushuzan: it rose; a nashiz hill is a raised hill; nashaza in his seat yanshuzu: he rose slightly; anshaza al-shay': he lifted it from its place. [Lisan al-Arab, root: n-sh-z].

(8) al-Sarf: turning a thing from one state to another; sarafa al-sajin: he released the prisoner; sarf al-qulub: turning hearts from guidance to misguidance: {Allah has turned their hearts (127)} [al-Tawba], i.e., turned them. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/374].

(9) Sabā, yasbū: he inclined and loved; God said: {And unless You turn away from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant (33)} [Yusuf], i.e., I would incline toward them and do what would entice me. Sabā ila al-lahw: he yearned for and longed for it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/368].

(10) al-Jahl: recklessness, foolishness, and transgression without right; al-jahl is the opposite of knowledge, which is the absence of knowledge; the active participle is "jahil", and the intensive form "jahul"; the meaning of ignorance is determined by what fits the context. God said: {But most of them are ignorant (111)} [al-An'am]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/135], adapted.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 33:

One might ask: why did Yusuf's statement come in the plural, when he said, ﴿The prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me﴾ (12:33)?

This is despite the fact that it was the wife of the ʿAzīz who said, ﴿And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned﴾ (12:32).

We say: Yusuf (peace be upon him) must have seen from them gestures or winks that suggested to him that he should not expose himself to that predicament which would lead him to prison. Therefore Yusuf (peace be upon him) included, in his statement in the singular, "the wife of the ʿAzīz," within the plural of the women whom the wife of the ʿAzīz had gathered, and who were the ones who had asked him, by a wink or a sign, to extricate himself from this situation.

Perhaps more than one of them had looked at him in an attempt to win him over, and the eyes, emotions and features of the face have a more eloquent expression than the expression of words. Their eye-signals may have indicated to Yusuf the desire that each one of them sought. In such gatherings, the language of the eyes plays an important role.

Here is Abu Dalama the poet, who sat in the assembly of the caliph. Abu Dalama was известный for a great capacity for satire (hijāʾ)(2). The caliph wanted to tease him, so he said to him: "I insist that you satirize one of us."

Eyes went around the assembly, and everyone present gestured to him discreetly that he would be granted a generous reward if Abu Dalama refrained from satirizing them. And since Abu Dalama was known for greed, and feared that he might lose any of the gifts, he therefore composed satire against himself, and said:

Ask, on your behalf, Abu Dalama, for he is not among the noble, nor is he of nobility.

When he wears the turban he becomes an ape, and a swine when he takes off the turban.

Thus he got out of the Amir's oath, and gained the gifts that those present in the assembly had promised him.

Here, in the verse we are contemplating, we find that Yusuf (peace be upon him) grouped the wife of the ʿAzīz together with the women; so he said:

﴿My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me﴾ (12:33)

That is: the prison is better in his estimation than agreeing with the wife of the ʿAzīz to commit indecency, or agreeing with the women to their invitation that he free himself from prison by yielding to them, and then go out to them from the palace afterwards.

But Yusuf (peace be upon him) called upon his Lord, saying:

﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ (12:33)

One might ask: why did Yusuf not say "O my God," while he knows that the basis of obligation in divinity is "do" and "do not"?

We say: Yusuf wished to call upon his Lord by the name of Lordship (al-rubūbiyya), acknowledging His bounty, since He, may He be exalted, is the One who raised and nurtured him; and here he calls upon Him by the name of Lordship, that He not abandon him in this situation.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) knows that he is human; and if God did not turn away their plot from him, he would have responded to their seduction, and would have become one of the ignorant who do not heed the consequences of matters.

Although the prison is a loathsome thing, he preferred it over disobedience to his Creator; and because he took refuge with the First Nurturer, so that the response would come from Him, may He be exalted.

The Truth says: ﴿So his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plot. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ (12:34)

1 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir [4/3507] "that each one of them asked to be alone with him to counsel him concerning the wife of the ʿAzīz, the purpose being to blame him [rebuke him] regarding her right, and to order him to assist her, so that perhaps he would respond. Each one of them then became alone with him separately, saying: 'O Yusuf, fulfil my need, for I am better for you than your mistress,' each one calling him to herself and soliciting him. He said: 'O Lord, there was one, and they became a group.'"
2 - Hajāʾ (هجاء), from hajā yahjū: to abuse someone in verse; it is the opposite of praise. Al-Layth said: it is the disparagement in poetry [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: h-j-w].
3 - Al-Jazl: great, abundant; ajzaltu lahu al-ʿaṭāʾ means I increased the gift for him; ʿaṭāʾ jazl and jazīl means abundant; and he was granted a great gift when it became large [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: j-z-l].

And thus Allah showed favour to him, the One who created him, took charge of his upbringing and protection, and turned away from him their scheming, which was embodied in their urging him to yield to what the wife of the ruler (al-'Aziz) was calling him to, and then their seduction of him by allusion rather than by explicit statement.

That seduction was embodied in the words of the King after that:

﴿He said, "What was your business when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?" They said, "Allah forbid! We know of no evil in him."﴾ [Yusuf: 51]

Thus Allah saved him from the plotting of the women. He—may He be exalted—has perfect hearing and perfect knowledge; nothing is hidden from Him, and He responds to those who are sincere in supplication.

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him for a time.﴾ [Yusuf: 35]

1 - Al-khatb (ألخطب): the matter in which address and questioning take place. The Most High said: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ [al-Hijr: 57], meaning: what is your concern? [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/198]. In Lisan (al-'Arab) it says: "al-khatb: a matter or affair, whether small or great; from it the saying 'jall al-khatb', meaning the matter or affair has become grave."

2 - Ibn 'Abbas said: "The shirt is among the signs, and the testimony of the witness is among the signs, and the cutting of the hands is among the signs, and the women's magnifying of him is among the signs." Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir [4/3508].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 35:

After the signs testifying to the innocence of Yusuf (peace be upon him) had become apparent before the Ruler (al-'Aziz) and his counsellors, and the deviation of the Ruler's wife and her persistence in trying to bring Yusuf into the shameful act with her had been revealed to them, without shame or fear of scandal.

Therefore the Ruler and his counsellors saw that Yusuf (peace be upon him) should be placed in prison, so that this would create a separation between him and her, until the uproar of the scandal subsided, and so that it would appear to the people that he was responsible for all this evil that had appeared in the Ruler's house.

Also, the phrase ﴿ليسجننه..﴾ (﴿they should imprison him...﴾ [Yusuf, 35]) contains a kind of preservation of the love that the Ruler holds for Yusuf. He did not order his killing or his banishment far away; rather, he kept him away from the wife who insisted on betrayal, and away from the society that chews over those events.

Prison, as we know, is the confinement of the prisoner to restrict his movement in existence. It is a measure that a judge or ruler takes as a punishment intended to humiliate the prisoner, or to protect society from his evil.

We know that a person does not dare to defy rulings except when he thinks or knows that he has power and dominance. So the judge or ruler announces the end of that dominance and power, orders his entry into prison, and a jailer guards the restriction of his freedom; he may be exposed to beating or humiliation.

This is the prison known in ancient and modern times, where the prisoner is isolated from society, though some members of society may show him compassion, and some of his relatives may visit him, bringing food and necessities.

However, there is a religious prison established by the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), when the community isolated the believer from the prisoner. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) ordered that none of the three(1) who stayed behind from going out with him to fight be spoken to, for baseless excuses. This isolation even extended until it became isolation from their families, until he (peace be upon him) ordered the end of this isolation after its purpose had been achieved.

And what was Yusuf's state in prison?

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men(2). One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine(3)." And the other said: "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good(4)."﴾ (36)

1 - These three are: Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' al-'Amiri, and Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi. Muslim in his Sahih [2769] recorded the hadith of Ka'b, which contains their full story of staying behind from the military expedition with the Messenger of Allah in the Battle of Tabuk.
2 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3511]: "He said 'fityan' (two young men) because they were slaves, and a slave is called a fata (young man), whether small or great, as mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Qushayri said: Perhaps 'fata' was a name for a slave in their usage, and for this reason He said: ﴿his fata seeks to seduce him from himself (30)﴾ [Yusuf]."
3 - Khamr: the intoxicating drink that covers the intellect and removes it. It is either derived from khamartu al-shay' (I covered the thing), meaning I concealed it, because it conceals the intellect, or from khammartu al-'ajin (I put leaven in the dough), when the leaven is put into it and reacts with it until it ferments. In its making, leaven is put into the juice and left until it ferments, and then the khamr is taken from it. The Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin...(219)﴾ [al-Baqarah]. His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine...(36)﴾ [Yusuf], i.e., I press grapes so that it becomes khamr, is a metonymy (majaz mursal) whose relation is what it will become. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 1/209], adapted.
4 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3512]: "His goodness was that he used to visit the sick and treat them, and console the grieving. Al-Dahhak said: When a man among the prisoners fell ill, he would attend to him; when he was in hardship, he would relieve him; when he was in need, he would gather for him and request on his behalf."

The companionship into which two of the young men entered with him in prison is a companionship of person (ma'iyyah dhat). It has been said that they were the baker and the cupbearer. It has also been said that the reason for their entering was the desire of the courtiers of the ruler of Egypt (al-'Aziz) to create confusion over a great scandal, namely the solicitation of Yusuf by the wife of al-'Aziz, and Yusuf's refusal of that.

The confusion was the spreading of news of a plot against al-'Aziz, and that the cupbearer and the baker had been caught attempting to put poison into al-'Aziz's drink.(1)

After a period of the two men's life with Yusuf inside the prison, and after daily association with him, Yusuf's conduct as one of the doers of good (al-muhsinin) became clear to them.

It happened that each of them saw a dream, so they resolved to ask him to interpret these two dreams, since the prisoner is often full of anxious thoughts and is not secure about his tomorrow. For this reason they turned to him in the matter that concerned them:

﴿One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine." And the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation. Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good."﴾ [Yusuf 36]

From the context of the speech we know that they were two dreams: one of them saw in his sleep that he was pressing wine, and the second saw that he was carrying bread on his head, of which birds were eating. Both of them, or each of them separately, turned to him asking for the interpretation of the two dreams, or they asked for the account of the interpretation of this matter which they had seen.

The basis of their turning to him is their saying:

﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the doers of good.﴾ [Yusuf 36]

This shows that goodness (ihsan) is a matter known to all mankind, even to people of deviant souls. No one can judge another to be a doer of good unless his deeds agree with the standards of goodness in the mind of the one who issues this judgment.

Every soul knows evil, and every soul knows goodness. But people look at goodness and evil through the subjectivity of their own selves. Yet if they looked at the totality of the movement of those who move in the universe, and looked at any matter that relates to others as it relates to them, they would know that goodness is a common measure shared by all.

We find, for example, that the thief is not troubled that someone should steal, but he is troubled if someone steals from him. Thus we see goodness stirring within him when evil is directed at him, and then he recognizes the station of goodness. But when he practices theft, and evil is directed by him at others, he neglects the station of goodness.

So, if you want to know the station of goodness in the standards of virtues and morals, then understand the matter in relation to yourself, both positively and negatively.

The example I always give is this: before you cast your eyes on the women who are unlawful to others (mahārim ghayrik), and you consider that this is not evil, here you must know its measure of good if you transfer the matter to the reverse case, when the eyes of others turn toward your own unlawful women.

Here you will find the scale of your judgment of matters balanced. If you want the scale to be balanced in every act, then look at the act as it comes from you toward others, look at the act as it comes from others toward you, and look at which of the two weighs more in your soul, and you will find the balance of your judgment disciplined.

And I always say: when the Truth, glory be to Him, forbade you to steal from others, He did not restrict your freedom; rather, He restricted the freedom of millions so that they would not steal from you, and this is a gain for you.

So, the one who knows the station of goodness does not attribute to others the act that proceeds from him, nor the act that proceeds from others toward him; rather he looks at both together. What he finds ugly coming from others toward him, let him find ugly coming from him toward others.

The two prisoners judged Yusuf to be one of the doers of good, and Yusuf, peace be upon him, knew from their judgment of him that the standards of goodness were present with them. Therefore he looked at the matter for which they had come to him, and made use of this issue, not to fulfill their need from him, but to fulfill his need from them.

For he saw in them a trace of belief in goodness and belief in the doers of good. So why would he not seize the opportunity and take his need from them before giving them their need from him?

It is as if he said to them: What have you seen of my goodness? Have you seen the goodness of my treatment of you? Or has each of you seen the precision of my choosing of good speech? You may not know that I have, by the grace of God, more than this, and that is what the Truth, glory be to Him, says afterward in the following verse:

﴿He said, "No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is from what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion (millah) of a people who do not believe in God, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter."﴾ [Yusuf 37]

1 - Among what has been mentioned in this regard is what has been said: the king became angry with his baker and his cupbearer. That is because the king had been deceived about them and became displeased with them, so they sent to his baker and his cupbearer that they should poison him together. The baker agreed, but the cupbearer refused. The cupbearer went and informed the king of that, so the king ordered that they be imprisoned, and they became familiar with Yusuf. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3511], abridged.

2 - Millah: religion, whether true or false. From the true usage is the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion (millah) of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself...﴾ [al-Baqarah 130], which is the true religion; and from the false usage is His saying: ﴿Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion (millatihim)...﴾ [al-Kahf 20], which is a false religion. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/236].

And with that he made clear to them that they could only see the outward appearance of his conduct, but there are hidden matters behind it. It is as if he were developing in them a sense of his station, his goodness, and his ability to inform them of the qualities and kind of any food they are given before it arrives.

This is not a particular privilege of Yusuf, nor something from his own resources, but rather knowledge received from God, which God teaches to His virtuous servants; so God reveals to them some of the secrets.

The two prisoners could likewise become like him if they perfect their faith in God. Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, continues:

﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me. Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in God and who, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ [Yusuf: 37]

It is as if, by this, he guides them to the path that makes them among the virtuous, to whom God gives some of the gifts of goodness, so that they know things that are hidden from others.

This shows us that when a believer sees in a person a sign (mukhayyilah) of goodness, he should nurture that sign in him so that he attains greater good. In this way he does not reserve the privilege for himself, so that he does not cut off the good example, and so that the servants may aspire to God's manifestations upon them and His illuminations.

Accordingly, Yusuf, peace be upon him, made clear to the two prisoners that he had left the religion of a people who do not believe in God in the manner befitting belief in Him, glory be to Him, and who do not believe in the Resurrection and the Reckoning, with reward of Paradise or punishment of the Fire.

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues with what came on the tongue of Yusuf, peace be upon him:

﴿And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq, and Ya'qub. It was not for us to associate anything with God. That is from the bounty of God upon us and upon mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾

1 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir [4/3512]: His saying: ﴿You will not be brought food as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation (37)﴾ [Yusuf] means: no food will come to you tomorrow from your dwelling except that I will inform you of its interpretation, so that you know that I know the interpretation of your dreams. This was from the knowledge of the unseen, specific to Yusuf, and he showed that God singled him out with this knowledge because he left the religion of a people who do not believe in God, meaning the religion of the king.

2 - "Innahu lamukhayyil lil-khayr" means: he is fit for goodness. One says "akhala fihi khalan min al-khayr" and "takhayyala 'alayhi takhayyulan," both meaning: he chose him and discerned goodness in him. "Takhawwaltu fihi khalan min al-khayr" and "akhaltu fihi khalan min al-khayr" mean: I saw his mukhayyilah (sign of promise). "Takhayyala al-shay' lahu" means it resembled him; "takhayyala lahu annahu kadha" means it appeared to him that it was so; one says "takhayyaltuhu fa-takhayyal li," like "tasawwartuhu fa-tasawwar," "tabayyantuhu fa-tabayyan," and "tahaqqaqtuhu fa-tahaqqaq." [Lisan al-Arab, root: kh-y-l]

3 - It is reported from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon them." Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [3116], Ahmad in his Musnad [2/332, 416], and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak [2/346].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 38:

Thereby Yusuf (peace be upon him) made clear that he had abandoned the creed (millah) of the people who do not worship Allah as He truly deserves to be worshipped, and who do not believe in the Last Day, and that he followed the creed of his forefathers Ibrahim, then Ishaq, then Ya'qub. They are the ones whom Allah sent to guide creation to monotheism (tawhid) and to belief in the Hereafter, with reward of Paradise and punishment of Hellfire.

This is from the grace of Allah in sending down the guiding method, and His grace, glory be to Him, has encompassed the forefathers of Yusuf with the honour of conveying His message on His behalf. For this reason, one who knows this must not associate anything with Allah, for associating partners with Allah means resorting to multiple gods.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Had there been in them any gods besides Allah, they would surely have been ruined. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ [al-Anbiya] 

Hence, if there were other gods besides Allah, glory be to Him, each god would have created something that the other god could not create, and the matter would have become a conflict between mutually repellent gods.

And from the grace of Allah (thus Yusuf, peace be upon him, made clear) that He sent down His method to the prophets, among them his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub, so that they might convey His method to His creation. They did not withhold this grace coming from Allah; rather, they conveyed it to the people.

﴿But most people are not grateful.﴾ [Yusuf]

Whenever you read or hear the words: ﴿but most people are not grateful﴾ [Yusuf, 38]

Know that the matter you are concerned with is, by the measures of reason and sound human nature, deserving of gratitude, and there is no gratitude except for a blessing.

Had people reflected, they would have thanked the prophets and messengers for the method they conveyed from Allah, because it guides them to the good management of this world and, beyond that, guides them to Paradise.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says, after that, what Yusuf continued to say to the two prisoners:

﴿O two companions of the prison, are many lords varied better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ (39)

1 - Rabb: is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He is the Lord of everything, that is, its owner, and He has lordship over all creation with no partner. He is the Lord of lords, and the Lord of everything: its owner and the one deserving it. The word rabb in the language is applied to the owner, the master, the manager, the nurturer, the companion, the guardian and the bestower of blessings. [Lisan al-Arab, root: r-b-b] with adaptation.

2 - Qahara, yaqharu, qahran: he overpowered him and humiliated him. The Exalted said: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾ [al-Duha], and al-Qahir is an active participle; the Exalted said: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am], meaning: the one who controls them. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/136] with adaptation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 39:

The word "ṣāḥib" (companion) means one who is constantly in attendance (mulāzim)[1]. What joins Yusuf and the two prisoners is the prison. We say: "So-and-so is a ṣāḥib al-dirāsa (companion of study)" or "ṣāḥib ḥajj (companion of pilgrimage)." The thing that links two or more people is either attributed to the place, or attributed to the circumstance that brought that group of companions together.

Yusuf posed the question:

﴿Are many scattered lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf 39]

When you pose a question through an opponent, you already know that he understands that scattered lords are not better than one God. It is as if Yusuf was certain that their answer could only be, "Rather, the worship of one God is better."

He would not have asked unless he knew that they would direct all the answers themselves, so they would find no answer except the one he intended.

They had worshipped multiple gods, and by the standards of things it should have been that those gods would spare you the need to turn to one who worships the One God.

So, in human powers we find that plurality enriches and magnifies the work, but in divinity we find that association (shirk) weakens the work.

For this reason the Sufi says: "Work for one face, and it will suffice you all faces."

Therefore Yusuf, peace be upon him, said to the two companions of the prison:

﴿Are many scattered lords better..﴾ [Yusuf 39]

If their dispersion were a dispersion of essences, they would be without a perfection for which they deserve worship. If their dispersion were a dispersion of repetition, this repetition would have no necessity. If their dispersion were a dispersion of specializations, this means that each of them has a point of strength and points of weakness; and this dispersion of theirs is a proof of deficiency.

For this reason the Truth, Exalted is He, showed mercy to us, the believers in Him, so that we worship one God, and He said:

﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners quarreling [mutashākisūn][2], and a man belonging wholly to one man. Are they equal in comparison? Praise be to Allah! But most of them do not know.﴾ [al-Zumar 29]

Yusuf, peace be upon him, tried to guide them to the worship of the One God, and after that said to them what the Truth, Glorified is He, had brought:

﴿You worship not besides Him except names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority. The decision is only for Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the correct religion [al-dīn al-qayyim][4], but most of mankind do not know.﴾ [Yusuf 40]

---

[1] al-Ṣāḥib: said of one whose companionship is frequent. ṣaḥiba, yaṣḥabu, and ṣāḥaba mean to live in company with someone; al-ṣāḥib is the companion. [Lisān al-ʿArab, root ṣ-ḥ-b]

[2] Shakasa: his character became bad and he was overcome by love of dispute; tashākasa al-qawm means the people quarreled and their disagreement intensified. Allah says: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners quarreling..(29)﴾ [al-Zumar]. That is the example of the polytheist slave who has many gods disputing over him. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 1/354].

[3] al-Silm and al-Salm: safety and absence of war, as in: ﴿Enter into peace completely (208)﴾ [al-Baqara]; in reconciliation, truce and submission: ﴿and offer you peace..(90)﴾ [al-Nisā']. They made peace with you, submitted to you and surrendered to you. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a man belonging wholly to one man..(29)﴾ [al-Zumar], i.e., a private possession of his, which no one disputes with him. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 1/324].

[4] al-Qayyim: the firm, straight one with no crookedness; or the one who sets things right and balances them, or who watches over and oversees them. From this is His saying: ﴿a straight religion..(161)﴾ [al-An'ām], i.e., upright, or one that rectifies the earlier religions. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 2/143].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 40:

We note that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had not yet spoken to the two prisoners about what they had asked of him, namely the interpretation of the two dreams. Had he spoken first about what was asked of him, the minds and attention of each of the two prisoners would have been diverted to the fulfilment of their needs from him, and they would not have turned afterward to what he was calling them to. And that to which he was calling them is the more lasting matter, the general affair that relates to every movement of life.

In this way Yusuf, peace be upon him, was giving preference to the two prisoners. He wished to draw their attention to the essential matter before speaking about the small particular they were asking about. He wished to correct the outlook of both of them toward the general method by which a person manages all the details and particulars of life. In this there is a preference (īthār) that is not self-serving.(1)

Here the Truth, glorified is He, said on the tongue of Yusuf, peace be upon him:

﴿What you worship besides Him are but names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.. (40)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: what you worship of many gods is merely the worship of names without meaning and without existence; names you inherited from your fathers or that you yourselves coined. You disbelieved by inventing names for gods that do not exist, just as your fathers disbelieved, a disbelief of forgetting the obligation or denying the obligation.

Names are normally assigned to indicate the named. When we pronounce a name, the image of the named comes to mind. That is why we name a child after his birth with a name that distinguishes him from his siblings, so that when the name is uttered it turns to the specific, individual person.

When one name is applied to several persons, the one who assigns the name must clarify what distinguishes each individual from the others.

An example from the Egyptian countryside: a father who looks for good omen in the name "Muhammad" names all his sons with this name, but he distinguishes between them by saying "Muhammad the elder," "Muhammad the middle," and "Muhammad the younger."

As for when a name is assigned to a named thing that does not exist, this is unacceptable or unreasonable. They assigned names to gods that do not exist, so there came to be names without anything named.

On the Day of Resurrection these people will come, to be asked at the moment of reckoning:

﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where are those you used to associate with Allah, besides Allah?" They will say, "They have departed from us," and [further], "We had not been calling upon anything before." Thus does Allah leave astray the disbelievers.(73-74)﴾ [Ghafir]

Thus these people acknowledge that there were no gods; rather, there were names without named things.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, says here:

﴿What you worship besides Him are but names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.. (40)﴾ [Yusuf]

It is as if Yusuf were asking: if you have a need that you seek from the heavens, would you ask a name that has no named thing?

Would a name without a named thing help you?

Yusuf, peace be upon him, knows that the worshipped one cannot be a name without a named thing. He knows that the true God has a name which He makes known to His messengers, and sends down with them a method that is summarized in "do" and "do not."

They have named names that have no named thing, and what does not exist cannot send down a method or answer one who is in need.

Therefore the Qur'an follows what came on the tongue of Yusuf, peace be upon him, in describing those names that are without named things, saying:

﴿What you worship besides Him are but names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.. (40)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: for which Allah has sent down no proof.

The noble verse continues what came on the tongue of Yusuf:

﴿Legislation is only for Allah. He has commanded that you worship none but Him.. (40)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: when I speak, and the speech is Yusuf's, I am only conveying a ruling from Allah, not from my own self, nor from my own authority, nor from my own desire; because it is He, glorified is He, who has commanded that you worship none but Him, meaning: do not obey any command or prohibition except what Allah has sent down in His method, which guides to truth and goodness.

The noble verse concludes:

﴿That is the correct religion, but most of the people do not know.. (40)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: this is the upright religion and no other, but most people do not know. The meaning is that the messengers have conveyed the method to them, but they did not put this knowledge to use in their deeds.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, began to interpret for them what they had asked.

The Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿O two companions of prison, as for one of you, he will give drink to his lord of wine; but as for the other, he will be crucified and birds will eat from his head. The matter has been decided about which you both inquire.(1) (41)﴾

1 - Ātharahu ʿalayhi: he preferred him, favoured him. Ātharto fulānan ʿalā nafsī (I preferred someone over myself) is from īthār (preference). It is said: he took it without self-interest (athara) and without self-interest (ithra) and without monopolising (istiʾthār), meaning he did not monopolise over others nor take the best [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: a-th-r].
2 - Istaftāhu: he asked him for a fatwa, asked his opinion on a matter and he gave him a fatwa, answered him. God the Exalted said: ﴿Fa-staftihim a-li-rabbika al-banātu wa-lahumu al-banūn (149)﴾ [al-Saffat], and He said ﴿Wa-yastaftūnaka fi al-nisāʾi qul Allāhu yuftīkum fīhinna (127)﴾ [al-Nisa'].

Thus Yusuf (peace be upon him) returned to the matter of the two prisoners. He interpreted the dream of the one who would give the wine to drink, saying that he would be released from prison and would return to give his master to drink. As for the other, he would be crucified, and birds would eat from his head, because the symbolism of the dream says that the birds would eat from his head; meaning that his head would become food for the birds.

The interpretation of dreams is a knowledge that Allah casts into the hearts of those whom He has taught the interpretation of narrations (ahadith). It is an ability to decode the riddle of a dream, and Allah gives it to whomever of His servants He wills.

Yusuf had said to the one who said: ﴿Indeed, I saw myself pressing wine﴾ (36) [Yusuf] that he would attain pardon according to what the dream he related revealed; and as for the other, the birds would eat from his head. That is, he would be crucified, as the symbols of the dream indicated.

We observe that Yusuf (peace be upon him) was preoccupied with the judgment that the two dreams made clear, rather than with the two men who had the dreams.

This is evidence that a judge must have his mind fixed on the ruling, not on the one being judged. Yusuf heard from both of them, and he did not know who would attain acquittal and who would be punished.

So Yusuf removed himself from the matter and did not allow his desire to enter his heart, because desire colors judgment, and no one can control his emotion; a judge, at the moment he issues a ruling, must completely strip himself of desire and personal inclinations.

Allah, glorified is He, teaches us this when He revealed to us in His Book the story of our master Dawud (peace be upon him):

﴿And has the news of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the wall of the prayer chamber? (21) When they entered upon Dawud and he was alarmed by them, they said: "Do not fear; we are two adversaries, one of us has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth, and do not exceed justice, and guide us to the right path. (22) Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe, and he said, 'Entrust it to me,' and he overpowered me in speech." (23) He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. Indeed, many associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they." And Dawud thought that We had tried him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and fell down bowing and turned in repentance. (24)﴾ [Sad]

Mentioning the number of his brother's ewes was meant to win Dawud (peace be upon him) over to his side; he wanted to portray the injustice that had befallen him. Dawud ruled that whoever took the ewe to add it to his own ewes was the one who had done wrong. Dawud felt that he had not been successful in the judgment, because he had mentioned in the basis of the ruling the ewes of the one who wanted to take his brother's ewe.

Thus taking alone was, for Dawud, the justification for condemning the one who wished to seize what was not his right; therefore he regarded this whole matter as a trial in which he had not succeeded, and he sought Allah's forgiveness through bowing and repentance.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) was wise when he gave the interpretation of the dream detached from personal interest, and he concluded the interpretation with the words:

﴿The matter has been decided concerning which you both inquire. (41)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: there is no room for returning to or retracting from the occurrence of that which he had reached by way of interpretation; the interpretation came in accordance with what Allah had taught him.

There are many narrations about the hardships Yusuf endured before the well and before the prison. It is said that his paternal aunt, the daughter of Ishaq, who was the eldest of his siblings, received him after his mother died to raise him, and she grew attached to him; she loved no one as much as she loved him.

Yaqub's soul longed for his son, so he went to her and said: "Hand Yusuf over to me." But she said: "By Allah, I cannot bear for him to be absent from me for a single hour, and I will not leave him."

When Yaqub (peace be upon him) left her, she resorted to an item(5) of the inheritance of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which the eldest of the sons would inherit, and she placed it under Yusuf's clothes.

The prevailing custom was that if someone stole something and was caught, he would be transformed from a free man into a slave. When Yaqub was about to leave with his son Yusuf to return to his house, the aunt announced the loss of the item her father Ishaq had given her, and they searched Yusuf and found the missing item.

His aunt said: "By Allah, he is indeed a thief (salam, that is, a slave)," and the custom was that whoever stole something would become the slave of the owner of the item.

Thus Yusuf remained with his aunt, deprived of his father for a period, and the father could not reclaim him until after the aunt died.

Then came the incident of the well, and after it the attempt of the wife of the governor (al-Aziz) to seduce him. Despite the governor's certainty of his innocence, he was imprisoned; and the narrators say:

"Yusuf (peace be upon him) was known in prison for generosity, trustworthiness, truthfulness in speech, good bearing, abundant worship, knowledge of interpretation—that is, the interpretation of dreams—and kindness to the people of the prison.

When these two youths entered the prison with him, they became attached to him and loved him greatly, and they said to him: 'By Allah, we have loved you with an exceptional love.' He said: 'May Allah bless you both; indeed, no one has loved me without harm coming to him because of that love. My aunt loved me, and harm came upon her because of it; my father loved me, and I was harmed because of him; and the wife of the governor loved me, and so it was.'

That is: he entered the prison and became with them without any sin he had committed.

The two prisoners said: 'We cannot do otherwise.'"

Then Allah, glorified is He, mentions what Yusuf said to the one who thought he would be saved from the prison:

﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved: "Mention me to your lord." But Satan caused him to forget the mention of his lord, so he remained in the prison for several years. (42)﴾

1 - Tasawwur (climbing): to scale and mount it. Allah says: ﴿And has the news of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the wall of the prayer chamber? (21)﴾ [Sad] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/335].
2 - Shatat: injustice and exceeding the limit in everything. Allah says: ﴿We have certainly uttered an outrageous lie (14)﴾ [al-Kahf], that is, a wrongful statement exceeding the limit [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/349].
3 - Ukfilniha: that is, make me its guardian, caring for its affairs and owning it; ʿazzani fi al-khitab: overpowered me and subdued me [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/18, 167].
4 - Kharra rakiʿan: he hastened to bow and submit to Allah as if he had fallen from a height. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/190].
5 - This item is Ishaq's waistband, as mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir [2/486]. The mintaqah is whatever a person tightens around his waist, and "intaqata" means he tightened the belt around his waist [Lisan al-Arab, root n-t-q].
6 - Al-samt: good intention and course in matters of religion and worldly affairs. Khalid ibn Janba said: samt is following truth and guidance, good neighborliness, and little harming [Lisan al-Arab, root s-m-t].
7 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir [4/3511] that the lord of the prison loved Yusuf, so he made things easier for him there, then said: "O Yusuf, I have loved you with a love I have never felt for anything." He said: "I seek refuge in Allah from your love." He said: "Why?" He said: "My father loved me, and my brothers did to me what they did; my mistress loved me, and what you see befell me."
8 - "Rabb" is applied to the owner, the master, the companion, the guardian of the household and its head [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/251], with adaptation.

The intended one here is the prisoner who saw in a dream that he was pressing grapes. It was he whom Yusuf interpreted his dream for, saying that he would be saved, and he continued his task of making wine for his master.

As for His saying, glorified is He:

﴿And he said to the one he knew would be saved..." (42)﴾ [Yusuf]

This means that the matter of his deliverance had not yet been made certain, and had not become knowledge.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, had instructed him:

﴿Mention me to your lord...(42)﴾ [Yusuf]

Remembrance (dhikr) is the presence of a thing in the mind. This thing had a connection of reception in his mind, like any matter you knew before, then left and forgot for a period, then remembered again anew.

Thus we know that a person has receptions of perceptions, and these do not remain at the focus of consciousness all the time, because the mind cannot be occupied except with one thing. If something else comes, it pushes the first matter to the edge of consciousness, so that the new matter settles in the focus of consciousness.

The example I always give is throwing a stone into water: the stone makes circles that grow, and their diameters expand successively. Likewise is the focus of consciousness when it receives a new matter or thought.

So the new thought pushes all the other thoughts away from the center to the periphery, then something comes that reminds you of what is on the periphery of consciousness, so the thought or matter you had forgotten returns to you, and you remember it with all its details, because human memory works on two levels: it preserves information, and it also retrieves information.

Yusuf said to the one who thought he would be saved:

﴿Mention me to your lord...(42)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: mention what you found with me of good before your master.

Some exegetes said: when Yusuf, peace be upon him, uttered this statement, God willed that he should remain in prison for several years. It was not fitting for him, as a messenger, to involve another in the matter of mentioning him favorably before that prisoner's master.

Yusuf, as a messenger, receives only from God through revelation, and he had said to that prisoner and his companion:

﴿No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you. That is of what my Lord has taught me...(37)﴾ [Yusuf]

This means that he receives directly from God, and he was to remain connected to the source that overflows upon him.

The Truth, glorified is He, continues:

﴿So Satan made him forget the remembrance of his lord, and he remained in prison several years (42)﴾ [Yusuf]

The forgetting of the remembrance of God contains a kind of punishment, or carries some discipline for Yusuf. Thus we see that Satan himself assists the Truth in His purposes concerning His creation.

This explains for us Yusuf's remaining in prison for several years. We know that "bid'" (a few) among years means from three years to ten years, and some scholars specified it as seven years.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I have seen seven fat cows being eaten by seven emaciated ones, and seven green spikes and others dry. O eminent ones, explain to me my vision, if you should interpret visions."(43)﴾

1 - ʿajafa: became lean, so he is aʿjaf and she is ʿajfāʾ. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿yaʾkuluhunna sabʿ ʿijāf (43)﴾ [Yusuf] refers to the lean cows that have no flesh or fat on them, and are struck as an example for seven years in which there is no rain and no fertility [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: ʿ-j-f].
2 - What is meant by al-malaʾ here are the people of knowledge and insight in soothsaying, astrology, augury and magic, and the nobles of his people. [See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3520].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 43:

The land in which that story took place, and across which it unfolded, is Egypt, and we already knew this when the Truth, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And the one who had bought him from Egypt said...﴾ (12:21)

Thus we know that there is a "king" and there is an "ʿAzīz" (minister).

We know that the rulers of ancient Egypt were called the Pharaohs. After the "Rosetta Stone" was discovered and the riddles of the hieroglyphic script were deciphered, we learned that the rule of the Pharaohs had disappeared for a period, when the kings of the shepherds, who are called the Hyksos, occupied Egypt.

This was the period in which Joseph appeared, and Joseph and his brother worked with them. When the Pharaohs regained rule over Egypt, they drove out the Hyksos and killed those who had been their allies.

The Qur'an's account of the presence of a king in Egypt during the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, is among the miraculous prophecies of the Qur'an.

And when you read:

﴿And the king said: "Indeed, I saw seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean ones..."﴾ (12:43)

Then he asks for the interpretation of his vision; this means it was a dream seen in sleep.

As for the word ﴿fat (sammān)﴾ (12:43), it means full of flesh and health, and the word [ʿijāf] means the emaciated, as common people say, "its skin is on its bones." So how can the lean eat the fat, when the reverse might be more acceptable?

The king added:

﴿And seven green ears of grain and others dry...﴾ (12:43)

The king did not describe any action proceeding from the ears of grain. Then he asked those around him from among the notables of the people, who occupy the front of gatherings and fill the eyes: ﴿Explain to me my vision, if you are able to interpret visions.﴾ (12:43)

The word [taʿburūn] is derived from "ʿabara al-nahr," meaning to cross from one bank to the other, as if he were asking them for the meaning hidden within the vision.

From this meaning we derive the word "ʿibrah" (lesson), which is an experience from which we benefit, and also "ʿibārah" (expression), which is when something is concealed within the self, and we render it and make it manifest through expression.

From it also comes "ʿabrah" (tear): the drop that falls from the eye expressing some feeling, whether sorrow or joy. The whole root revolves around defining the unknown by the known.

In this way the interpreter of dreams, by means of its symbols, crosses from the imaginary to the real.

The notables around the king had no interpretation of the vision he had seen in his sleep.

The Truth, glory be to Him, relates what came from their tongues:

﴿They said: "Confused dreams (aḍghāth aḥlām), and we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams."﴾ (12:44)

1 - ḍaghth (aḍghāth): a handful of mixed branches of plants. The Almighty's words ﴿aḍghāth aḥlām﴾ (12:44) mean mixed, jumbled, confused dreams, indistinct, by way of metaphor, like mixed things. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 1/394].

Thus the chiefs declared that the king's dream was nothing but a confused jumble of dreams without meaning.

The word "ḍigh<u></u>th" (ضغث, a bundle of mixed herbs) is a bundle of grasses of various kinds. It is as if the king's dream had no interpretation according to them, because they are not people who can distinguish in interpretation.

This is a truthful stance on the part of the courtiers: that none of them informs about something unless he has knowledge of it. And it is no shame for one of them to declare his ignorance of a matter he does not know.

Whoever declares his ignorance of a matter to the one asking, while he actually knows it, makes him ask someone else; but if he gives an answer, he may cause him to persist in that answer.

For this reason the scholars said, to open room for honesty in giving legal opinions: "Whoever says 'I do not know' has issued a fatwa," because when he says "I do not know," he will compel you to ask someone else.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And the one of the two who was saved and who remembered after a period (of time) said, "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾

1 - "Idhkar" (ادكر): its original form is "idhtakar" on the pattern of "ifta'ala." The "ta" of the iftiʿāl was changed to "dāl," the "dhāl" of the verb was changed to "dāl," and the two "dāl"s were assimilated (idghām). Cf. ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 17] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/244].

2 - "Ummah" (الأمة): the period, the span of time, and the interval. The verse ﴿and remembered after a period (ummah)...﴾ [Yusuf: 45] is explained by this. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-ddakara baʿda ummah" with a ha' (ummah-h), and "ummah" here means forgetfulness and heedlessness, i.e., he remembered after forgetting. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/34].

The one who was saved of the two prisoners heard the king's words and the response of the chiefs, so he recalled to his memory what had passed over him in prison, how he had seen the dream, and how Yusuf had interpreted it.

And His saying: ﴿And he remembered after a period of time (ummah)...﴾ [Yusuf: 45]

That is: he exerted his mind and intellect, and made an effort to remember, because a considerable period of time had passed. The word "ummah" means a period of time, as in the saying of the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted:

﴿And if We delay the punishment from them for a counted ummah (period), they will surely say, "What holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the Day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾ [Hud: 8]

And "ummah" may refer to a community of people, and it may also refer to a man who combines all the qualities of goodness, as Allah the Exalted said in describing Ibrahim, peace be upon him:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah (community unto himself), devoutly obedient to Allah, upright, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [An-Nahl: 120]

That is: all the qualities of goodness were gathered in Ibrahim, upon him and upon our Prophet be peace.

After the king's cupbearer made an effort and strove to remember what had happened to him over a period of some years—the days when he was a prisoner and saw a dream whose interpretation was given to him by Yusuf—the cupbearer said to the chiefs and to the king concerning that dream:

﴿I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth.﴾ [Yusuf: 45]

With this he asked permission to go to someone who would interpret the king's dream for him.

And His saying: ﴿So send me forth﴾ [Yusuf: 45]

That is, the interpretation is not from him; rather, he knows the one who is able to interpret dreams.

We note that the Qur'an did not place on this man's tongue where he would go, because that is known to him and to us, we who are reading the surah.

The Qur'an then moved from the request to be sent forth to the meeting with Yusuf, peace be upon him. Allah the Blessed and Exalted says what came on the tongue of the king's cupbearer:

﴿Yusuf, O man of truth (al-siddiq), explain to us concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others dry, so that I may return to the people, that they might know.﴾ [Yusuf: 46]

1 - Al-qunut (devout obedience): obedience and supplication. "Qanata al-mu'min bi-Allah" means he obeyed Allah and acknowledged servitude to Him; "qanata fi salatihi" means he was humbly submissive and calm; "qanata" means he supplicated and prolonged the supplication. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/134].

2 - Al-siddiq (the one of great truthfulness): pronounced with a kasra on the sad and a shadda on the dal, it is an intensive form derived from truthfulness. ﴿Those are the siddiqun (truthful ones)...﴾ [Al-Hadid: 19], and the feminine form is siddiqah: ﴿and his mother was a siddiqah...﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 75], referring to Maryam, peace be upon her. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/272].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 46:

﴿Joseph, O man of truth (al-Siddiq), give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others withered, so that I may return to the people, so that they may know.﴾ (46)

His saying: ﴿O man of truth (al-Siddiq).. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

indicates that they had tested him in several matters, and his truthfulness had been established.

The meaning of "al-siddiq" is not limited to his being truthful in all his words, truthful in all his actions, and truthful in all his states; rather its meaning is broad enough to show us that truthfulness was constantly attached to him, in speech and in deed.

As for speech, his truthfulness is evident, because he utters a verbal proposition that has a reality outside which confirms it.

As for the truthfulness of deeds, it means that you do not test him in a statement and then his action comes contrary to that statement; and this is the one to whom the term "siddiq" is applied.

We know that human movements in life are divided into two kinds: either speech or action. Speech has the tongue as its instrument, and action has all the limbs as its instruments.

So: there is speech, and there is action, and both are work. Speech is work; seeing with the eye is work; hearing with the ear is work; touching with the hand is work.

But speech is specific to the tongue, while the remaining limbs take on action, because action is the means of communication between a speaker and a listener, and it took the share of action.

Thus we know that action is of two kinds: either speech or deed.

The siddiq is one who is truthful in his speech, so that the verbal statement corresponds to reality, and truthful in his action, by not saying what he does not do.

For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do (3)﴾ [al-Saff]

We know that the king's cupbearer had two experiences with Joseph:

The first experience: his living with him in prison, he and his fellow baker, and their saying to him:

﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers (36)﴾ [Yusuf]

And this saying of theirs was the basis of their asking him to interpret the two dreams for them:

﴿One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine," and the other said, "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread on my head, of which the birds eat. Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers." (36)﴾ [Yusuf]

The second experience: the occurrence of the reality of life's movement after that corresponding to his interpretation of the two dreams. For this reason he says to him here:

﴿Joseph, O man of truth, give us your interpretation concerning seven fat cows which seven lean ones devour, and seven green ears of grain and others withered, so that I may return to the people, so that they may know. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: give us your interpretation of the dream of seven fat cows, which seven cows of extreme leanness devour, and seven green ears, and seven others withered, so that I may return to the people, so that they may know.

His saying: ﴿Give us your interpretation.. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

clarifies that he is not asking about a dream concerning himself; rather it concerns a dreamer he has not specified, though we have known that it is the dream of the king.

His saying: ﴿so that I may return to the people.. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

is a precaution and caution regarding a matter he does not affirm with certainty; it is caution regarding a reality decreed by God for man, and the questioner adopted the manner of caution in order to save himself from being a liar, for he knows that the matter of his return is not in his hand. For this reason God teaches us:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," (23) except [with the addition], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right conduct." (24)﴾ [al-Kahf]

And when you say, "If Allah wills," you have removed yourself from the circle of lying; and as long as you have mentioned God, He, glory be to Him, is able to guide you to the appropriate choice in every matter in which you face a choice.

So God teaches His servants to preserve themselves, by being truthful in their words and deeds; for however you plan, you plan with a mind granted to you by God; and when you undertake any action, any action, however small, needs many and numerous factors, of which you possess none; therefore you must return every matter to the one who possesses it.

And here the cupbearer said:

﴿so that I may return to the people.. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

and by this the Truth, glory be to Him, teaches us caution.

And the Truth, glory be to Him, added on the tongue of the man:

﴿so that they may know (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

As if the man knew that when he takes the interpretation from Joseph, peace be upon him, and returns with it to the people, he does not know how they will receive this interpretation.

Will they receive it with acceptance, or with dispute about it? Or will they receive the interpretation with confirmation, and know your worth and station, O Joseph, so that they free you from what you are in of the affliction of prison?

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿so that I may return to the people.. (46)﴾ [Yusuf]

may lead a questioner to say: Who assigned the cupbearer to go to Joseph; was it the king or the courtiers?

We say: the cupbearer attributed it to all of them, for the sake of administrative caution.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿He said, "You will sow seven years in succession; so what you harvest, leave in its ear, except for a little of which you eat. (47)﴾

1 - al-Siddiq: with a kasra on the sad and a shadda on the dal: an intensive form from truthfulness (ṣidq). ﴿Those are the siddiqun (the truthful)..(19)﴾ [al-Hadid], and the feminine is siddiqa: ﴿and his mother was a siddiqa..(75)﴾ [al-Ma'idah], referring to Maryam, peace be upon her. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/272].
2 - al-Maqt: the most intense hatred; maqtahu yamqutuhu: he hated him. He, exalted be He, says: ﴿The hatred of Allah is greater than your hatred of yourselves..(10)﴾ [Ghafir]. He said: it means: the hatred of Allah toward you when you were called to faith and did not believe is greater than your hatred of yourselves when you saw the punishment. [Lisan al-'Arab, root m-q-t].
3 - Tahajja: they disputed and contended with proofs, each of them trying to establish that he is the one in the right. He, exalted be He, says: ﴿And when they argue in the Fire..(47)﴾ [Ghafir], i.e., they dispute. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/143].
4 - Da'aba 'ala al-amr: he became accustomed to it. Al-da'b and al-da'b: habit and custom. He, exalted be He, says: ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah..(31)﴾ [Ghafir], i.e., their habit and manner. And He, exalted be He, says: ﴿He said, "You will sow seven years in succession (da'aban)..(47)﴾ [Yusuf], i.e., [in a steady manner]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/219].

This is the beginning of the interpretation of the king's dream.

Ad'ab (persistence, diligence) means constancy; it is as if Yusuf (peace be upon him) had asked that the people of Egypt cultivate with persistence and without laziness.

He continues: ﴿Then what you reap, leave it in its ears, except a little of what you eat﴾ [Yusuf 47].

That is: what you harvest as a result of cultivation with earnest effort, you may eat a little of it, and leave the rest preserved in its ears.

The preservation in the ears teaches us the worth of the Qur'an, the power of the One who sent down the Qur'an (glory be to Him), and the knowledge that Allah, exalted is He, gave Yusuf (peace be upon him) in all aspects of life, including economics and the requirements of storage, and other gifts of Allah. Modern science has confirmed that when wheat is stored in its ears, that is a protection and safeguard for it from weevils.

Some scholars, in their interpretation of this verse, said: the intended meaning is storing wheat in its ears and stalks.

I say: the intended meaning is only leaving the wheat in its ears, because the stalks are animal fodder.

We know that the wheat grain has two coverings: a covering that protects it, which separates from the kernel during the process of "threshing" (ad-dars), then flies off during the process of "winnowing" (at-tadhiyah), separating from the wheat grains.

The wheat grain also has a covering that remains attached to it, the husk that separates from the grain when we grind the wheat, which we call "ar-radda" (bran). It is of two kinds: "coarse bran" and "fine bran."

It is the habit of some people to separate the pure flour from the bran, and these people ignore, or do not know, the scientific fact that has confirmed that eating bread made from white flour free of bran causes constipation of the stomach.

Thus this husk attached to the wheat grain is not only for protecting the grain; rather it contains great nutritional value.

The wealthy of the countryside in Egypt used to purify the ground flour of bran, calling it "the flour of distinction" (ad-daqiq al-'alamah); if you put a spoonful of it in your mouth, you feel constipation; whereas if you put a spoonful of natural flour mixed with the bran contained in the grain, you will not feel this constipation.

Allah bestows His favour upon His servants with this, in His true word:

﴿And the grain having husk, and the fragrant plant﴾ [ar-Rahman 12].

The scholars of this age have been guided to the active value in grinding wheat while preserving what is in it of wheat husk, and it has been established for them that whoever eats bread made from extremely pure flour suffers a nutritional imbalance that compels him to eat bread made from wheat husk alone, which is called "as-sinn bread," to compensate in his nutrition for what he has lost of nutritional value.

Here the Truth (glory be to Him) says: ﴿Then what you reap, leave it in its ears, except a little of what you eat﴾ [Yusuf 47].

Thus Yusuf, who was asked by the cupbearer to interpret the king's dream, informed him of what they must do in anticipation of the seven lean years that follow the seven years flourishing with greenery and abundance: they should not eat to fullness, but take from the wheat only what suffices them: ﴿except a little of what you eat﴾ [Yusuf 47].

The Truth (glory be to Him) continues what came on the tongue of Yusuf (peace be upon him) of the rest of the interpretation of the king's dream: ﴿Then after that will come seven hard years which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you store﴾ [Yusuf 48].

1 - "Ye'sur al-habb dhu al-'asf": that is, having straw or the leaf that wraps it. Al-'asf, al-'asifah: the leaves of the ear. Ibn Kathir said in his interpretation of this verse [4/271]: "The meaning of this, and Allah knows best, is that grain such as wheat and barley and the like has in its state of growth 'asf, which is what is on the ear, and rayhan, which is the leaves wrapped around its stalk."

2 - Al-Qurtubi said in his interpretation [4/3526]: "That is: what you withhold in order to sow, because in retaining the seed lies the preservation of the sustenance. Abu 'Ubaydah said: tuhsirun, 'you store up'; Qatadah said: tuhsinun, 'you store up'; and the meaning is one."

Thus Yusuf (peace be upon him) clarified what would happen in Egypt: a drought lasting seven lean years after seven years of cultivation, which requires an unflagging resolve.

As for His words, glorified be He, describing the seven "years" as: ﴿severe﴾ [Yusuf]

The meaning is that the drought in them would exhaust the people. If there is no yield stored from the produce of the previous seven years, famine may strike. The people should therefore hold back their stomachs during the first seven years and eat only in the measure of necessity, so as to secure their confrontation with the years of drought.

We know that a human being sustains his life through breath, food and drink. Food is what nourishes a person and gives him the strength with which he faces life.

But most of our food is not aimed at strength alone; we also seek enjoyment from it. Had a person sought only to ward off the pangs of hunger, he would have been satisfied with boiled food, or with bread and condiment alone. But we eat for enjoyment.

The Truth, glorified be He, speaks of this when He says: ﴿So eat it, wholesome and agreeable﴾ [al-Nisa']

That is, without it harming you, and without this food compelling you to digestive medicines.

This is the intended meaning of His words: ﴿wholesome..﴾ [al-Nisa']

As for the intended meaning of His words: ﴿agreeable..﴾ [al-Nisa'],

it is food that benefits and supplies the body with energy only, though its taste may not be pleasing.

Here the Truth, glorified be He, says: ﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you have preserved﴾ [Yusuf 48]

Naturally we understand that it is not the years that consume; rather, it is the people who live in those years who eat.

We understand this because we know that any event requires a time and a place; sometimes the event is ascribed to the time, and sometimes it is ascribed to the place.

An example of ascribing the event to the place is the saying of the Truth, glorified be He: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we travelled..﴾ [Yusuf 82]

Clearly we understand that what is meant is asking the people of the town where they were, and the owners of the caravans that were with them.

Here, in the verse about which we are offering our reflections, we find the event ascribed to the time: "they will eat what you have stored, except a little," because after they eat they must keep a quantity of grain and seed to use as seed in the following year, after seven years described as drought.

His words, exalted be He: ﴿what you have preserved﴾ [Yusuf 48]

are derived from the root "ḥ-ṣ-n," which denotes protection and inaccessibility. It is said: "they stayed inside the fortress (ḥiṣn)," meaning that if enemies attacked them, they would be secure against them and the enemies could not reach them.

The Truth, glorified be He, says: ﴿And [forbidden are] the chaste women (al-muḥṣanāt) among women..﴾ [al-Nisa' 24]

That is, those who abstain from unlawful intercourse, and they are the free women.

And the Truth, glorified be He, also says: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity (aḥṣanat farjahā)..﴾ [al-Anbiya' 91]

That is, she who perfected the preservation of her chastity, and she is the Lady Maryam the virgin (peace be upon her). Thus we find that the root "ḥ-ṣ-n" denotes protection.

The Truth, glorified be He, then says: ﴿Then after that will come a year in which people will be given rain, and in which they will press (juice)﴾ [Yusuf 49]

1 - Al-ghawā'il: that which destroys; al-ghawl: hardship [Lisan al-Arab, root: gh-w-l].
2 - Hanu'a yahna'u hanā'a: it was made easy without hardship, and its matter was facilitated, and its doer was made happy by it. A "hanī' food" is wholesome and beneficial, making its eater happy. The Almighty said: ﴿So eat it, wholesome﴾ [al-Nisa' 4], meaning lawful and good, with no prohibition in it and no sin upon you in eating it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/309].
3 - Mari'a al-ta'am: it was easy in the throat, its consequence was sound, and it was free from distress. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/20].
4 - This style is called in rhetoric majāz through ellipsis (ḥadhf). [Dala'il al-I'jaz of al-Jurjani].
5 - Al-'ir: the caravan; al-'ir: a people who have with them their beasts and loads of food. The Almighty said: ﴿O caravan, you are surely thieves﴾ [Yusuf 70], meaning: O travelling people. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/44].
6 - Al-batul among women: the virgin cut off from husbands; it is also said: she who is devoted to God, Mighty and Majestic, cut off from the world. [Lisan al-Arab, root: b-t-l].
7 - Ibn 'Abbas said: they press grapes and oil. Ibn Jurayj said: they press grapes into wine, sesame into oil, and olives into olive oil. It is also said: it means milking the milk-animals because of its abundance, and this indicates abundance of vegetation. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3527].

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary notes that what Yusuf (peace be upon him) spoke of here lies outside the interpretation of the dream, because what the king's dream contained was seven lean cows devouring seven fat cows, and seven green ears of grain and others dry.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) finished interpreting the dream, and after that he came to judgment on matters by way of reason, since ordinary fertility returns to give them what it used to give them before that.

This may be called "ghawth" (relief), because we say "aghātha fulānan" (he relieved so-and-so), meaning a'natha fulānan (he helped so-and-so), since he is in need of help, and "al-ghayth" (rain) descends from the sky to end drought.

As for His saying: ﴿Then will the people be given rain (yughāth al-nās)...﴾ [Yusuf: 49]

That is: they will be relieved (yu'ānūn) by what comes to them of God's bounty, with the necessities of food that keep life sustained for them.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿And therein they will press (yaʿṣirūn)﴾ [Yusuf: 49]

That is: what can be pressed of grains or fruits, such as sesame, olives, grapes, sugarcane, or dates. You will not press those grains or fruits unless you have what overflows beyond the sustenance of yourself and those you support.

Thus Allah, glory be to Him, made clear to us that they will be provided with good that overflows beyond relief, and they may store it. What preceded in the verses of the dream and its interpretation is a dialogue between Yusuf the Truthful (peace be upon him) and the king's cupbearer.

We have observed how the Qur'an moved from the scene of the courtiers' inability to give an opinion on the matter of the dream, and the cupbearer's offering to be sent to bring them the interpretation of the dream, and then it came directly with the dialogue between Yusuf and the cupbearer.

Here the Qur'an moves to what happened after the king learned the interpretation of the dream. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." But when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what is the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾ [Yusuf: 50]

1 - ʿajafa: to be emaciated, so he is aʿjaf, and she is ʿajfāʾ, meaning thin. At-taʿjīf: poor nourishment and thinness. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿yaʾkuluhunna sabʿ ʿijāf...﴾ (43) [Yusuf]: they are the emaciated ones with neither flesh nor fat upon them, struck as an example of seven years with neither rain nor fertility. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: ʿ-j-f]
