2 - ghayth: rain. Al-ghayth: pasture that grows from the water of the sky; the original meaning is rain, then what grows by it was called ghayth. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: gh-y-th]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 50:

The meaning of that is that the cupbearer went directly to the king's assembly and conveyed to him the interpretation of the dream. The king insisted that they bring this man to him, for he was convinced that it was necessary to benefit from him. The cupbearer returned to take Yusuf out of the prison in which he was.

But he was surprised by Yusuf's refusal to leave the prison, and by his saying to the one who came to escort him to the king's assembly:

﴿Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot.﴾ [Yusuf]

Thus Yusuf was keen not to respond to the one who came to free him from the torment of the prison in which he was, unless his innocence was cleared in a manner the king would recognise, for it is probable that they had concealed it from the king's ear.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, intended by this that the king should investigate that matter with these women who cut their hands and who invited him to indecency.

Yusuf was content with alluding to that by his saying:

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot.﴾ [Yusuf]

This saying conceals within it what the women had said before to Yusuf about the necessity of obeying the wife of the ʿAzīz in her demand for indecency.

Thus we find the Qur'anic narrative giving us the lesson that serves us in the reality of life; those stories are not for entertainment, but for the lesson that serves us in the matters of life.

The clearing of any person's innocence is an important matter, so that any suspicion about the person is removed before any task is assigned to him.

Thus Yusuf, peace be upon him, requested the clearing of his innocence, lest any speaker say, by way of slander or rumour, "scoffing or defaming" (1): "Is this not Yusuf, the subject of the story with the wife of the ʿAzīz, the one who solicited her to herself?"

And here is our Messenger (ﷺ) saying:

"I am amazed at the patience of my brother Yusuf and his generosity—may Allah forgive him—when a messenger came to him asking him to interpret the dream, and had I been I would not have done so until I had come out. And I am amazed at his patience and generosity—may Allah forgive him—when he was told to come out but he did not come out until he informed them of his excuse. Had I been in his place I would have rushed to the door, but he wanted there to be an excuse for him" (2).

Our Prophet (ﷺ) wished to make clear to us Yusuf's standing in patience, self-respect, uprightness and dignity, so he said:

"The noble one, the son of the noble one, the son of the noble one, the son of the noble one is Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim." He said: "Had I remained in prison as long as he remained, and then the messenger came to me, I would have answered." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited:

﴿So when the messenger came to him, he said: Return to your lord and ask him what was the matter with the women who cut their hands...﴾ (50) (3) [Yusuf]

Thus the Messenger (ﷺ) explained to us Yusuf's standing in patience and uprightness, and his fear that he would leave the prison and be pointed at: "This is the one who solicited his master's wife."

In the Messenger's saying (ﷺ) there is an indication of Yusuf's thoroughness in that matter, and it would have been more cautious for him to leave the prison and then work to uncover his innocence.

The meaning of that is that the noble person does not exploit situations in a foolish exploitation, but takes each situation according to its measure and arranges for it; Yusuf was confident of his innocence, but he wanted that the king should not be the last to know.

Our Messenger (ﷺ) spoke truly when he said: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt, for truthfulness is tranquillity and falsehood is doubt" (4).

He (ﷺ) held that faith in Allah requires that the believer not stand in a position of suspicion, because some people, when they see someone's intelligence, may be moved by envy of his acuteness, and so they speak against him.

Therefore, you must guard yourself by not standing in a position of suspicion, and whatever matter brings you suspicion, you must keep away from it.

We have in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a good example. His wife Safiyya bint Huyayy came to visit him while he was in seclusion (i'tikaf) in the last ten nights of Ramadan, and she talked with him for an hour after the 'Isha' prayer, then she rose to return (yanqalibu), i.e., to return to her chamber, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose with her, until when she reached the door of the mosque by the dwelling of Umm Salama, the wife of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), two men of the Ansar passed by them; they greeted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and then hurried on (5). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Slow down, it is only Safiyya bint Huyayy." They said: "Glory be to Allah, O Messenger of Allah!" and what he had said was grave to them. He said: "Satan flows through the son of Adam like the blood flows, and I feared that he would cast something into your hearts" (6).

Here, in the situation we are reflecting upon, we find the king summoning the women who cut their hands, who had solicited Yusuf to himself, as Almighty Allah mentions:

﴿He said: "What was your affair when you solicited Yusuf to himself?" They said: "Far be Allah from imperfection! We know of him no evil." The wife of the ʿAzīz said: "Now the truth has become manifest (ḥaṣḥaṣa). It was I who solicited him to himself, and indeed he is of the truthful."﴾ (51)

1 - al-lamz: faults in the face, its origin being a gesture with the eye, head and lips together with a hidden speech; al-hamz: backbiting and disparaging people and mentioning their faults. [Lisan al-'Arab, roots: l-m-z, h-m-z].
2 - Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir [11640]. al-Haythami said in Majma' al-Zawa'id [7/40]: "In it is Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Qurashi al-Makki, who is abandoned (matruk)." al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur [4/548], attributing it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh by various routes from Ibn 'Abbas.
3 - Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [2/332] and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [3116], who said: "a hasan hadith." Likewise al-Hakim in his Mustadrak [2/346], all from the hadith of Abu Hurayra. al-Hakim said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not narrate it with this wording," and al-Dhahabi remained silent on it.
4 - Narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in his Musnad [1178], likewise Imam Ahmad in his Musnad [1/200], and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [2518], who said: "hasan sahih", from the hadith of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali.
5 - al-nafadh: passing through; in al-Muhkam: the passing of a thing and getting clear of it. You say: nafadha, i.e., he passed and went beyond. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: n-f-dh], i.e., they passed by and went beyond them.
6 - Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih [6219] and Muslim in his Sahih [2175], from the hadith of Safiyya bint Huyayy.
7 - ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq: it became clear and manifest after being hidden; al-ḥaṣḥaṣa: the clarifying of the truth after concealment, i.e., it appeared and emerged [Lisan al-'Arab, root: ḥ-ṣ-ḥ-ṣ].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 51:

We know that the first solicitation of Yusuf came from the wife of the ruler (al-ʿAziz); Yusuf remained steadfast. Then she invited the women to her gathering, and they cut their hands when they were taken aback by the beauty of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Gestures and calls of excitement and agitation came from them.

Yusuf said about them what Allah, glorified is He, related:

﴿And if You do not avert from me their plot, I will incline toward them and be of the ignorant.﴾ [Yusuf]

The king summoned the women and asked them: ﴿What was your situation (khatbukunna) when you solicited Yusuf for himself?﴾ [Yusuf]

Al-khatb (lit. "affair," "matter") is a grave event: an unusual occurrence that people speak about. It is not a matter kept between a person and himself; rather, they speak of it in a way that shakes the city, because such an incident has occurred.

This is why we find Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said to a group of angels: ﴿He said, "Then what is your business (khatbukum), O messengers?" They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people."﴾ [al-Dhariyat]

That is, the angels reassured Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that they were on a mission to punish a criminal people.

And Musa, peace be upon him, when he returned to his people and found that al-Samiri had made for them a calf of gold from the ornaments they had taken from the people of Pharaoh, said to al-Samiri: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O Samiri?"﴾ [Ta-Ha]

The king's statement in the verse under our present reflection: ﴿What was your situation when you solicited Yusuf for himself?﴾ [Yusuf]

indicates that he had heard the account with its details, so he was shaken by it and regarded it as a grave matter. This makes clear to us that the values are the same in every time and place.

The women began to speak, and said: ﴿حاشا لله، ما علمنا عليه من سوء﴾ [Yusuf: "Far be Allah from it! We know of him no evil."]

They did not mention the matter of their own solicitation of him; the important thing was to clear Yusuf's name before the king.

Their words ﴿Ḥāsha lillāh﴾ [Yusuf] mean: we exalt Yusuf above this, and our exalting Yusuf is a matter from Allah.

Here the wife of the ruler intervened: ﴿The wife of al-ʿAziz said, "Now the truth has become evident"﴾ [Yusuf]

That is, she acknowledged that there was no longer room for concealment, the truth had become clear after being hidden, the portion of truth had emerged from the portion of falsehood, and it was necessary to confess what had happened: ﴿It was I who solicited him for himself, and indeed he is of the truthful.﴾ [Yusuf]

The wife of al-ʿAziz continued her confession in the following verse: ﴿That is so that he will know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the betrayers.﴾ [Yusuf]

1 - Ṣabā yaṣbū: he inclined and loved. ﴿Asbu ilayhinna﴾ [Yusuf, 33]: that is, I incline toward them and do what they tempt me with. Ṣabā ila al-lahw: he longed for and yearned after amusement. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/368].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 52:

﴿That is so that he (al-Aziz) may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plotting of the betrayers.﴾

She said this so that the innocence of Yusuf, peace be upon him, would be proclaimed, and that she had not seized the opportunity of his absence in prison to take revenge on him, because he had not responded to her seduction, and she had not, during his absence, spun for him schemes, intrigues, and plots.

This shows us that a person's violent desire may flare up for a specific purpose, and when that purpose subsides and passes, the person returns to his perfect balance within himself. He may make a first slip in his mind a means to goodness in matters where he has no weakness, so that a good deed covers over an evil one, in confirmation of the words of the Truth, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ [Hud]

If a person commits an evil deed and another exposes him for it, then the one who exposes that evil deed is depriving society of the good deeds of the one who committed the evil.

Therefore I say: cover up the faults of the one who errs, for they may inspire him to offer some good that wipes out his evil deeds.

And so they have said: if you survey the history of people, you will find that those with strong souls in morals and values have, in them, some weaknesses and lapses, and they try to do good deeds so that their evil deeds may be removed from them, because the mind of each of them is occupied with his weakness, which burns him, so he rushes to do good works.

After the wife of the al-Aziz had confessed to what she had done, she said:

﴿And that Allah does not guide the plotting of the betrayers.﴾ [Yusuf]

That is: she acknowledged that He, glorified and exalted is He, does not let the plotting of the betrayers take effect, nor does He let it reach its goal.

The wife of the al-Aziz continues, saying:

﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil, except those on whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This statement is part of the speech of the wife of the Ruler (imra'at al-'Aziz), and it seems she is explaining why she attended this gathering; she did not attend to clear herself.

﴿Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those on whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (12:53)

The coming of the words of the Truth, the Exalted, affirming that the soul, in its absolute sense, is commanding to evil, leads us to say: Joseph too is a human soul.

Some scholars⁽¹⁾ have said that this statement is from the words of Joseph, as a reply to her when she said:

﴿It was she who sought to seduce him from himself, and he is certainly among the truthful. [He said], "That is so he will know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plan of the betrayers."﴾ (12:51-52)

And it would have been appropriate for Joseph, peace be upon him, to reply with the words: ﴿And I do not acquit myself; indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those on whom my Lord has mercy...﴾ (12:53)

This statement may be attributed to Joseph as a kind of caution, so that the pride of faith does not touch him, for he is a messenger of Allah who knows that Allah, the Exalted, is the One who turned their plotting away from him.

This is a form of Allah's mercy toward him; for he, as a mere human without infallibility and without a guided path, could have fallen into error, but the Truth, the Exalted, preserved him from slipping.

And by the kindness of Allah, He said of the soul that it is "commanding to evil." This gives a sufficient clarification of the nature of the soul's action: it is not one that commands to evil in the sense that it orders a person to commit a sin once, and the matter ends.

Rather, be attentive, O human, to the reality of the soul's work: it is always commanding to evil. You know that all divine obligations are either commands or prohibitions. Commands may come to you as a duty that burdens your self, and you know that prohibitions keep you from actions that may be desirable to you, because in their outward appearance they are pleasurable and answer the call of human instincts. Therefore the Chosen Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires."⁽²⁾

That is: sins may tempt you, but the wise person is the one who controls his soul, considers distant consequences, and does not look only at the passing, momentary pleasure, unless he looks also at the end to which that pleasure leads; for a thing you enjoy for a moment may make you suffer for a long time.

For this reason we say: one who indulges himself excessively is heedless of the reward of obedience and the punishment of disobedience; and if he kept in mind the reward for obedience and the punishment for disobedience, he would refrain from indulging himself.

For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "No adulterer commits adultery while he is a believer, no thief steals while he is a believer, and no drinker drinks wine while he is a believer."⁽³⁾

So, at the moment of committing a sin, you find the person concealing his faith, and he does not put in his mind that he may die before repenting of his sin or before expiating for it.

A person errs in calculating his lifespan, because no one knows the time of his death, or the interval between him and the reckoning of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, for his sins. Each of us is required to keep in mind the saying of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him: "Death is the Resurrection; whoever dies has had his resurrection."⁽⁴⁾

We have a good example in ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, the third Caliph of the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, who, whenever he stood at a grave, would weep until his beard was wet. He was asked about that, and it was said to him: "You remember Paradise and Hellfire and do not weep, but you weep when you stand at a grave?" He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, say: 'The grave is the first of the stages of the Hereafter. If its occupant is saved from it, what comes after it is easier than it; and if he is not saved from it, what comes after it is harder.'"⁽⁵⁾

Therefore, no one should consider unlikely the appointed time of his meeting with death.

The verse continues: ﴿except those on whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (12:53)

We know that there are things that cure disease, and there are things that protect a person and give him immunity so that disease does not strike him. The Truth, the Exalted, is Forgiving, meaning He forgives sins and erases them; and the Truth, the Exalted, is Merciful, meaning He grants a person immunity so that disease does not strike him and he does not fall into another slip.

And the Truth, the Exalted, is the One who said: ﴿And We send down of the Quran that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers...﴾ (17:82)

When you hear the Quran, it heals you from the disease you suffer from psychologically, strengthens your ability to resist disease, and brings forth the healing powers latent in your depths.

It is a mercy to you when you take it as a method and apply it in your life; it grants you an immunity that protects you from illness. It is thus both a curative medicine and a preventive medicine at once.

1 - Related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim. The most famous view, and the one most fitting to the context of the story and the meanings of the speech, is that it is from the words of the wife of the Ruler, because the whole context is her speech in the presence of the king, and Joseph, peace be upon him, was not with them; rather, the king had him brought after that. [See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir 2/481] with adaptation.
2 - Narrated by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad [3/153, 254], Muslim in his Sahih [2822], and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [2559], from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.
3 - Agreed upon. Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih [2475], and Muslim in his Sahih [57], Book of Faith, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.
4 - Mentioned by al-Ajluni in Kashf al-Khafa' [hadith no. 2618] from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, and its complete form: "Increase your remembrance of death, for if you remember it in prosperity, it will trouble you, and if you remember it in hardship, it will expand it for you," the hadith...
5 - Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [1/63], Ibn Majah in his Sunan [4267], and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [2308], who said: "a hasan gharib hadith," from the hadith of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will select him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence."﴾ (12:54)

We note that the king said, ﴿Bring him to me﴾ (12:54) twice.(1) The first time was after he heard the interpretation of the dream, but Yusuf refused to leave the prison until his innocence was established; or else he did leave and attended the confrontation with the women, including the wife of the ruler (al-Aziz).

The king saw in Yusuf lofty character and breadth of knowledge.

The first meeting ended so that the king might reflect and think about the qualities of this man, and about the peace of mind that filled the king's soul, and how this man had entered his heart.

The second time was when the king wished to select him for himself and make him his advisor.

The Truthful, glorified is He, expresses this meaning in His saying: ﴿Bring him to me; I will select him for myself. So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence."﴾ (12:54)

This selection came after the king had spoken with Yusuf, and after he had perceived Yusuf's detachment from his own self; and the king became certain, following the dialogue with Yusuf, that he was a man who had guarded himself against the most violent of instincts, the instinct of sex. He became certain that Yusuf had accepted imprisonment and lived in it for a long period; that he was a man of knowledge, as this was confirmed by the interpretation of the dream; and that he had done so while a prisoner, and had not agreed to leave prison except to establish his innocence, or after his innocence had been established.

For all this, he became one of those trusted by the king, who declared the matter by his saying: ﴿Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence﴾ (12:54). This was to close the door to slander against him or plotting against him. The station of "al-Makin" (the established one) is a standing from which no one can be harmed. Therefore we find that the Truthful, Exalted is He, when speaking of the revelation from Jibril, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of power, with the Owner of the Throne, established [in rank]﴾ (81:19–20).

The meaning is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was worthy of trust with the ruler; he would be the one who executes affairs and has contact with the governed. If he is established in rank with the ruler, he is also trustworthy with the governed.

The problem in our contemporary societies arises when the ruler prefers those he sees as trustworthy over those with expertise and integrity, so the balance of justice is upset. The wise ruler must choose those who possess both qualities: integrity toward the governed and trust in the eyes of the ruler; by this, life is set right on the path of God.

When Yusuf, peace be upon him, heard this statement from the ruler, ﴿Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence﴾ (12:54), he resolved to ask him for something related to the interpretation of his dream, which Yusuf had previously interpreted: ﴿He said, "You will sow for seven years in succession; so what you harvest, leave in its ear, except for a little which you eat. Then after that will come seven hard years which will consume what you have stored up for them, except a little of what you store. Then after that will come a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [juice]."﴾ (12:47–49) This is an economic process requiring planning, implementation, follow-up, good management, firmness, and knowledge. Therefore Yusuf's request, peace be upon him, contained an affirmation that the coming reality would come in accordance with his interpretation of the dream. The verses say: ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the storehouses(3) of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾ (12:55)

(1) The first time is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me." So when the messenger came to him, he said, "Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plot."﴾ (12:50). The second time is in His saying here: ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will select him for myself. So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established and trusted in our presence."﴾ (12:54).

(2) "Daaban" (persistently): one who is diligent in his work and keeps to it without slackening; i.e., persevering and striving. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/219], adapted.

(3) "Al-Khaza'in" (storehouses): plural of "khizana," the place where useful things are kept. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir [2/482]: "They are the granaries in which the crops are gathered for the years they were told of, so that they may be managed in the most cautious, most beneficial, and most rightly guided manner."

This statement is a confirmation of Yusuf's confidence that the one who comes to govern this land needs wisdom in management, one who does not squander what will come in the years of plenty, so as to ensure security in the years of hardship; and that task requires preservation and knowledge.

It has already been established that Yusuf, peace be upon him, possessed these two qualities.

Someone may say: Is there not in Yusuf's words a suggestion of seeking authority? And the principle (1) states: one who seeks authority is not appointed.

But Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not seek authority; rather he sought reform, so that he might take his reform as a path for his call and as the fulfilment of his mission, since he was one who commands and is obeyed, not one who is commanded under compulsion, being confident in faith and trusted in his faith.

Circumstances may arise that do not tolerate trial with people, so whoever is confident in himself that he is capable of carrying out the task may offer himself for it.

An example of this: Suppose a people have boarded a ship; then the winds rose, the storm blew, matters became complicated, and the captain was confused, and someone came to him saying that he is able to resolve this matter for him and to manage the steering of the vessel well, and the captain had previously known this of him.

Here the captain must allow this expert to steer the ship; and after the difficult situation ends, the captain must thank this expert and return to steering his own ship.

Thus: a person has the right to seek authority when it becomes incumbent upon him, by seeing a matter being approached by an inexperienced person who would corrupt it, while he knows the way of its righteousness; and here intervention becomes an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) for the rescue of society.

In such a case, one who seeks authority possesses two kinds of courage:

The first courage: that he sought authority for himself, out of his confidence in bringing the task to success.

The second courage: that he prevented the one who has no experience from assuming a post whose management he does not know; and thereby falsehood ceases to dispose of affairs.

Thus the face of truth becomes apparent, and the domination of falsehood is removed.

For this reason we find Yusuf, peace be upon him, saying to the king: ﴿Appoint me over the treasures of the land; indeed I am a guardian, knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 55].

The treasures contain what enables one who controls them to lead the economy.

It has been said: Yusuf asked the king to appoint him over the treasures of the land, in order to set an economic policy with which they would face seven years of drought, and that is a matter requiring wisdom, preservation and knowledge.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, would take from every person seeking grain payment in gold and silver; and whoever did not possess gold and silver would bring precious stones, or bring livestock to take food in exchange. And whoever possessed none would bring some of his sons to be enslaved; that is, the poor head of the household would say: Take this boy to be a slave in exchange for my taking food for the rest of the family.

Yusuf, peace be upon him, would manage the matter well in the years of drought so that each person would tighten his belt, so that one would not eat with seven intestines but with one intestine, as our Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, says in the noble hadith: "The believer eats with one intestine, and the disbeliever eats with seven intestines." (2)

Provisioning in years of drought requires precise planning and admits no extravagance. Since everything has a price that must be paid, each person would take according to what he had; and after the years of drought ended and the years of plenty came, Yusuf returned to each person what he had taken from him.

When he was asked: "Why did you take from them if you had decided to return to them what you had taken?"

He answered: "So that each person takes only the minimum that suffices him in the years of drought."

Something similar happens among us when we find some people buying subsidised bread to feed to livestock, and when the price of bread rises we find each person buying within the limits of the money he has, and eager not to throw away anything of what he has bought. The state's capacity in times of drought was limited, so it became necessary for each individual to act for himself.

We see this matter, and it recurs in our lives: when a person cannot find the price of meat, perhaps his soul does not yearn for meat, and he may proudly declare: "My stomach can no longer bear meat." The poor man may declare his love for small fish because its flesh is tasty, in contrast to large fish whose flesh is "mutafallal" (stale/insipid), or he may express his admiration for fresh radish because it is delicious food. And long ago in the early years of life, when we lived far from our families' homes during our years of study, and we came back to find only one patty of "ta'miya" (falafel), we would divide this patty so that it would suffice for the last morsel of the loaf. But if we entered and found five patties of ta'miya, each of us would eat half a patty with a single morsel. Thus each one bears according to his movement and his capacity.

And the poet says:
The soul is eager when you make it eager,
and when it is brought down to little, it is content.

1 - The evidence for this principle is what Muslim transmitted in his Sahih [1733] from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "By Allah, we do not appoint to this office anyone who asks for it, nor anyone who is eager for it."
2 - Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih [2060] [184], Book of Drinks, from the hadith of Jabir and Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

And thus did We establish Joseph in the land, to dwell in it wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers. (12:56)

Thus was God's establishment of Joseph, peace be upon him, in the land, such that he managed the affairs of Egypt in a firm and just manner. When the famine came, it did not strike Egypt alone; rather, it spread to the lands around it. The evidence is that there were people from other lands who came seeking their sustenance from it. The clearest example is the brothers of Joseph, who came from al-Sham seeking food for themselves and for those waiting for them in their own land. This is proof that the area of hardship was vast.

As for the words of the Truthful One, may He be glorified: ﴿And thus did We establish Joseph in the land, to dwell in it wherever he willed..﴾ (12:56) [Joseph]. From this we understand that he made for himself a dwelling in more than one place. Let no one suppose that this is a kind of extravagant luxury. But why not look at it with eyes that reveal the reality of administrative officials in some countries? As soon as they learn that a residence for the rulers exists in a certain region, and that the ruler may visit it, they take care of the entire region in which this residence lies. We see this in our contemporary life: when the ruler visits a certain area, they re-pave the streets, repair the utilities, and may even bring in plant pots to beautify the place. So how much more so if they learn that a residence for the ruler exists in a certain place? They will surely continue to attend to every detail related to the utilities in that location.

Therefore, the words of the Truthful One here concerning Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿where he willed..﴾ (12:56) [Joseph] mean: the spread of care for services to all who live in this land. Do not take the matter as mere luxury and honor, but take this statement as a responsibility from which those around him will benefit, whether they were intended by it or not.

This is a picture showing that dwelling wherever he willed was not only mercy toward him, but also mercy toward the people. Therefore the Truthful One says in the same verse: ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will..﴾ (12:56) [Joseph]. Whoever was living without clean water will be reached by pure water; and whoever was struggling to live in a comfortable place will find the area in which he resides transformed into a comfortable place with all the requirements of the age in which he lives. So Joseph, established in the land, has a dwelling adjoining him, and he will find care from the administrative apparatus wherever he goes, and care will cover everyone, as mercy from God to him and to the people around him.

The Truthful One concludes the noble verse with His words: ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers (12:56)﴾ [Joseph].

The good-doer is one who does something beyond what was asked of him.

Here we find that goodness is attributed to Joseph, because when he established for himself a dwelling in more than one place, he benefited the people of those places where he had homes, by raising the standard of services in utilities and other things.

And He, glorified be He, rewards the good-doers with complete and full recompense, and He rewarded Joseph, peace be upon him, with establishment in the land together with the love of those who were entrusted to his affairs.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 12, verse 57:

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾ (57)

Here He, glory be to Him, makes clear that He does not reward the good-doers only in this world, but recompenses them with a better and more enduring reward in the Hereafter. The word "khayr" (good, better) is used in two ways:

The first: that one thing is better than another; that is, both are sharers in goodness. This is the meaning intended here. The example is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

("The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and in each there is good. Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, 'If only I had done such and such,' but say, 'Allah decreed it, and He does what He wills,' for 'if only' opens the work of Satan.")(1)

The second use of the word "khayr": it is the opposite of "sharr" (evil). The example is the saying of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He:

﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. (7) And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it. (8)﴾ [al-Zalzalah]

The Truth, glory be to Him, wills that the balance of life's movement be equitable. The balance of life's movement would not be equitable if we said to man in absolute terms: you will receive the reward of your good deeds in the Hereafter, because only the believer would accept that.

As for the disbeliever, he may oppress, shed blood, steal, and corruption spreads in the earth.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, willed to make recompense of two kinds: recompense in this world for whoever does good, whether he is a believer or a disbeliever, and recompense in the Hereafter, which is specific to those who believe in Him, glory be to Him.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says here:

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾ (57) [Yusuf]

That is: it is greater in good than the reward of this world, because the reward of the Hereafter lasts forever, unlike the worldly good which you may miss or which may pass from you, given that the world is limited for you by your lifespan in it; but the Hereafter has the permanence that Allah, glory be to Him, willed for it.

1 - Related by Ahmad ibn Hanbal in his Musnad [2/366, 370], and Muslim in his Sahih [2664], and Ibn Majah in his Sunan [79], from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).
2 - al-Mithqal: a known weight of measure. The Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight (40)﴾ [al-Nisa'], that is, the amount of the weight of an atom; He does not wrong anything, small or great. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/109].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 58:

﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him, and he recognised them, but they were unknowing of him.﴾

Joseph did recognise them, but they did not recognise him. They had cast him into the well when he was a young boy, and his journey through life then continued after some of the caravan (al-sayyarah) found him and sold him to the ruler of Egypt (ʿAzīz Miṣr). Thus there passed over him a succession of events: his physical maturing and exceptional beauty, the seduction attempt by the wife of the ʿAzīz, and then the seven years of imprisonment.

Each of these events left its mark on a person's features. Moreover, they came to him while he was in his high position, which imposed upon him a dignified appearance and clothing.

As for him, he recognised them because he had left them when they were grown men, their features already settled. We know that when a person passes a decade of years, that time may further define his features if he is mature and adult, but it does not change them the way time changes the features of a child as he grows and reaches maturity.

What drove them to come was the famine, which did not affect Egypt alone but also affected the regions adjacent to it.

The matter of Joseph, peace be upon him, had spread, for he had stored up provisions in anticipation of that famine. Their father had sent them to seek from him provisions (al-mīrah) and food, and they never imagined in any way that the one before them was their brother whom they had cast into the well.

Footnote 1 – al-Mīrah: food that a person procures, i.e., brings in; māra ahlahu: he brought them food. The Almighty said: ﴿And we will bring provisions for our family and guard our brother...﴾ [Yusuf: 65]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/246].

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 12, verse 59:

Almighty Allah says: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provision, he said, "Bring me a brother of yours from your father. Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?" (59)﴾

It is certain that he spoke with them about their circumstances, and let them tell him about their father and their brother, and that they had asked for grain; and he ordered that it be prepared for them.

The word "al-jihaz" (provision, equipment) is used here for that which caused them to move from their homeland to meet Yusuf in search of grain.

Then he asked them, after that, to bring their brother Benjamin with them, and said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of hosts?﴾ In this there is a reminder to them that he gives full measure completely. It appears that they had asked him for an increase in the grain, on the claim that they had a brother whom they had left with their old father, so Yusuf asked them to bring their brother so that he might give them an additional measure of grain, because he does not like to give anyone without clear evidence, out of his commitment to justice.

Each of them had come on a camel, carrying goods which they would pay as the price of what they took. When they come back with their brother, they will take a camel's load over and above what they took this time. They had said this to their father when he asked them about sending their brother with them on the journey, as Yusuf (peace be upon him) had requested. Therefore the verse says: ﴿and we will get an extra camel-load.﴾ (65)

His saying: ﴿and that I am the best of hosts (59)﴾ means that he welcomes guests. They sensed this from the good place where they were lodged, with its comfort and fine reception, and the presence of everything a guest needs during his stay.

The word "manzil" (one who lodges/host) apparently is the opposite of "mu'alla" (one who is raised up); its true meaning is: a host from among those who lodge, in a place where all the requirements of life are present. The Almighty says of Paradise: ﴿a welcome (nuzul) from the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful (32)﴾ [Fussilat]. That is, He, glory be to Him, has prepared Paradise with what surpasses human imagination, and with the absolute attributes of forgiveness and mercy. And if the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is the one who prepares, then what He has prepared must be beyond human imagination.

I once said to my brothers who were dazzled by a luxurious hotel in San Francisco: when a person sees something good, or something refined, or something beautiful with another person, he receives it in one of two ways; his self appears in it. If he is envious, he looks at things with hatred and resentment; but if he is a believer, he rejoices and says: this blessing that I see increases my longing for Paradise, because this blessing that I see was made by a human for humans; so what of God's making of Paradise? He who created the whole universe, with all its human beings?

And I always say: I have never seen blessing with anyone without my faith increasing, [realizing] that the blessing I see was prepared by humans for humans; so what of what the Creator of humans has prepared for the believing humans?

As for one who looks at the blessing in another's hand with envy, he deprives himself of the longing for that blessing that is with its owner; for the blessing has a longing (sababah) for its possessor and clings to him. If you rejoice in the blessing with a person, be assured that the blessing will knock at your door; and if you dislike it with someone else, you will have disliked the blessing coming to you.

If you want the good that is with another, you must love the blessing that is with that other, so that the blessing will strive toward him, without burdening yourself with managing or maintaining this blessing, because it will come to you by the power of the Almighty.

Yusuf's saying (peace be upon him) in this verse, which is the subject of our reflections: ﴿and that I am the best of hosts (59)﴾ is a statement from him confirming the justice with which he received them, the full measure, and the good hospitality; and there is no doubt that when they bring their brother, they will find the same reception.

(1) Jihaz of the bride, the traveler and the army: it is what they need and what is necessary for them on their journey. The meaning here is that he gave them full measure and provided the food for which they came. [See Tafsir Ibn Kathir 2/483, and al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/134].

(2) "Al-Suddi and others mentioned that Yusuf (peace be upon him) spoke to them, saying to them as one disapproving of them: What brought you to my land? They said: O Chieftain, we have come for grain. He said: Perhaps you are spies? They said: God forbid. He said: Where are you from? They said: From the land of Canaan, and our father Ya'qub is a prophet of God. He said: Does he have other sons besides you? They said: Yes, we were twelve; our youngest went off and perished in the wilderness, and he was the dearest of us to our father, and his full brother remained, so his father kept him back to console himself with him. Then he ordered that they be lodged and honored." [Tafsir Ibn Kathir 2/483].

(3) Nuzul: arriving at a place, and nuzl and nazl: what is prepared for a guest when he alights at someone's house. [Lisan al-'Arab, root n-z-l].

(4) Nuzl: a dwelling, and what is prepared for a guest to lodge in. The Most High said: ﴿abiding therein, a welcome from God...(198)﴾ [Al 'Imran]. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/260].

(5) Sababah: longing. One says: "I longed for the thing with longing (sababah), so I am a passionate one (sabb), a lover longing." [Lisan al-'Arab, root s-b-b].

Almighty Allah continues with what was said by the tongue of Yusuf: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me, and you shall not come near me﴾ (60). Yusuf, knowing in advance how difficult it would be for their father to trust them with their brother, issued this warning to them: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure (of grain) for you with me...﴾ (60).

He said this to them, while he knew that the return (al-ma'ad) would be a return of drought, dearth and famine(1).

Yusuf added: ﴿and you shall not come near me﴾ (60), i.e., do not come to the region of this land which I govern; and for this reason we will find them saying to their father after that:

﴿O our father, the measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us that we may obtain a measure, and indeed we will be its guardians﴾ (63).

(1) al-Ma'ad: the place of return and final destination, i.e., that your return is to a land of drought and famine, and it is the homeland from which they had come. Al-ma'ad and al-mu'adah: the gathering place to which one returns. [Lisan al-Arab, entry: '-w-d].

They said: "We will seek to persuade our father about him, and we will surely do it."

Their words, "We will seek to persuade (sanurawidu) our father about him..." (12:61), mean that the matter is not easy. They know what they did before with Joseph. Murawada (persistent seeking, coaxing, pressing) means back-and-forth effort and requires cunning (ihtiyal). The meaning was already explained in the words of the Truthful, Glorified be He: "And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself..." (12:23).

They reinforced their statement with "and we will surely do it" (12:61), meaning that they will exert all their efforts so that their father will agree to send their brother with them, while they know that this is a demanding goal, difficult to achieve.

1 - That is: we will be keen to bring him to you by every possible means and will spare no effort, so that you know we are truthful in what we have said. [Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir, 2/483].

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And he said to his servants, "Put their merchandise back into their saddlebags, so that they may recognize it when they return to their family; perhaps they will come back."﴾ That is, Yusuf (peace be upon him) ordered his attendants to return the goods which these men had brought with them, so that they might exchange them for the grain and food they had taken. The attendants of Yusuf (peace be upon him) had to carry out his order by placing these goods discreetly in the saddlebags on which they rode, and in this there was an encouragement for them to come back again.

1 - Qayyada (qāyada) muqayadah: if he gives him a commodity and takes in return another commodity. Al-qay (qayd) means "exchange" or "return." [Lisan al-Arab, root: q-y-d].
2 - Ibn Kathir mentioned several opinions on this, among them: that Yusuf feared they would not have other merchandise with which to return for provisions. It was also said: he was ashamed to take from his father and brothers a return for the food. [See Tafsir Ibn Kathir, 2/483].

When they returned to their father, they said: "O our father, the measure has been withheld from us, so send our brother with us that we may get our measure, and indeed we will be its guardians."

This was the first news they gave their father upon their return, with the provisions in hand. It seems they wanted to make clear to the father that they would be prevented from going to Egypt in future unless their brother was with them.

They told their father their story with the ruler of Egypt, and that if the father agreed to send their brother Benjamin (Bunyamin) with them, then they would be given their measure, and they would guard their little brother.

In this statement, they were trying to remove the father's suspicion regarding what had happened to Joseph (Yusuf) earlier.

Here the Real (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, brings what their father Ya'qub (peace be upon him) said:

﴿He said: "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted his brother to you before? But God is the best guardian, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

Here their father reminds them that they had not previously offered anything that would reassure him about this. They had lost their brother Yusuf, and they had said: "A wolf has eaten him."

He added: ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Yusuf: 64]. This is a statement in which we perceive that he has consented to Binyamin's going with them, and that he is calling upon the Real to protect his son.

The sons of Ya'qub began to open their goods after the journey, and after the discussion with their father.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 65:

Allah, glory be to Him, says:

﴿When they opened their belongings, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. They said: "O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us. And we will bring provisions for our family, and protect our brother, and gain an extra camel-load. That is an easy measure."﴾ (65)

Thus they discovered that the merchandise they had carried with them on their journey to Egypt, to barter with and to pay as the price for what they wished to obtain of food and provisions (mira), had been returned to them. They announced to their father that they did not desire more than that, for they had obtained the provisions (mira) by which they and their families would be sustained.

They must accompany their brother on the next trip, and they will protect him, and they will return with an additional camel-load, and this is a light matter for the ruler of Egypt.

However, their father Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said what Allah, glory be to Him, relates here:

﴿He said: "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in Allah's name that you will surely bring him back to me, unless you are encompassed entirely." And when they gave him their solemn covenant, he said: "Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾ (66)

1 - Al-mithaq and al-mawthiq (covenant): a firm pledge. Allah, exalted, says: ﴿And His covenant with which He bound you⋯﴾ [al-Ma'idah 7], meaning the pledge that He made you swear to and obligated you to fulfil. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/319].

2 - Al-ihatah bi al-shay' (encompassing a thing): surrounding it from all its sides. His words ﴿unless you are encompassed entirely⋯﴾ [Yusuf 66] mean: unless you are prevented or your way of escape is blocked. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/178].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 66:

We note here the tenderness of Ya'qub's heart and how quickly he agreed to send his son Binyamin (Benjamin) with them to Egypt. This tenderness had already appeared earlier in his saying: ﴿So Allah is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Yusuf: 64]. He asked them to swear a binding oath that they would return from their journey to Egypt, bringing their brother Binyamin with them if he went with them, unless some matter beyond human will should overtake them, such as enemies surrounding them and destroying them and destroying Binyamin along with them. This is from the prudence of prophethood. Therefore he said: ﴿Unless you are encompassed [by calamity]...﴾ [Yusuf: 66]. The sons of Ya'qub swore to that and gave their father the oath and pledge to bring Binyamin back, and so that Allah would be a witness over them. Ya'qub said: ﴿Allah is Trustee over what we say﴾ [Yusuf: 66], meaning that He, glory be to Him, is aware and watchful; so if you betray, then He, glory be to Him, is the Avenger.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 67:

Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, enjoins his sons, the Asbat (the tribes):

﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates. And I cannot avail you against Allah at all. Judgment is only for Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely [indeed] rely."﴾ (67) Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said these words the second time they went to Egypt, after he had learned of Yusuf's good reception of them, that their merchandise had been returned to them, and he knew from this that they had become favoured by the Ruler of Egypt.

Whenever you see a person who has standing, you expect that he will be an enemy, and so Ya'qub feared lest someone plot against them, because they were strangers.

From here he commanded them to enter Egypt by different gates. In earlier times cities had gates that were opened and closed at specified times, and when they enter individually, no one will notice that they are a group. Ya'qub feared for his sons from envy, and we know that envy exists.

Allah, glorified is He, has taught us to seek refuge in Him from envy, because He, glorified is He, knew from eternity that envy is a matter beyond the power of people to repel, and He is the One who said:

﴿Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak (1) from the evil of what He created (2) and from the evil of darkness when it settles (3) and from the evil of the blowers in knots (4) and from the evil of an envier when he envies."﴾ [Al-Falaq]

Regarding envy, you cannot seek refuge in someone equal to you, because envy comes from something unknown and unperceived. The ray that emanates from the eye may blaze with resentment toward everyone who possesses a blessing. In our age, the age of material advancement, people have arrived at using radiation to disintegrate things.

So it is possible that envy is like those radiations, which Allah may place in the eyes of some of His creatures, so that the glance is like a piercing arrow or a deadly bullet.

And the Truth, glorified is He, said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.. (31)﴾ [Al-Muddaththir]

If someone says: Why does Allah, glorified is He, give some of His creatures these properties?

I say: He, glorified is He, gives some of His creatures capacities which they then use in the wrong place. Every person in some form has the capacity for a glance, but it is resentment that kindles the harmful spark. You may look without envy if you say: "Mashallah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, Allahumma barik" (1).

By this the arousal necessary to ignite the harmful spark is not realised. You may seek refuge in Allah, the Creator of mankind and Knower of secrets, and recite the words of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿Say, "I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak (1) from the evil of what He created (2) and from the evil of darkness when it settles (3) and from the evil of the blowers in knots (4) and from the evil of an envier when he envies."﴾ [Al-Falaq]

And you may say the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he sought refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, saying: ("I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and venomous creature (2), and from every evil eye (3).") (4). And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ("Your father, Ibrahim, used to seek refuge with them for Isma'il and Ishaq, peace be upon them.")

Likewise, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, "when a matter distressed him, he would stand and pray" (5). For the meaning of a matter distressing the Messenger of Allah, or one of his followers, is that this matter lies beyond human capacity.

Here a person must take refuge in the One who causes causes, for He is the firm support, after you have taken the means that Allah has extended to you from His hand. Thus your going to the Truth is the going of one who is compelled, not the going of one who is idle in taking the means.

And the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Is He who responds to the compelled one when he calls upon Him and removes the evil.. (62)﴾ [An-Naml]

The compelled one is he who has exhausted all his means and does not call upon his Lord until he has taken all the extended means. So do not ask of Allah's Essence before you have taken what He has provided for you by His hand of means.

Here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, we find Ya'qub, peace be upon him, having enjoined his sons not to enter Egypt by one gate but by different gates, out of fear of envy. The matter of faith, with what it requires of submission to Allah's will, was aroused, so he said: ﴿And I cannot avail you against Allah at all.. (67)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning: my caution will not make me any richer than the decree of Allah. It is merely caution; the benefit of that caution and planning is from the command of Allah. For this reason he said: ﴿Judgment is only for Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and upon Him let those who rely [indeed] rely. (67)﴾ [Yusuf]. All creation's affairs return to Allah, upon Him Ya'qub relies, and upon Him every believer relies.

1 - The Exalted says: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except in Allah"?.. (39)﴾ [Al-Kahf].
2 - Al-Hammah: singular of hawam, meaning snakes and scorpions, and every poisonous creature that kills with its venom. As for what does not kill and sting, it is al-sawam. [Lisan al-Arab, root h-w-m].
3 - Al-lammah: what you fear of touch or fright; al-lammah also means the evil eye that afflicts a person. [Lisan al-Arab, root l-m-m].
4 - Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [1/270], al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [2060], and Abu Dawud in his Sunan [4737], from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Tirmidhi said: "A hasan sahih hadith."
5 - Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad [5/388] and Abu Dawud in his Sunan [1319], from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman.

The sons of Jacob carried out what their father had commanded them. Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿And when they entered from where their father had ordered them, it did not avail them at all against Allah; it was only a need within Jacob's soul which he fulfilled. And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most of the people do not know.﴾ (68)

That is: their entering from where their father had ordered them did not ward off from them a matter that Allah, glorified is He, had willed. Nothing turns back the decree of Allah. Perhaps their father wished to ward off from them the envy of the envious, or that someone might plot against them or suspect them, but nothing can prevent the decree of Allah.

For this reason Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿except a need within Jacob's soul which he fulfilled..﴾ (68) [Yusuf]. Jacob knew that nothing can turn back the decree of Allah, and Allah, glorified is He, did not give precautionary measures by which people could prevent the decree of Allah.

Allah, glorified is He, says here about Jacob: ﴿And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him..﴾ (68) [Yusuf]. That is: he knew the place of the causer and the place of the causes, and he knew that taking the means does not contradict reliance upon Allah, since Allah, glorified is He, created the causes out of mercy for His servants.

﴿But most of the people do not know.﴾ (68) [Yusuf]. That is: they separate the causes from the Causer, and this is what wearies the world.

1 - "Qada hajatahu" (he fulfilled his need): he reached it and attained it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿except a need within Jacob's soul which he fulfilled..﴾ (86) [Yusuf]. That is: he reached it and obtained it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim: 2/122].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 69:

Then He, glory be to Him, says after that: ﴿And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself. He said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not be distressed by what they used to do."﴾ That is: when they entered upon Joseph, he received them with the best reception and honoured their hospitality, after they had fulfilled their promise to him and brought their brother, his full brother Benjamin, with them. Joseph, peace be upon him, had been longing for his full brother Benjamin.

We have already known that he is Joseph's only full brother, for the two are from one mother, whereas the rest of the brothers are from other mothers.

The words of the Truth, glory be to Him, about Joseph: ﴿he took his brother to himself..﴾ [Joseph] indicate that Joseph was yearning to see his brother.

And His saying: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I am your brother, so do not be distressed by what they used to do."﴾ [Joseph] makes clear to us that Joseph's brothers had kept Benjamin apart for a period, and had not treated him well, and Joseph sought to comfort his brother and to remove the distress he had suffered because of what his brothers were doing.

1 - Al-wafd (delegation): the honoured riders. Al-Asma'i said: Fulan wafada, yafidu, wifada, when he went out to a king or a commander. [Lisan al-'Arab, root w-f-d].
2 - Istafrada fulanan: to be alone with him. Istafrada al-shay': he took it out from among its companions; and afradahu: he made it singular. [Lisan al-'Arab, root f-r-d].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 12, verse 70:

﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions, he put the drinking-cup (1) in his brother's saddlebag. Then a crier called out: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!" (70)﴾

That is: Yusuf, peace be upon him, had arranged the provision of grain for them, as he had promised them, and as he had equipped them on the previous occasion. He wished to keep his brother with him in Egypt. But how could he take him from his brothers and keep him with himself, when their father had taken a covenant from them that they would not lose him and would not neglect him, just as they had done with his brother before?

So: there must be a stratagem by which he could keep his brother with him. And God mobilised for him in this matter his brothers, who used to be hostile to him and used to harbour resentment against him and his brother.

Here comes the account of the king's cup, which the king drinks from and which is used as a measure, and he placed it in his brother's saddlebag.

The word "al-siqaya" (the drinking-cup, al-saqaya) is used in several senses from the root "sqy" (s-q-y), that is: "s", "q" and "y". It is applied to giving people and pilgrims water to drink.

The Noble Qur'an says: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque equal to [the deeds of] one who believes in God and the Last Day...? (19)﴾ [al-Tawba]. So the meaning of al-siqaya is also the place where water is put so that people may drink from it. Or: "al-siqaya" is applied to the vessel by which water is brought out for those who drink.

Here the word "al-siqaya" is applied to the vessel from which the king would drink, and which is used as a measure, and this is evidence of the preciousness of what is measured.

The word "sawa'" (cup, sa') is also applied to such an instrument from which one drinks, or by which water is raised from a place to the mouth of the drinker; it is also used for measuring, and its singular is "sa'".

The Truthful, glorified is He, says here about Yusuf's stratagem to keep his brother with him: ﴿He put the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag...(70)﴾ [Yusuf]. That is: he ordered some of his helpers to place the "siqaya" in his brother's saddlebag. The "rahl" is what is placed on the camel, and in it is all the traveller's baggage.

After the brothers of Yusuf had mounted their camels in preparation for returning to al-Sham, the surprise befell them, of which the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿Then a crier called out (2): "O caravan, you are surely thieves!" (70)﴾ [Yusuf]. That is: "O company of that caravan, you are thieves." Theft is a shameful act when a penalty falls upon the thief as a consequence, and what is stolen is a valuable thing.

It seems that this stratagem was carried out with the agreement of Benjamin, so that he would remain with his brother Yusuf until his parents (3) came to Egypt.

One may ask: how did Benjamin consent to this, when it is a matter that increases Ya'qub's grief? And how does Yusuf accuse his brothers of a theft they did not commit?

I say: look at the precision of the Qur'an, and let us understand it well, so that we may see that Ya'qub's grief over the loss of Yusuf had overwhelmed him, so the loss of Benjamin would not affect him much.

The proof of this is that when Ya'qub, peace be upon him, was told by his sons of the story of the theft and the detention of Benjamin in Egypt, he said: ﴿Alas for my grief over Yusuf...(84)﴾ [Yusuf].

Ya'qub did not mention Benjamin.

As for their being accused of theft: the verse here does not specify exactly what they had stolen, while in Yusuf's view they had stolen him from his father and thrown him into the well.

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, brings the position of the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿They said, turning towards them: "What is it that you are missing?" (71)﴾

1 - "Al-siqaya" is applied to the vessel with which one gives drink. It was a silver cup with which they used to measure food [Lisan al-'Arab, root: s-q-y].
2 - "Adhdhana ta'dhinan wa adhanan": he informed of the matter; the doubling of the letter indicates abundance and repetition. The Exalted said: ﴿Then a crier called out, "O caravan, you are surely thieves!" (70)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning: he called out, informed, and repeated the calling and informing [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/16].
3 - By "his parents" is meant: his father Ya'qub, and his maternal aunt, the wife of his father, because Rachel, the mother of Yusuf and Benjamin, had died in childbirth with Benjamin [see Tafsir al-Qurtubi 5/3598].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 71:

That is: the brothers of Joseph turned to those who were accusing them of theft, asking: "What have you lost? And why do you accuse us?"

Here the Truth, glorified is He, relates what those who accused them said:

﴿They said: "We have lost the king's goblet, and for whoever brings it is a camel-load [of grain], and I am its guarantor."﴾ (72)

1 - Al-za'im (the guarantor): the surety, the bondsman, and the chief. One says "za'ama bi-al-amr" meaning he took responsibility for the matter, so he is a za'im, that is, a guarantor. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/286].

Al-Sha'rawi said: That is, those who proclaimed them to be thieves said to them: "The drinking-vessel of the king has been lost," and it is called "al-sawa' (the goblet)." Whoever brings it out from the place where it is hidden will receive a reward of a camel's load. So perhaps the king's goblet has been put into the load of one of you without intention.

The herald affirmed that he would guarantee the reward to whoever brings out the king's goblet, and produces it without searching, namely a camel's load of provisions (al-mirah, food supplies).

Here the brothers of Yusuf, peace be upon him, said:

﴿They said: "By Allah, you know well that we did not come to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves."﴾ (12:73)

Their words, ﴿By Allah﴾, are an oath. The "ta'" (تاء) is commonly attached to the word Allah (لفظ الجلالة) in an oath that is meant to express astonishment. That is, the brothers of Joseph swore in amazement at being accused of stealing, since everyone knew about them that they had not come with the intention of causing corruption through theft or anything else; no one had previously accused them of such a charge.

Here the Truth, glorified is He, brings what was said on the tongues of those who announced that a theft had occurred, and that the stolen item was the king's goblet (ṣuwā' al-malik).

He, glory be to Him, says what came from their own tongues:

﴿They said, "What is its penalty if you are lying?"﴾ (12:74)

This is a question from Yusuf's aides to Yusuf's brothers about the punishment prescribed in their law for one who steals. What should we do to the one in whose baggage the king's goblet is found, once your lying is established, that you did not steal it?

The Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 75:

It was well known that whoever was caught in theft under the law of the family of Ya'qub (Jacob) would be enslaved or would remain in the service of those whom he had robbed; just as Yusuf's aunt did, for she loved him and he lived with her after his mother's death. When his father wished to take him back, she concealed in Yusuf's garments an precious thing (shay'an 'aziz) that she had inherited from her father Ishaq (Isaac), and by that means she kept Yusuf with her. His father did not take him except after his aunt had died.

Yusuf (peace be upon him) therefore had the aim of keeping his brother with him, and he had known this ruling beforehand. Thus Yusuf (peace be upon him) left them to pass the judgment themselves, the judgment that he longed for, namely that his brother remain with him.

Almighty Allah relates their words:

﴿They said: "The recompense for it is that he in whose bag it is found, he himself is the recompense for it. Thus do we recompense the wrongdoers."﴾

Thus they pronounced the judgment themselves, and they confirmed it by their saying: ﴿Thus do we recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ [Yusuf]

Thus they helped Yusuf to achieve his purpose of keeping his brother with him, and Yusuf ordered the caravan to be searched.

And the Exalted says:

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother; then he brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed. We raise by degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is One, the All-Knowing.﴾ (12:76)

The purpose of beginning the search with their bags, they being ten, before the bag of his full brother, was to negate the possibility of their suspicion that he had asked them to bring their brother with them so that he could plot this matter himself. He then searched his brother's bag after that, in order to extract from it the king's goblet and to apply to him the law of the religion of the family of Jacob, so that he would retain his brother with him. This is evidence of wise cunning.

Thus God, the Exalted, made the scheming work in Joseph's favour, He who said: ﴿Thus did We devise for Joseph..﴾ (12:76), meaning: the scheming was for his benefit.

He continues: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed..﴾ (12:76), meaning: Joseph could not have taken his brother under the king's law that governed Egypt, were it not for the ruling of the brothers that their law required this.

He continues: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is One, the All-Knowing.﴾ (12:76)

Thus God raised Joseph's standing, devised for him, fulfilled his hope, and he deserved all of that; and God raised him to high degrees of knowledge and wisdom.

The scheming was not for the purpose of bringing torment or loss upon his brother; rather, We desired for Joseph and his brother elevation. Many calamities befall people while they do not know that within the trial there are gifts.

The believer should know that any difficult matter that befalls him, without any choice of his own, must be felt to contain some benefit from God for the human being.

As for Joseph's brothers, they had earlier schemed against him, so what was the outcome of their scheming? God, the Exalted, willed to make the entire scheme work for Joseph's benefit, and He made him a possessor of knowledge, so He said: ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is One, the All-Knowing.﴾ (12:76)

﴿Possessor of knowledge (dhu 'ilm)⦆ means: a person who has knowledge, and the two are separate: there is the "possessor" and there is the "knowledge." The possessor exists first, and afterwards knowledge comes to him, so he becomes a possessor of knowledge. But above him is ﴿the All-Knowing (ʿAlīm)﴾ (12:76), meaning that knowledge is intrinsic to Him, and He is God, the Exalted and Most High.

So what was the stance of Joseph's brothers? Naturally, they must have been stunned. The first action they took was to turn upon the brother in whose saddlebag the goblet had been found; they began to rebuke him, because he had embarrassed and disgraced them, and they sought reasons of their own for resentment against him, not for gentleness toward him.

Their prior attitude toward him is known from their saying: {Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we, though we are a band (ʿuṣba)(1)..} (8) [Joseph]

They knew that Joseph and his brother were from another woman, named "Rachel", and had they been full brothers to them, they would have been gentler with him(2). He clarified to them: whoever placed the merchandise in my saddlebag is the one who placed the merchandise in your saddlebags.

Here one of the brothers said: "By God, O sons of Rachel, how much calamity has come upon us from you!" Benjamin replied: "The sons of Rachel have suffered from you calamity beyond what has come upon you from them."

1 - ʿuṣba: a closely bound group; ʿuṣba and iṣāba: a group of between ten and forty [Lisan al-Arab, root ʿ-ṣ-b].
2 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir [5/3569] that his brothers, "when they saw that, lowered their heads and turned to him saying: Woe to you, O Benjamin, we never saw you today; your mother Rachel bore two thieves." Their brother said to them: "By God, I did not steal it, and I have no knowledge of who put it in my belongings."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 77:

Almighty Allah here presents their statement: ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before." But Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them. He said: "You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you allege."﴾

Thus they claimed that the disease of theft had been transmitted to Benjamin from a full brother of his before him. They said this in order to clear themselves, and thus the features of their enmity toward Joseph and his brother became evident.

Their saying: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before...﴾ is called in the language a conditional proposition (al-qadiyyah al-shartiyyah). The meaning of a conditional proposition is that one event occurs because of an event that occurred before it. There is an event that occurs on its own, and there is an event that occurs on condition that another event has occurred before it.

An example of this is your saying to a student: "If you study your lessons, you will succeed." Here there are two events, studying and succeeding. The occurrence of success is conditional upon the occurrence of studying, and the condition must occur first; then the second event occurs. Here it is their saying: ﴿a brother of his had stolen before...﴾ as a justification for Benjamin's theft.

An example from the Qur'an as well is: ﴿But if they deny you, messengers before you were denied﴾ [Al 'Imran: 184]. It is as if Allah is clarifying to the Messenger (ﷺ): if they deny you now concerning what you convey to them of news from heaven, do not grieve or be distressed, for this denial is a phenomenon that all the messengers before you suffered from, because they bring what the recipients first reject, so denial must occur. Thus the conditional structure holds, because Almighty Allah has here turned the thing away from its cause, so the answer of the condition came after the time in which the condition occurred.

Here Almighty Allah said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his had stolen before...﴾ That is: do not be surprised, O Chief of Egypt, for this is a trait in the sons of Rachel. They said this while not knowing that they were speaking to Joseph, son of Rachel!

Every event that happens to upright dispositions must necessarily move those dispositions from their state. We see this at the moment when someone utters a word that takes an upright person out of his condition and disturbs him, and the upright person perceives through it what pains him, and is moved by an emotion that makes him inclined to respond. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) advised us: "If one of you becomes angry while standing, let him sit; if the anger leaves him, well and good; otherwise, let him lie down."(1) So that he helps himself to suppress his distress and anger, and so that part of the energy that charges him with emotion may drain away.

But Joseph (peace be upon him) did not incline to respond, therefore Almighty Allah said: ﴿So Joseph kept it hidden within himself...﴾ He could have told them what had happened to him from his aunt, who falsely accused him of theft so that she might keep him in her custody out of excessive love for him. But Joseph (peace be upon him) wished to remain unknown to them, so that matters might take their course: ﴿So Joseph kept it hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them.﴾

This happened although their statement had affected him, but he stated his opinion of them to himself: ﴿You are worse in position, and Allah is most knowing of what you allege﴾ because you are the ones who took me as a child to play, then threw me into the well, and left my father without companionship... and I did not steal, rather I was stolen; and thus you stole a son from his father.

If he said this within himself, his emotion at this statement must have appeared on his features, and meaning may appear on the features so that the meaning reaches them; speech is nothing but words through which the meaning of the discourse reaches a listener. And the meaning reached them through Joseph's emotion.

As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what you allege﴾ that is: He, glory be to Him, is most knowing of what you describe, and of the signs and marks you display, and the word "tasifun" (you allege) prevailed in the discourse.

An example of this is the saying of Almighty Allah: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues allege falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful"...﴾ [An-Nahl: 116]. That is: what you say itself suggests that it is a lie. Thus we know that the words "tasif" and "tasifun" in their usage became predominant for speech that carries with it the evidence of its falsehood.

1 - Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad [5/152], and Abu Dawud in his Sunan [4782], and Ibn Hibban [1973 - Mawarid al-Dham'an], from the hadith of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Haythami said in al-Majma' [8/71]: "Ahmad narrated it and its narrators are the narrators of the authentic (collection)."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, brings about what came from their tongues after that: ﴿They said: "O Chief of Egypt, indeed he has an aged father, so take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers."﴾ (78) Thus they entered into discussion with Joseph and began to appeal to his compassion, by their saying: ﴿Indeed he has an aged father...﴾ (78)

We note that the word "kabīr" (kabīr, great/aged) is used in multiple senses. If you mean old age, it comes from "kabura yakbaru" (kabura yakburu, to grow old), and if you mean greatness of station, you would say "kabura yakburu" (kabura yakburu, to be great in status).
