And the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Terrible is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie.﴾ (5) [al-Kahf]

Greatness (al-kibr) is one of the meanings of majesty, whereas old age (al-kibr fi al-sinn) is different. Here they said: ﴿Indeed he has an aged father...﴾ (78), which may be a softening by his honour, or a softening by his weakness. That is: indeed he has an aged father, great among his people; and when it reaches him that his son has been detained for theft, this is a painful matter. Therefore, consider that, as you are the Chief of Egypt, and we hope you will preserve for the father his honour, his glory and his greatness, and conceal this matter for the sake of the father's esteem and station.

Or: their saying may be intended to convey that the father is a decrepit old man who cannot bear the shock, especially since he has already lost a son.

Then they present another proposal, saying: ﴿So take one of us in his place. Indeed, we see you are among the good-doers.﴾ (78) That is: they asked him to complete his kindness towards them, for he had received them hospitably and had previously lodged them in a noble dwelling, given them provisions, and not taken their goods as payment for them. One who does such a thing would not withhold from them the granting of their request, by taking one of them in place of their younger brother.

All of these are softenings from them towards his heart. But the rule is that no one is held to account for a sin except its perpetrator; therefore this matter was not lost on Joseph, and the Truth, glorified is He, brought what clarifies that: ﴿He said: "God forbid that we should take except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers."﴾ (79)

Yusuf, peace be upon him, seeks refuge in Allah from taking anyone in place of the one in whose belongings the king's goblet was found. What fault is his in this matter? No one can be punished for a sin committed by another.

When you read "إذا" with tanwin, know that there is an omitted clause, meaning: Yusuf said, "If we take other than the one in whose possession we found our property, then we would be among the wrongdoers."

The tanwin came in place of the omitted clause that we have mentioned.

Another example from the Qur'an is the saying of the Truthful, glorified is He: ﴿And you, at that time, are looking on (84)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah]

This happens when the soul reaches the throat, and the tanwin came in place of the entire clause.

Thus Yusuf wanted to remind them that it is not right for him to take one of them in place of Benjamin, because he is the one in whose belongings the king's goblet was found; and it is not proper for him to wrong anyone, or to take anyone for the crime (al-jarirah) of another.

Here the sons of Ya'qub knew that the matter could not be decided easily, because it concerns a grave affair.

¹ Al-jarirah: the offence and sin that a man commits (Lisan al-Arab, root j-r-r).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 80:

The Truthful (subhanahu wa ta'ala) portrays their state, saying:

﴿So when they despaired (1) of him, they withdrew to confer privately (4). Their eldest said: "Did you not know that your father has taken from you a binding covenant (2) in the name of God, and before this you failed in regard to Joseph? So I will not leave (3) this land until my father permits me, or God judges for me, and He is the best of judges."﴾ (80)

It is said: "yaàisa" means he cut off hope in a thing. They did not merely cut off hope; rather they "istay'asu," and this is a matter beyond despair (yas).

They began to employ every kind of softening (means); but there was no benefit. Whenever they brought forward a softening plea, they found the door before them closed.

It is as if by that they were insisting that despair should come to them, because the surrounding circumstances and the surrounding atmosphere bear no glimmer of hope at all. Whenever a glimmer of hope appears and they seek it, they find the way closed. It is as though they were seeking despair from Joseph's permitting the sending of their brother Benjamin with them on the journey back to their father. And here: ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (4)..(80)﴾ meaning: they separated from him, and from the eyes of those present: the Aziz Joseph, and those around him of his helpers, and their brother who was the subject of dispute, and they withdrew with themselves. Withdrawal is secret conversation (munajah), and secret conversation is a matter of confidence; and confidence only exists in a matter you do not want others to see.

We note that ﴿khalasu (they withdrew)..(80)﴾ is plural, and ﴿najiyyan (to confer privately)..(80)﴾ is singular. This is among the places where those who do not possess Arabic linguistic faculty ask: how does the Qur'an use a singular after a plural?

We always say: if they had possessed the language as a faculty, they would have known that this is entirely permissible. An example of this is the saying of the Truthful (subhanahu wa ta'ala): ﴿And the angels after that are a supporter (5) (4)﴾ [At-Tahrim]

They do not understand that the language contains words in which the singular and plural are equal, as if the angels combine the strength of each one of them so that it becomes one strength.

Another example: the saying of Abraham, the Friend of the Most Merciful: ﴿He said: Have you considered what you have been worshipping (75), you and your forefathers (76)? Indeed, they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds (77)﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara'] meaning: Abraham, peace be upon him, gathered the many deities they worshipped and made them one enemy to him.

Likewise we can do the same with the word "sadiq" (friend), and likewise the word "adl" (just/justice). When the judiciary considers a case, the judge does not issue the ruling alone; rather he issues it after consultation with advisers, and the ruling is issued by the three: the president of the court, the member of the right, and the member of the left, both of whom are of the rank of adviser.

It is said: "the judges judged 'adlan' (justly)," and it is not said that each adviser or judge has 'adl'.

Likewise: ﴿najiyyan (privately)..(80)﴾ in the verse which is the subject of our reflections: when they despaired of Joseph, they withdrew with themselves to confer privately. Customarily the first opinion belongs to the eldest brother, who usually has the experience and wisdom that enables him to put forward the right opinion.

Here the Truthful (subhanahu wa ta'ala) says: ﴿Their eldest said: "Did you not know that your father has taken from you a binding covenant in the name of God, and before this you failed in regard to Joseph? So I will not leave this land until my father permits me, or God judges for me, and He is the best of judges."(80)﴾

Their eldest may be the oldest of them in age, or he may be the leader of the journey. When he saw them accepting the idea of returning without their brother whom the Aziz of Egypt had detained, he told them his opinion, warning them not to overlook that their father had taken from them a covenant before God, unless they were encompassed (by calamity); and that they must not forget that they had a prior precedent when they took Joseph and lost him. On that basis his resolve settled that he would not leave the place, and would not return to his father unless he was permitted to do so, or God judged in his favour by the Aziz of Egypt releasing his brother to him, or that he would die right here in this land.

This statement, outwardly, is a defence of himself, and a shame at returning to his father without Benjamin; and for this reason he left his brothers to bear that confrontation with the father.

This matter appears harsher upon the father, because in the first journey he lost Joseph, and in the second journey he loses his son Benjamin, as well as the eldest son who heads the journey. In this there is an escalation of harshness upon the father, and it was expected that there would be deliberation among the brothers in that secret conference, but the eldest brother, or the leader of the journey, settled the matter.

1 - istay'asa: he despaired of him after effort and hardship [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/366].
2 - al-mithaq and al-muwaththaq: the affirmed covenant. God the Exalted said: ﴿And His covenant with which He bound you (7)﴾ [Al-Ma'idah], meaning: His covenant which He made with you, and obliged you to fulfil. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/319].
3 - barraha al-ard: he departed from it and left it; the saying of the eldest of Joseph's brothers here means: I will not leave the land of Egypt. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/61] adapted.
4 - najawahu yanjuwhu najwan: he spoke to him secretly and singled him out for conversation. Fa-khalasu najiyyan means: conferring with one another; tanajā al-rajulan: each of the two made his conversation known to the other in secret. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/255] adapted.
5 - al-zahir: the helper who assists, as if he supports the back of the one who aids him. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/418] adapted.

Then, when they asked him, "What shall we do, our elder?", his saying came, which the following verse conveyed:

﴿Go back to your father and say, "O our father, indeed your son has stolen, and we bear witness only to what we know, and we were not guardians of the unseen."﴾ (12:81)

Thus the eldest brother, or the leader of the journey, ordered his brothers to return to their father and tell him exactly what had happened. He had been accused of theft, and we say these words only after the young men of the Governor found the king's goblet in his baggage. We do not know whether someone planted it for him, or whether it was a stratagem and a plot (hilah wa-makidah)?

We say to you, O our father, only what has reached us of information. The Governor has taken him according to our law. With our knowledge of our brother, we do not testify that he stole. However, the establishing of the presence of the king's goblet in his baggage is the cause of all of that.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 12, verse 82:

The eldest brother knew that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) might disbelieve his sons, because they had a previous record with him. Therefore the eldest brother, or the leader of the caravan, instructed them to say to their father, if he disbelieved them, what the truth had put on their tongues: ﴿And ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful﴾ [12:82].

Meaning: O our father, if you doubt our words, you can seek other evidence from the place where we were, because this matter has caused an uproar and happened before a large crowd of people, and the caravans that were with us witnessed the incident. A crier announced the theft, and the caravan's goods were searched openly.

So if you want to be certain of the truth of our words, ask the caravan that travelled with us on the road, and they know this affair as we know it, or ask the people of the town we came from.

We note here that the Exalted has related the words of Yusuf's brothers to their father Ya'qub: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came (82)﴾.

We know that every event must have an agent, an object upon which it falls, a place in which it occurs, a time in which it occurs, a cause that necessitates it, and a power that carries it out. In some cases we find that the place is the apparent and prominent element of the event, so it is attributed to it, and it is said: ﴿Ask the town...(82)﴾.

The intended meaning, naturally, is to ask the people of the town, or: the matter was so clear that even inanimate things know its details, or: you are a prophet and God reveals to you, so ask Him to make the earth tell you what happened upon it.

Likewise their saying: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan...(82)﴾. We know that the "ʿayr" (caravan, ʿayr) is the riding beasts, whether they are she-camels, camels, donkeys or mules that carry goods. When it is said: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan...(82)﴾, the meaning is that the caravan had a part in the matter beyond all the circumstances.

An example of this is what happened at the Battle of Badr. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to intercept the caravan coming from Syria, loaded with goods, in order to seize it to compensate for the wealth the disbelievers had seized from the emigrants that was in Makkah. Only a few guards and herdsmen were with this caravan.

But when He spoke of the fighters who came from Makkah, He described them as the ﻿nafīr (a company that marches out to confront the camp of faith), that is, the group who set out to face the camp of faith.

So every event takes its prominent aspect.

Here the Exalted relates what was said on the tongues of Yusuf's brothers when they returned to their father, without their brother Benjamin; likewise their eldest brother or the leader of the caravan stayed behind. The Exalted says: ﴿Ask the town in which we were... (82)﴾.

It is possible that their search took place in a place somewhat distant from inhabited areas, where Yusuf's soldiers or helpers searched their belongings, in which they found the king's goblet.

The place was called "qarya" (town), just as we do today when we designate a place for customs, where we inspect goods leaving or entering the country. So their saying: ﴿Ask the town in which we were... (82)﴾ means: ask the people of the place where the search took place. Likewise their saying: ﴿and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾.

That is: ask those who were with us, whom we came along with from the other caravans.

They repeated their saying: ﴿and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾ because they knew of their previous lying before that; therefore they wished here to establish their truthfulness. When their father Ya'qub asks, he will find that they are indeed truthful, and they did not seek the testimony of others except that they are confident of their truthfulness this time.

The Exalted brought this nominal sentence: ﴿and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾ because they had understood that their father had doubted them before, when they brought a lying blood and claimed it was Yusuf's shirt, and that a wolf had eaten him. The Exalted then brings what was said on the tongue of Ya'qub: ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you, so patience is fitting. Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise" (83)﴾.

Matters that contradict the conscience, from which a person feels shame and fears their consequence, are matters that resist the soul; the soul needs treatment to bring them forth, and needs someone to facilitate them for it, so that it proceeds to do the reprehensible deed. This is what is called "taswīl" (making something seem attractive). The saying of the Exalted on the tongue of Ya'qub: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you...(83)﴾ means: your souls made easy for you a matter that upright souls find difficult to accept. Ya'qub had said earlier, at the moment they brought him Yusuf's shirt with its false blood: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you, so patience is fitting; and God is the one sought for help against what you describe (18)﴾.

Here Ya'qub (peace be upon him) asked for help, which shows that what they said, and the events of the story, would not stop at this point; rather, after what they said, events would come that require mustering the powers of patience within the soul and require the help of God.

The matter differs here, in the verse we are contemplating, from what came after the discussion of the soul's making things attractive and seeking patience from God. The gifts of relief had drawn near, so he said: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise (83)﴾. In this verse is the expression of hope that suggests relief; and it came to pass.

Some of those overtaken by heedlessness ask: why did Ya'qub say: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me...(83)﴾, when the absent ones were Yusuf and his brother?

We say: and why do you forget the eldest of the brothers, who refused to leave Egypt until his father permits him, or God relieves him?

Ya'qub had lost three of his sons: Yusuf, Benjamin and Shim'un. Therefore he said: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me...(83)﴾, and did not say: "bring me the two of them."

The Exalted concludes the noble verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise (83)﴾.

So God, glory be to Him, knows where they are, because He is the All-Knowing of everything, and He is the All-Wise in what He brings upon us of circumstances.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 83:

A repeated text, because it shares [its subject] with verse 82: The elder brother knows that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) may disbelieve his sons, because there are precedents for them. Therefore the elder brother, or the head of the caravan, instructed them to say to their father, if he disbelieves them, what the Truth had put on their tongues: ﴿And ask the town (7) in which we were and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful﴾ (82).

That is: O our father, if you doubt our words, you may seek other evidence from the place where we were, because this matter has caused a commotion and happened before a large crowd of people, and the caravans that were with us witnessed the incident. A crier announced the theft, and the caravan was searched openly.

So if you wish to confirm the truth of our words, ask the caravan that travelled with us on the road, and they know this affair as we know it, or ask the people of the town from which we came.

We notice here that the Exalted has related the words of Yusuf's brothers to their father Ya'qub: ﴿And ask the town in which we were and the caravan in which we came (82)﴾.

We know that every event must have an agent, an object upon which it falls, a place in which it occurs, a time in which it occurs, a cause that necessitates it, and a force that carries it out. In some cases we find that the place is the apparent and strong aspect of the event, so it is attributed to it, and it is said: ﴿And ask the town... (82)﴾.

The intended meaning, naturally, is to ask the people of the town, or: the matter was so clear that even inanimate things know its details, or: you are a prophet to whom God reveals, so ask Him to make the earth tell you what happened upon it.

Likewise their saying: ﴿And ask the town in which we were and the caravan... (82)﴾. We know that the caravan (al-'ir) means the beasts of burden, whether they are she-camels, or camels, or donkeys, or mules that carry goods. When it is said: ﴿And ask the town in which we were and the caravan... (82)﴾, it means that the caravan had in the matter something beyond all the circumstances.

An example of this is what happened at the Battle of Badr. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to intercept the caravan coming from Syria, loaded with goods, in order to seize it as compensation for what the disbelievers had taken of the wealth of the emigrants that was in Makkah. Only a few guards and herdsmen were with this caravan.

But when He spoke of the fighters who came from Makkah, He described them as the nafir (the force), that is, the group who rose up to confront the camp of faith.

Thus, every event takes its most prominent aspect.

Here the Truth, glorified is He, relates what was said on the tongues of Yusuf's brothers when they returned to meet their father, and their brother Binyamin was not with them; likewise their elder brother, or the head of the caravan, had stayed behind. The Exalted says: ﴿And ask the town in which we were... (82)﴾.

It is possible that their search took place in a place somewhat distant from the inhabited area, and that Yusuf's soldiers or helpers inspected their belongings, in which they found the king's goblet.

The place was called "the town", just as we do now when we designate a place for customs, where we inspect goods leaving or entering the country. So their saying: ﴿And ask the town in which we were... (82)﴾ means: ask the people of the site where the search took place. Likewise their saying: ﴿and the caravan in which we came, and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾.

That is: ask those who were with us, whom we came with, from the other caravan owners.

They repeated their saying: ﴿and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾ because they knew of their earlier lying before that; therefore they wished here to establish their truthfulness. When their father Ya'qub asks, he will find that they are truly truthful, and they did not seek the testimony of others except that they are confident of their truthfulness this time.

The Exalted brought this nominal sentence: ﴿and indeed we are truthful (82)﴾ because they had understood that their father had doubted them before, when they brought a lying blood and claimed that it was the shirt of Yusuf, and that a wolf had eaten him. The Exalted then brings what was said on the tongue of Ya'qub: ﴿He said: Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you, so patience is fitting. Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise (83)﴾.

Matters that contradict conscience, and of which a person feels shame and fears their consequences, are matters that resist the soul, and the soul needs treatment before it brings them out, and needs someone to facilitate for it when it proceeds to do the reprehensible act; this is what is called "sawwala" (to make attractive, to embellish). The saying of the Exalted on the tongue of Ya'qub: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you (83)﴾ means: your souls have made easy for you a matter that upright souls find difficult to accept. Ya'qub had already said, at the moment they brought him Yusuf's shirt with the false blood upon it: ﴿Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you, so patience is fitting, and God is the One whose help is sought against what you describe (18)﴾.

Here Ya'qub (peace be upon him) sought God's help, which indicates that what they said, and the events of the story, would not stop at this point, but would come after what they said with events requiring the mobilization of the powers of patience in the soul and requiring God's aid.

The matter differs here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, from what came after the talk of the soul's embellishment: the drawing on God for patience. The gifts of relief had drawn near, so he said: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me. Indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise (83)﴾. In this verse is the request of hope that suggests relief; and it happened.

Some of those overtaken by heedlessness ask: why did Ya'qub say: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me (83)﴾, when the absent ones were Yusuf and his brother?

We say: and why do you forget the eldest of the brothers, who refused to leave Egypt until his father permitted him, or until God released him?

Three of his sons were absent from Ya'qub: Yusuf, Binyamin and Shim'un. Therefore he said: ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me (83)﴾, and did not say: He will bring me the two of them.

The Exalted concludes the noble verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise (83)﴾.

So God, glorified is He, knows where they are, for He is the Knower of everything, and He, glorified is He, is Wise in what He brings upon us of dispositions.

Almighty Allah then says: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my grief over Joseph!" And his eyes became white from the grief, and he was suppressing it.﴾ (12:84)

Ya'qub (peace be upon him) turned away from them. What they brought him was news that saddened him, and he withdrew into himself, because in his human nature he grieved over Joseph; the pattern of calamities for him was the loss of Joseph.

When you hear a cry over something painful, such as "Oh my sorrow!" or "Oh my sadness!" or "Oh my calamity!", this means that the soul is constricted by events and is saying, "O distress, this is your time, so be present!" Or it is as He said: ﴿"Oh, my grief over Joseph..." (12:84)﴾, because his brother Benjamin was the most similar of people to him. So his grief over Joseph was a wave of distress that descended upon him, and it was followed by another wave of distress, which is the loss of Benjamin.

As for the saying of Almighty Allah: ﴿"And his eyes became white..." (12:84)﴾, it means that Ya'qub's tears increased until the black part of the eye appeared white as if it had turned white; or it means: his eyes became white from the intensity of his grief, which he does not disclose to anyone and which he suppresses.

He may suppress his anger at everything that has happened, but emotions, no one is able to control them.

We find our Messenger (ﷺ) weeping, his eyes shedding tears out of grief at the death of his son Ibrahim. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Are you weeping? Did you not forbid weeping?" He said: "No, but I was forbidden from two foolish, wicked sounds: a sound at a calamity, slapping of faces, tearing of collars, and the wailing of Satan."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "The eye sheds tears and the heart grieves, and we say nothing except what pleases our Lord, and indeed we are grieved by your separation, O Ibrahim."

Thus we know that Almighty Allah does not want a person to be a block of stone or a rock that is unaffected by events; rather He wants him to be affected by events, because this is a quality that must exist in his humanity, and this is an emotion that Allah wants to preserve, and it is upon the believer to elevate it.

So He, glory be to Him, is the One who created emotion and instinct in man. Had Allah wanted man without emotion or instinct, He would have done as He willed, but He willed emotion and instinct in man for a purpose.

And at the moment an emotion or instinct departs from its purpose, the method says to you: No. For the function of the method is to refine emotion for you.

An example I give here is a person's love of enjoying food: the method says to him, "Eat what benefits you and do not be gluttonous."

Another example: the instinct of curiosity. The method says to you: know what benefits you, and do not use this instinct to spy on people.

The sexual instinct Allah intended for the preservation of the species and to bring about offspring and descendants, but do not use it as savage outbursts. Thus the method guards the instincts and emotions so that they remain within the framework of their purpose.

Emotion, for example, is what makes a father tender toward his young son and care for him; accordingly, the believer must elevate his instincts and emotions.

As for the saying of Almighty Allah about Ya'qub: ﴿"...so he was suppressing it" (12:84)﴾, it means that he restrained his outburst according to its measure. The word "kazim" (كظيم) is derived from "kazamtu al-qirba" (كظمت القربة), meaning we tightly sealed the mouth of the waterskin so as to prevent water from leaking out of it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 12, verse 85:

The Truthful One (Allah), glorified is He, says after that: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill (ḥarḍan) or become among the perished."﴾

One may ask: Who was it that said this to Jacob, since the previous verse mentioned that he turned away from them?

We say: Jacob lived with his sons and grandchildren. It is related in a report that some people came to visit him and said to him, "By Allah, you have been broken (inhashamta), O Jacob, and you have not reached the age of your father Isaac." The meaning was: you have become an old man, weak and broken. He said, "It is only Joseph who has broken me." So Allah rebuked him for this statement and made clear to him: "Do you complain of your Lord to His creation?" He raised his hand and said, "A sin I committed, O Lord, so forgive it for me." He said, "I have forgiven it for you."(21)

And some of his sons or grandsons admonished him, saying: ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become among the perished.﴾ That is: you will not stop remembering Joseph and what happened to him, until you come close to ruin. And "ḥarḍ" (fatally ill, one brought close to death), as we know, is one who is close to ruin, or who actually perishes.

The reply came from Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and Allah, glorified is He, related it: ﴿He said: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know."﴾ (12:86)

Complaining of a matter to Allah is a form of worship directed to Allah. Al-bath (the anguish) is the calamity that no one has the power to conceal, so it spreads out. When a person in a higher position is struck by something that the one below sees as evil, the one below divides into two kinds. One kind seeks the favour of the stronger, shows him tenderness, softens toward him, asks his forgiveness and seeks his indulgence. Another kind refuses to submit to the one afflicted, rebels, and the state of such a person says: "Let him do what he wishes."

Allah, blessed and exalted, says in His Book: ﴿So why, when Our might came to them, did they not humble themselves?﴾ (6:43)

So at the moment the might comes and we humble ourselves before Allah, the might will have washed us of sins and of forgetting the remembrance, and returned us to Allah, the One who alone removes the might.

As for the one who rebels and exalts himself over events, woe to him for that rebellion. And when Allah, glorified is He, afflicts a person with a calamity, He is gentle toward the one who calls upon Him.

Some have asked: why did Ya'qub not say what our Messenger (ﷺ) taught us: ﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return."﴾ (2:156)

We say: this is among the blessings that Allah, glorified is He, has singled out for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). When some people entered upon 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face and be pleased with him, while he was suffering from a fever and was groaning, they said to him: "O Abu al-Hasan, do you feel pain?" He said: "I am not ashamed before Allah (to complain)."

And here, in the verse we are reflecting upon, Ya'qub (peace be upon him) declares that he complains of his grief and his concern only to Allah, for He is the One able to remove harm, since Ya'qub (peace be upon him) knows from Allah what his sons or grandsons do not know.

For he felt in his inner being, and from the doubts he had at the moment they informed him of the fabricated story of the wolf, that Yusuf was still alive, and that the vision Yusuf had recounted to his father, Allah would surely grant its fulfilment.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 87:

The Exalted Lord mentions what came from the tongue of Ya'qub, saying:

﴿O my sons, go and seek news (tahassassu) of Yusuf and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy (rawh) of Allah. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾

We observe that those who were absent were three: Yusuf, Binyamin, and the elder brother who insisted that he would not leave Egypt until his father permitted him, or until Allah brought about relief.

Here in this verse, mention is made of Yusuf and his brother, and there is no mention of the elder brother or the leader of the journey. We say: Yusuf and his brother are the weak group who suffered the opposition of the rest of the brothers, and they had both been separated from the father while young. As for the elder brother, he is able to devise a plan and to return at the time he wishes.

As for Ya'qub's saying: ﴿Go and seek news of Yusuf and his brother...﴾ (87)

In it we find the word [tahassassu], which derives from al-hiss (sense perception), and hiss is pluralized as "hawass" (senses). The senses are the channels through which information is perceived by the human soul. Information arises in us from sensible matters, and our senses perceive them so that they become rational propositions.

Thus we know that the senses are channels of knowledge, and they are not restricted to the five outward senses; rather, scholars have discovered that there are other, non-apparent senses, and we have already addressed this matter on many previous occasions.

﴿So seek news of Yusuf and his brother...﴾ (87) means: employ your senses with all the energy they contain, so that you may reach the truth.

We know that the word "jasus" (spy) has been applied to one who eavesdrops, watches, and sniffs out the news and movements in the camp of the enemy; he is also called an "ayn" (eye).

In our common usage we say to one who professionally gathers news: "Sniff out for us the story of such-and-such a matter."

Ya'qub continued his speech: ﴿And do not despair of the mercy (rawh) of Allah. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾ (87) That is: beware of saying that we went, we exerted ourselves and tried every stratagem, but found no solution, because Allah exists and Allah's mercy is still there.

The saying goes: "No distress, while You are the Lord," and whatever is difficult for you according to your own laws, turn to Allah in it.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught us that whenever a matter distressed him, he would stand and pray.

Thus he turned to the Lord of the causes, and He, Glorified is He, is above all causes. Try this in any matter that stumps you, and none of you will reach the end of the prayer without finding a solution to what had stumped him.

The word "rawh" is pronounced in two ways: "rawh" and "rūh." "Ar-rawh" is the fragrance that blows upon a person so that he is refreshed by it, just as a person sits on a hot summer day and then a light breeze blows and he is revived. The Exalted Lord says: ﴿Then rest (fa-rawh) and sweet scent (rayhan) and a Garden of delight﴾ (29) [al-Waqi'ah].

We may take an example of this rawh from perceptible things: when the heat intensifies, and we sit in a garden and a breeze of air blows, the atmosphere is perfumed by the flowers in the garden.

And the "rūh" (spirit) is that which the Exalted Lord breathes into inanimate matter so that it moves.

Here Ya'qub, peace be upon him, brings the principle that every believer follows, saying: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾ (87)

For whoever has no Lord is the one who despairs; therefore we find that the proportion of suicides among atheists is high, but the believer does not do this, because he knows that he has a Lord who helps His servants. And so long as the believer has taken the causes, He, Glorified is He, grants him from what is above the causes.

The Exalted Lord says: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out (2), and provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for everything a destiny (3)﴾ [at-Talaq].

This is a matter that happens to whoever fears Allah. I challenge anyone to find a believer who does not experience such things in his life so long as he takes the causes and fears Allah; he will find in a moment of distress that relief has come from where he did not expect, because Allah is the ultimate reserve of the believer.

Suppose you are walking along the road with one pound in your pocket, and that is all you have, and you lose it. Will you grieve? Yes, you will grieve. But if there are ten pounds in your house, your grief over the lost pound will be light. And if your bank balance were a thousand pounds, you would not grieve over the pound that was lost.

Whoever has a Lord, who exerts effort in taking the causes, will find the solution and relief from any distress, even that which lies beyond the causes.

And why does a person despair?

It is the atheist who despairs, because he does not believe in a god. And if he did believe in a god, that god either would not know of the distress this unbeliever is in, or it is a god who knows but does not help those who worship it, either out of inability or stinginess. In all these states it is not a god, and it does not deserve to be believed in.

As for the true believer, he knows that he worships a powerful God, who gives through the causes and beyond the causes; and when He withholds, that withholding is itself giving, because He may take away what would harm him and not benefit him.

When they entered upon him, the Almighty takes us to another scene, the moment they entered upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, in his residence in Egypt. Let us read His saying:

﴿When they entered upon him, they said: "O Chief! Hardship has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable."﴾ (12:88)

The Almighty did not mention the name of the one they entered upon, because he is the protagonist of the story. The pronoun in "upon him" must refer to something known. They addressed him with exaltation, saying:

﴿O Chief! Hardship has touched us and our family...﴾ (12:88) That is: hunger has reduced us to emaciation. They began by softening the heart of the one listening to them, after exalting him; for he is the High and they are the low.

Their speech continues: ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.﴾ (12:88)

We know that they had come to seek information about Yusuf and his brother, and they chose the approach of softening and exalting as a kind of cunning. The exaltation lies in calling him by "the Chief," i.e., the possessor of authority; this address means that what they will ask of him is within the reach of his power. The softening lies in complaining of their condition, from hunger that has reduced them to emaciation. They announced their arrival with "meager merchandise," i.e., goods used as payment for what they would take away.

The word ﴿مزجاة (muzjāh)﴾ means: pushed along by the one who buys or sells. The Almighty says: ﴿Have you not considered that Allah drives (yuzjī) clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap...﴾ (24:43). The word "yuzjī" means: drives or pushes. So what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿with meager merchandise (muzjāh)﴾?

To know the meaning by your own sense, try this in yourself, and observe how you pay for anything you buy. If you have old currency and new currency, you will find that you pay the value of what you buy with the old currency, and you will find yourself at ease at keeping the new currency for yourself.

The seller may say to you: "Take this old banknote that you pay me, and exchange it for me for a new one."

Since the money will be paid, you want to be rid of the old money, and you do that while at ease. In this way we can understand the meaning of ﴿meager (muzjāh)﴾, i.e., of poor quality. It is as if the harm that befell them made them unable to pay the prices for the provisions they would take, like the earlier prices, which were distinguished by quality.

The Almighty continues with what came from their tongues:

﴿So give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.﴾ (12:88) That is: they hope that the measure be made full for them and not diminished, if what they brought as payment does not match the value of the provisions; and they asked him to consider that fullness of measure a charity.

In this way they returned him to a price higher than what they had brought as payment, beyond the capacity of humans to pay; for charity is that for which the Almighty alone gives reward.

One may ask: Were they not sons of a prophet, and is charity not permissible for them?

We say: the impermissibility of charity is a matter singled out by the Almighty for the family of Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is a matter specific to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Charity is not befitting for the family of Muhammad; it is only the filth of people."

Consider what the softening words they spoke achieved: Yusuf, peace be upon him, looked at them and smiled, and when he smiled, his front teeth appeared, and those teeth were distinctive compared to the teeth of everyone who had seen him.

Divine Providence (al-Haqq, may He be exalted) then brings about what He said:

﴿He said: "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?" (89)﴾

The coming of this statement in the form of a question moves them to reflect and examine closely, so that they might recognize the identity of the speaker.

Then comes the gracious gentleness from him when he adds:

﴿What you did with Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant? (89)﴾

In this statement there is something by which he seeks to excuse them on the ground of ignorance. He did not address them with the pride of power or the arrogance of the high station he had reached. His aim was to lessen the shock of the surprise, so he reminded them that they did that in the days of their ignorance.

This is like one of them who wronged you long ago through unacceptable conduct, but the passing of days has removed the bitterness of his behavior from you. So you remind him of what he did long ago, saying to him: "Your action proceeded from you in the days of your recklessness, but now you have reached the level of reason and understanding of matters."

Joseph's (peace be upon him) saying this matter to them in this form of gentleness also expresses his being affected by their complaint. Then his smiling at them, and the appearance of his front teeth, prompted them to recall him (32), and there took place between them and him the dialogue that came in the following verse.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 90:

﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient - then indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost."﴾ So they became aware of Joseph's identity and recognized him, and they said: ﴿Are you indeed Joseph...﴾

Their words came in the form of an interrogative of affirmation, which they emphasized with "inna" (indeed) and the lam of emphasis, and they said this in a tone full of joy and amazement at their success in the search (tahassus) that their father had enjoined upon them.

So he replied to them: ﴿I am Joseph, and this is my brother...﴾ Naturally they knew Joseph's brother, Benjamin, and Joseph's mention of him here is evidence that Benjamin had shared with him in the blessing, and that Allah, glorified is He, had honoured both of them.

Joseph's gratitude to Allah for His blessing comes in his saying: ﴿Allah has been gracious to us...﴾

Joseph spoke these words which present the general matter that benefits them as brothers, and benefits every listener and everyone who recites it. Joseph, peace be upon him, said this after a clear proof drawn from the reality of events that had passed him, from the dream up to this situation.

It is a statement with evidence from lived reality: Allah bestowed His favour upon Joseph and his brother, through what the two of them had been tested with and what they had gathered after separation. Joseph explained this by saying:

﴿Indeed, whoever fears...﴾ meaning: whoever places between himself and disobedience of Allah a shield, and fears the attributes of majesty, follows His method, glorified is He, endures what befalls him, does not let his resolve slacken in the worship of Allah, and avoids every disobedience however it is made attractive to him.

So, glorified and exalted is He, He does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost, those who fear Him, and who by their piety have become deserving of His mercy and His beneficence in this world and the next.

Then comes the saying of the Truth, glorified is He, to convey to us what the brothers of Joseph said in this situation: ﴿They said, "By God, God has certainly preferred you over us, and we were certainly wrongdoers."﴾ (91)

"Tallahi" (by God) is an oath by God. And ﴿God has preferred you over us﴾ (91) means: He has singled you out with something beyond what He singled out others with. He did not prefer you through injustice toward anyone else, but you deserved what He preferred you with of kingship, elevated rank and standing.

Thus the brothers of Joseph confirmed what Joseph had said, and acknowledged their sin, when they tried to be close to their father as he was, but you, O Joseph, reached the point of becoming one brought near and given precedence with the Lord of your father and the Lord of the worlds.

The matter and the state we were in confirm that we were "khati'in" (sinners), and we must pay attention to the difference between "khati'in" (خاطئين) and "mukhti'in" (مخطئين).

The 'Aziz said to his wife: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners (al-khati'in)﴾ (29). He did not say to her "kunti min al-mukhti'in." The root is one: the letters "kha'", "ta'" and "hamza," but the meaning differs. The khati' (one who sins deliberately) is the one who knows the boundary of what is right and transgresses it, whereas the mukhti' (one who errs) is the one who has not reached what is right, because he does not know its place or the way to it.

And Allah the Exalted says, in what was spoken by Yusuf (peace be upon him) to his brothers after they had acknowledged their wrong:

﴿He said, "No reproach shall there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ (92)

The word tathrib (التثريب) means severe blame, and it is derived from ath-thurb (الثرب). When people slaughter an animal and draw out its intestines, they find around the intestines a thick layer of fat; this fat is called ath-thurb.

But if the animal is emaciated and has not been well fed, its intestines come out with that thurb having melted away from it.

Tathrib means that severe blame has melted the fat from the flesh, causing the blood to seep, and it nearly brings the person to ruin and wears him down.

And in a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "If the slave-girl of any one of you commits fornication and it becomes clear that she has fornicated, let him inflict the prescribed punishment upon her and not reproach her. Then if she commits it again, let him inflict the prescribed punishment upon her and not reproach her. Then if she commits it a third time and it becomes clear that she has fornicated, let him sell her, even for a rope of hair."(2)

That is: he should not say to her, "O you who did such-and-such," but rather he should punish her with the punishment that Allah has prescribed for such a crime. If she does not desist from the act, then he should sell her. Thus we understand that severe blame or reproach may breed obstinacy.

And Yusuf (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Today, may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ (92)

One may ask: why did Yusuf say this, when they may have already sought Allah's forgiveness before?

We say: Yusuf's supplication for their forgiveness came within the bounds of his knowledge, and to purify their souls of what had tainted them through this meeting.

His saying ﴿and He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾ (92) is an understanding of the reality that any mercy in the world, or from any person, is derived from His mercy, glory be to Him.

Yusuf said this while certain that his supplication would be answered, because he had already forgiven them their earlier wrong and pardoned them; and Allah is more worthy than he of pardoning them.

(1) Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim [11/223]: "The meaning of 'it becomes clear (tabayyana) her fornication' is that it is verified, either by evidence, or by witnessing, or by knowledge held by one who permits judging by knowledge in hudud matters."
(2) Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih [1703], from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Then the discourse between him and them returns to their father, and the Truthful One (Allah, glorified is He) relates what came from the tongue of Yusuf to his brothers, he who knew what had happened to his father after their separation from him:

﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight. And bring me all your family.﴾ (93)

Yusuf, peace be upon him, had known that his father's eyes were clouded from grief and that he was nearly losing his sight, so he commanded his brothers to take the shirt he had been wearing to his father.

The books of biography (kutub al-siyar) mention that his eldest brother, who refused to leave Egypt and said: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me, and He is the best of judges﴾ (80),

had said to Yusuf: "O Chief (al-'Aziz), I am the one who brought the shirt stained with false blood to my father, so let me carry this shirt to my father, so that this may wipe out that." (1) Yusuf spoke of what the shirt would do with the father: ﴿cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight..﴾ (93). We note that he did not say "the face of your father."

In his words ﴿the face of my father..﴾ (93) there is an indication of the paternal tenderness that they had lost since Yusuf disappeared, so that his father drowned in grief. And ﴿he will regain his sight..﴾ (93)

means: his sight will return to him, or he will see before him, whole.

Yusuf adds: ﴿And bring me all your family﴾ (93). This is a precise Qur'anic expression: that they should bring with them everyone who has a bond of kinship with them or who works with them. (2) Yusuf did not say "your parents" so that they would not bring only the notables.

We note that he did not mention his father in Yusuf's command to his brothers to bring everyone related to them by kinship, because in such a matter, coming from the position of the Chief of Egypt, it would be a compulsion on the father to come, and he honours his father above that.

1 - Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (5/3593): "al-Suddi related that the one who carried his shirt was Yahudhah. He said to Yusuf: 'As for the one to whom I brought your shirt stained with false blood and saddened him, I am the one who now carries it to gladden him, and so that his sight returns to him,' and he carried it."

2 - Masruq said: They were ninety-three, men and women. Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir [5/3593].

Almighty Allah says after that:

﴿And when the caravan departed, their father said, "Indeed, I sense the smell of Joseph, if you did not think me senile."﴾

"Fussilat" (departed) indicates something that was joined to another thing and then separated from it. "Fussilat al-ʿeer" means the caravan left the city and passed beyond it to continue its journey. The intended meaning is that the caravan had left the borders of Egypt, heading for the place of Yaʿqub (peace be upon him).

Here Yaʿqub said to those present with him of his grandchildren and great-grandchildren: ﴿Indeed, I sense the smell of Joseph...﴾

It is well known that the shirt he had sent with his elder son carried the scent of Joseph, but those of Yaʿqub's relatives around him did not believe his words, so he added: ﴿if you did not think me senile﴾, meaning, if you did not accuse me of senility, because al-tafnid (senility, see note) is the decline of the mind due to old age.¹

It is remarkable that in our own days we find science has established that images of mirrors and sounds leave traces in the air, despite what a person imagines, that they have vanished.

Science attempts, through means of rays, to reveal the image of any group that was sitting in a place and then left it an hour or two earlier, which indicates that images have a "ripeness" of light and shadow that remains in the place for a period before it disappears.

Likewise sounds: scientists try to recover the voices of those who have departed, and they say: nothing is lost in the universe; rather, everything that has existed in it is preserved in one form or another.

Smell too is not lost, as evidenced by the dog that picks up scent over great distances and now distinguishes narcotics by their odour; for this reason trained dogs are deployed in airports and at borders to expose any attempt to smuggle narcotics.

If the animal, created by the power of Allah, is able to pick up a scent from among thousands of odours, and if the knowledge bestowed by Allah upon humans is now investigating how to summon an image and recover a sound from the atmosphere surrounding a person, then we must realise that when the caravan left the walls of the city and took its path toward the place where Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) lived, Yaʿqub, by the power of Allah, was able to smell the scent of Joseph, which was carried by his shirt arriving with the caravan.

Someone may ask: why was Yaʿqub's perception of Joseph's scent linked to the caravan's departure from Egypt and its presence on the road to Yaʿqub's homeland?

We say: because while the caravan was in the city, the scent of Joseph's shirt would be mixed with other smells, for there are many other odours within any city, and it is difficult for one particular scent to penetrate and prevail over all others; the matter differs in the open countryside, where a breeze of scent can travel without anything obstructing it.

Thus we believe that everything in the universe is preserved and nothing is lost, in confirmation of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 10–11].

Whatever proceeds from you is recorded against you; therefore your record will be brought to you on the Day of Resurrection for you to read, and you will be sufficient as a reckoner against yourself.

¹ Al-khuraf: the corruption of the intellect due to old age. [Lisan al-ʿArab, root: kh-r-f].

They (the rest of Jacob's family) respond to his saying that he finds the scent of Joseph:

﴿They said, "By God, you are surely in your old error."﴾ It seems they had grown weary of his talk about Joseph, so they turned away from his words, saying to him: "How long will you remain in your error?" They did not mean "error" in the sense of departing from the path (of religion), but they meant "error" in the sense of the minor matters unrelated to religiosity: his intense love for Joseph, his attachment to him, his longing for his return, his frequent speaking of him, and his expectation of meeting him. They were the ones who thought that Joseph had died.

(1) Here, "ḍalāl" (error) means the intensity of preoccupation with the beloved, the frequent asking about him, and the continuous searching, in accordance with God's saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā 93:7].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 96:

The bearer of good tidings comes to Ya'qub (ʿAlayhi al-salam). The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So when the bearer of good tidings arrived, he cast it over his face, and he regained his sight. He said: "Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾

When the bearer(1) arrived, who, as the narrations say, was the eldest of the brothers; and it is also said that he was Yahudha (Judah), and he was the one who refused to leave Egypt unless his father gave him permission, or unless a solution came from heaven to the problem of Binyamin's remaining in Egypt, after the officials of the Aziz had accused him of theft, in accordance with what Yusuf had devised so that he would keep his brother with him.

When this bearer came, carrying the shirt of Yusuf, he cast it over the father's face, in execution of the command of Yusuf (ʿAlayhi al-salam).

Thereby the cause of Ya'qub's weeping was removed, and Ya'qub rejoiced greatly; for in the days of his grief over Yusuf, and the whitening of his eyes from excessive weeping, his heart informed him by inspiration from Allah that Yusuf was still alive. The weeping over him from that time on was weeping out of intense longing to see his son.

Likewise, Yusuf may have known by revelation from Allah that casting the shirt upon his father's face would return his sight, by permission of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, besides the fact that joy has psychological effects that are reflected in the state of health. Thus the victories of the Truth and of prophethood became manifest.

Ya'qub (ʿAlayhi al-salam) said:
﴿"Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?"﴾

He did not say this to humiliate them, but to give confidence and authentication to the reports of every prophet, and that reality had confirmed the words he had said to them:

﴿"O my sons, go and search for Yusuf and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people."﴾

So if a report comes to you from one who is infallible, beware of stopping with your intellects regarding it; for intellects grasp the perceptible things according to their measure, and there are things beyond the perceptions of intellects.

And when an infallible one speaks to you about what is beyond the perceptions of their intellects, beware of calling him a liar, whether or not you understood what he told you about, or failed to grasp his speech about what is beyond the perceptions of intellects.

1 - Al-Bashir (the bearer of good tidings): the one who gives people the glad news. It was said: he was Shim'un, and it was said: Yahudha. He said: "I will take the shirt today as I took it stained with blood," related by Ibn 'Abbas. And on the authority of al-Suddi, that he said to his brothers: "You know that I took to him the shirt of grief [sorrow], so let me take to him the shirt of joy [happiness]" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 5/3596].
2 - Tahassasa al-shay' and tahassasa minhu: to seek knowledge of a thing by careful investigation of it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O my sons, go and search for Yusuf and his brother (87)﴾ [Yusuf]. That is: follow their news and search for them with great diligence. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/154].
Reviewed against the original and its hadiths takhrij by His Eminence Shaykh Muhammad al-Sanrawi, adviser at al-Azhar, and Ustadh 'Adil Abu al-Ma'ati.

And here the brothers of Yusuf acknowledge their sins, so the True One, glory be to Him, says: ﴿They said, "O our father, ask forgiveness for us..."﴾.

Here they admit to the sin, and they address their father with the call of fatherhood so that he will seek forgiveness for them for the many sins they committed. They had hurt their father and made him grieve, and such a sin does not fall away unless the one who committed it acknowledges it. We note that they said: ﴿Indeed, we were wrongdoers﴾ [Yusuf: 97], meaning: they were knowing what was right, yet they did not do it.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 12, verse 98:

Al-Haqq (exalted be He) brings about what Ya'qub said: ﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Indeed, He is the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."﴾

We note that Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿"No reproach will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ [Yusuf: 92] Yet their father here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, says: ﴿"I will ask my Lord to forgive you..."﴾ [Yusuf: 98], and he did not say: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you now." This indicates that elders need more time than the young do; therefore Ya'qub postponed the seeking of forgiveness to a later time. Al-Alusi (Shaykh al-Alusi) says in his tafsir: "That was because the claims of righteousness owed by a brother to his brothers are not the same as those owed by a son to his father, since a brother does not have the same right as a father; therefore the father's anger is more severe than the brother's anger." Furthermore, their sins here are among the grave sins, the effects of which upon the father lasted a long time. It is said that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, delayed seeking forgiveness for them until the last part of the night (al-sahar), because supplication at that time is answered.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 12, verse 99:

From that point, Allah, glorified and exalted be He, transports us to the moment of the meeting between Yusuf (peace be upon him) and all of his family, after they had moved to where Yusuf lived. He, glorified be He, says: ﴿So when they entered upon Yusuf...﴾

We know that the grandfather Ishaq (Isaac) was not alive at that time, and they used to give precedence to the paternal side over the maternal side, and the maternal aunt entered with them, because the mother was not present.

It appears that Yusuf received them when they entered Egypt with the reception accorded to dignitaries. He met them outside the city once, to relieve them of the hardship of travel, and the notables and leading men of the city came out to receive them. This is the first entry, in which he took his parents to himself.

Then he brought them in on the second entry into the city, as evidenced by his saying: ﴿...Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [Yusuf: 99]. So there are two entries in the verse.

The words of Allah, glorified be He: ﴿He took his parents to himself...﴾ [Yusuf: 99] indicate the warmth of a meeting between two estranged people bound by tenderness. The father had been longing to see his son, and he must have heard from his brothers about his rank and station, while the son had been eager to meet his father.

The emotions of such a meeting are usually left to human feelings and are not regulated, for they are particular emotions composed of affection, love, respect and other things. There is one whom you meet and are content to greet with a handshake, and another whom you meet and your longing overcomes you so that you embrace him and say whatever words of welcome you wish. All those emotions are without any formal regulation of worship, as evidenced by the fact that Yusuf (peace be upon him) took his parents to himself and held them in his embrace.

"And the example from the life of our Messenger (ﷺ) in the context of the Battle of Badr: he was reviewing the fighters, and in his hand the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a staff with which he straightened the rows. He passed by Sawad ibn Ghaziyya of the Banu Adi ibn al-Najjar, who was out of line, i.e., outside the row, which made the row uneven. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck him in the belly with the staff and said to him: "Straighten up, Sawad." Sawad said: "You have hurt me, and Allah has sent you with truth and justice, so let me retaliate." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) uncovered his belly and said (ﷺ): "Retaliate." Sawad embraced him and kissed his belly. He (ﷺ) said: "What led you to do this, Sawad?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, the time of what you see has come, meaning war, so I wanted the last of my contact with you to be that my skin touches your skin." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed for good for him."

Then Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne...﴾

Joseph raised his parents upon the throne because he did not want to set himself apart from them. This conduct shows love, respect and honour. The throne ('arsh) is the royal seat from which the ruler directs the affairs of government. They fell down prostrating to God, for the sake of reuniting the family, and they did not prostrate to Joseph. Rather, they prostrated to the One to whom prostration is due, who is God.

To those who have debated the matter of the prostration of Jacob's family to Joseph, I say: are you more jealous for God than He is, glory be to Him? It is He, glory be to Him, who said this, and it is He who earlier commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam. So why do you take this statement as prostration to Adam?

The true believer understands the prostration of the angels to Adam as the carrying out of God's command to them to prostrate to Adam. God created Adam from clay and breathed into him of His spirit, and He commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam in gratitude to God who created this creation. Likewise, the prostration of Jacob's family to Joseph was an expression of gratitude to God who gathered their shattered family. It was He, glory be to Him, who said this statement, and He did not condemn their act, as is shown by the fact that they offered a greeting to Joseph, which he was able to return in kind. Their prostration to him was not for the purpose of worship ('ibadah), because worship is an act performed by the lesser in drawing near to the greater, to which the one worshipped does not respond in kind. If it were worship directed to other than God, God, glory be to Him, would punish for it, and that is among the forbidden matters.

As for worship of God, it is the following of His commands and the avoidance of His prohibitions. Therefore, the prostration here was a response to the call of gratitude by all, on account of the removal of grief and sorrow, and He, glory be to Him, rewards it. As for a greeting, it is offered by one servant, and the other servant may return it in kind or with something better. This is a matter God does not forbid, and worship has no bearing on it.

Therefore, we must be attentive to the fact that this matter must be interpreted logically, in agreement with the evidence of the language and the requirements of the situation. If we consider the condition of Jacob, peace be upon him, and what he was in of sorrow, and the situation of his sons, caught between the torment of conscience over what they had done and the hardships they had faced, we would be certain that the prostration intended was an expression of gratitude to the One in whose hand are the reins of affairs, rather than the creation of gaps without justification. As for their prostrating to Joseph, did they do it without God's knowledge? Certainly not.

After this, we find Joseph's statement to his father: ﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision from before. My Lord has made it true..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100]

The vision was the first scene in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, where God related what Joseph said to his father: ﴿"...Indeed I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me."﴾ [Yusuf: 4] His saying in the verse under our consideration, ﴿"My Lord has made it true..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100], means: a realised fact. Joseph's father and brothers saw it at the moment they prostrated to Joseph, a prostration of gratitude and greeting, not of worship. The eleven brothers prostrated, as did the father and the aunt who took the place of the mother. The visions of the prophets, as we know, must come to pass.

Someone may say: what about the vision of Abraham, peace be upon him, in which God commanded him to slaughter his son, and he set about carrying it out, and Isma'il submitted to the command of the vision?

We say: the prophets alone are under a legal obligation to carry out their visions, because Satan cannot deceive them; they are protected from Satan's deception.

As for a person who comes and says, "A vision came to me telling me to do such-and-such," we say to him: you are not obliged to carry out what you see in your dreams; no legal ruling binds you to that, and besides, Satan may deceive you.

As for Abraham's carrying out what he saw in the dream, that he must slaughter his son, and his attempt to carry it out, the reason was that he knew of his legal obligation to act on the vision.

God has related to us this event to show us the magnitude of the trials that Abraham endured, and how he strove to fulfil every command that came to him from heaven, and to carry it out with precision.

God said, portraying this: ﴿And when his Lord tried Abraham with commands, and he fulfilled them, He said, "Indeed I will make you a leader for the people..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]

The peak of the trials was that he would carry out the slaughter of his son with his own hands. Therefore I always emphasise that the prophets alone are obliged to carry out their visions. As for any other person whose vision contradicts the method (manhaj), he must regard it as a whisper from Satan. God continues what was said by Joseph: ﴿"...and He was kind to me when He took me out of the prison..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100]

Someone may ask: why did Joseph not mention the grave events that befell him in sequence, such as his brothers throwing him into the well?

We say: Joseph did not want to mention what would disturb the pleasure of the reunion of the family after long separation. Rather, he spoke of what happened to him afterwards: that he became a slave, how he entered prison because he did not yield to the seduction of the wife of the ruler, how God blessed him by bringing him out of prison, and that as soon as he came out of prison, the blessing appeared, and it was enough that he became a ruler.

Someone might say: the story here is not consistent with itself, because some of the events are mentioned and others are not.

We say: the story is entirely consistent, and there is a difference between historical narratives as history, and narratives that illustrate the important moments in history.

The occasion of this verse is the gathering of the brothers, the father and the aunt, and there is no need to mention what would spoil this meeting, especially since Joseph had said earlier: ﴿"No blame upon you today. God will forgive you, and He is the most merciful of the merciful."﴾ [Yusuf: 92] He had also previously said to them, gently, as one who seeks to excuse them on the ground of ignorance: ﴿"...Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?"﴾ [Yusuf: 89] And here, in the verse under our consideration, he mentions God's kindness to him, saying: ﴿"My Lord has made it true..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100]

He praises God, thanking Him for His kindness, saying: ﴿"...and He was kind to me when He took me out of the prison..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100] This is a kindness to him personally. Then he mentions God's kindness to the rest of his family: ﴿"...and brought you from the desert..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100]

The word "ahsana" (to be kind), as we know, sometimes takes the preposition "ila" (to), as in "ahsana ilayhi" (he was kind to him), and sometimes takes the preposition "bi" (with/by), as in "ahsana bihi" (he dealt well with him). Here it is in the construction "ahsana bi" ("He was kind to me"). That is, the kindness done through him has been connected to everything connected to him: He made him a ruler and brought his family from the desert. Whereas kindness done to him is restricted to himself and does not extend beyond him.

God made kindness here of two kinds: one kind for the person himself, and one kind for others. He considered the arrival of the family from the desert to be a kindness to him, because the desert people live according to their nature and in family isolation. They have no settled dwelling place, and no society gathers them, and they have no built houses in which to settle. Rather, they follow their sustenance from pasture and water sources, and carry their baggage on the backs of camels, moving from place to place. Their lives are free of the blessings of civilisation. In civilisation, everything you ask for is brought to you, but life in the desert requires a person to go wherever he finds good; therefore life is more settled in the towns than in the desert.

The poet Ahmad Shawqi, may God have mercy on him, gives us a picture showing the difference between the desert and the town, when he composed a debate between a woman who is partisan to the desert and another who is partisan to the town. He said:

*I am from the wilderness, O son of Juraij,*
*and from this harsh way of life,*
*from one who milks the sheep in one place,*
*and from one who lights the fire in a corner.*
*Our singers are Ma'bad and al-Gharid,*
*and our sounds are the howling of the hyena.*
*They eat the varieties of the cooks,*
*and we eat what the herds have cooked.*

So Ibn Juraij complains of boredom with life in the desert, where he sees only repeated scenes of milking a sheep or lighting a fire. Unlike the townspeople, he does not hear the voices of the famous singers of that time, but the howling of hyenas. He does not eat, as the townspeople do, what the cooks have prepared, but drinks milk, which is what the livestock provide for them. Layla, partisan to the desert, replies:

*Hind has wronged you, O son of Juraij,*
*and she was harsh in her cradle.*
*The desert is only the dwellings of the noble*
*and the abode of the protecting covenants.*
*For them is the qibla of the sun at its rising,*
*and for the town is the second qibla.*
*We are the basil filling the open space,*
*and they are the basil in vessels.*
*Love kills us, and the townswomen*
*rise from love in their vessels (of ease).*

Her phrase "i'tasafat" means "wronged", that is: Hind wronged the desert, O son of Juraij. Then she brings forward the qualities of the desert: the girls of the desert are like basil planted in the wide open space, unlike the girls of the towns, each of whom resembles a basil plant set in flower pots or some other container.

Then she comes to values, and boasts that the desert girl is killed by love and does not win anything from the one she loves, so she wastes away and dies. But the townswoman's health survives at the expense of love.

Here, in the verse under our consideration, Joseph gives thanks for what God bestowed upon him, and upon his family whom God brought from the desert to live in Egypt, the land of wide civilisation. In this way, he has magnified the difference between what they had been living in, of harshness of life, and a life of ease and comfort.

Then he touches on what his brothers did towards him, saying: ﴿"...after Satan had sown discord between me and my brothers..."﴾ [Yusuf: 100] This is a gentle touch on what happened. He attributed it to Satan and described it as a "nazgh" (a prick, a whisper). That is, it was not a settled matter of a single degree of evil. That is, what Satan did was merely a jab that alerts a person to something harmful, and he is moved by it. The word is derived from the goad with which a horse trainer spurs any horse. He pricks it with the goad, a light prick, and it listens and carries out what he commands. So "nazgh" is a prompting to a task, and differs from "ta'n" (a thrust).

God, glory be to Him, alerts us to what Satan does, saying: ﴿"And if an evil whisper from Satan comes to you, then seek refuge in God..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 200]

Each of us knows that Satan is an enemy with a long-standing enmity. When you seek refuge in God from Satan, you gain protection against Satan. And He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿"...when a passing thought from Satan touches them, they remember, and then they see clearly."﴾ [al-A'raf: 201] That is, when a person remembers the enmity between himself and Satan, he must fortify himself with faith's immunity against this prick.

God concludes the noble verse with Joseph's words: ﴿"...Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills; indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ [Yusuf: 100]

He, glory be to Him, is the Manager from whom nothing is hidden at all. The word "lutf" (subtlety, kindness) is the opposite of "kathafa" (density). The subtle is that which has a fine body, and the more a thing is subtle, the more it penetrates, because there are no obstacles to stop it.

Nothing ever hinders God, and He knows the position and place of everything. He combines subtlety with expertise, so His subtlety does not halt a

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 12, verse 101:

Then the Truthful One (al-Haqq, subhanahu) mentions Yusuf's private supplication (munajah) to Allah, glorified is He: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty...﴾

We know that rububiyyah (lordship, the sustaining and nurturing of creation) means creating from non-existence, and supplying from non-existence; and providing sustenance (iqatah) to preserve life, and marriage to ensure the continuation of offspring. All these processes proceed in great harmony.

So the Truthful One, glorified is He, brought into existence from non-existence, preserved individual life through sustenance, and preserved the life of the species through what He permitted of marriage and multiplication.

Every creature has a share in the bounty of rububiyyah, whether believer or disbeliever, and all the creatures of the universe are subjected (musakhkharah) for all creation. He, glorified is He, is the One who summoned creation into existence; therefore He guaranteed what would secure their life.

The Truthful One, glorified is He, singles out His believing servants with another bounty in addition to the bounty of rububiyyah; namely the bounty of ulluhiyyah (divinity), embodied in the methodology (manhaj).

Yusuf, peace be upon him, says, addressing his Lord in supplication: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty...﴾ [Yusuf: 101]. That is: it is He, glorified is He, who gave him that lordship, this authority and power; so no one possesses power against Allah, and even the oppressor does not possess power against Allah. Therefore the Truthful One says in another verse of the Qur'an: ﴿Say: "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty away from whom You will. You exalt whom You will, and You abase whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things competent."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]

The giving of sovereignty meets no resistance from the one who holds it; but the removal of sovereignty is what the one from whom it is removed resists.

The Truthful One is also the One who grants might to whom He wills, and He is the One who humbles whom He wills.

When this verse penetrates the soul of the believer, he becomes certain that there is no escape from destiny (qadar), that the giving of sovereignty is good, that the taking away of sovereignty is good, that exaltation is good and humiliation is good; so that man does not transgress, does not become arrogant, and does not dispute the faith of others.

Some people used to say: "You must assume an omitted word in the verse." They said this on the claim, based on assumption, that there are two goods in the verse and two omitted evils.

I say: No. What you think, O human, to be evil is in fact good that Allah wills; for everything Allah causes to happen is good. Yusuf's saying ﴿You have given me of sovereignty...﴾ [Yusuf: 101] requires us to understand the meaning of "al-mulk" (sovereignty) and the meaning of "al-milk" (ownership). We know that every person has something he owns, such as his clothes, his pen, or his household furniture, and similar things; this is what is called "al-milk" (ownership). As for "al-mulk" (sovereignty), it is that you possess authority over those who possess things.

Allah has given some of His creatures sovereignty over other creatures: He first gave them dominion over what is in their possession, and gave them dominion over others; and glorified is He, He takes sovereignty from one and grants it to another, so that matters do not become a fixed, unchanging monotony.
